10048-billie-bradley-and-her-inheritance:
Janet D. Wheeler's 1920 girls' book follows Billie Bradley and her inheritance, the queer homestead at Cherry Corners. It opens with an accident and a hundred dollars, as Chet helps and the last hope fades, worse and worse, until Debbie deserts.

A strange burglar, startling developments, ghosts and things, and old furniture follow, until Billie wins out and makes great plans at Cherry Corners. Wheeler writes brisk, cheerful adventure for girls. Readers get a heroine who faces trouble with spirit and turns a strange old house into a happy home. Wheeler wrote several Billie Bradley books for the same young audience.
10201-the-desert-of-wheat:
Zane Grey's 1919 novel opens in late June, when the vast northwestern desert of wheat begins to take on a tinge of gold. The endless, rolling, smooth world of treeless hills, miles of fallow ground and miles of waving grain, slopes up to the far-separated homes of heroic men who conquered sage and sand.

Their simple homes seem lost on soft gray and golden billows of land, dots on distant hills, in a country nature alone seems to account for. Grey writes of farmers, wheat, and the land with epic feeling. Readers get the American West as farmland, golden, austere, and fiercely contested.
11365-the-fern-lover-s-companion-a-guide:
George Henry Tilton's Fern Lover's Companion, a guide for the northeastern states and Canada, teaches readers to identify ferns by genera, fronds, and fruiting times. Contents cover polypodies, bracken, cliff brakes, lip ferns, chain ferns, spleenworts, hart's tongue and walking leaf, shield ferns, beech ferns, wood ferns. bladder ferns, woodsias, sensitive and ostrich ferns, flowering ferns, adder's tongue, and grape ferns, with a key, glossary, checklist, and fern literature.

Illustrations by Alice D. Clark, to whom the book is dedicated, show frond shapes, spore cases, and species like cinnamon fern and sensitive fern. Tilton quotes poetry on finding meaning in nature, setting a gentle tone. The guide suits beginners walking northeastern woods with a hand lens.
11753-experimental-determination-of-the-:
Albert A. Michelson, Master in the United States Navy, made this experimental determination of the velocity of light at the Naval Academy, Annapolis. Simon Newcomb, superintendent of the Nautical Almanac Office, accepted the paper as part of a series on celestial motions, noting it was done at private expense.

The work matters, Newcomb says, because measuring light speed may give the most accurate solar parallax now available. A second determination, with Professor A. M. Mayer of Stevens Institute, used a fork wedged in wood, a platinum tip on lampblacked paper, and a break-circuit clock timed by Western Union time-ball. The paper is a classic of precision measurement.
12380-two-thousand-miles-on-an-automobil:
An author calling himself Chauffeur published Two Thousand Miles on an Automobile in 1902, a desultory narrative of a trip through New England, New York, Canada, and the West. Frank Verbeek illustrations accompany the text, and the book is dedicated to L. O. E., who faced dangers for sixteen hundred miles with equanimity.

Chapters cover preliminary observations, the machine used, and roads that draw violently conflicting opinions from citizens who pretend to know. The truth, the chauffeur says, is that all roads are pretty good, meaning hilly and rather soft. The book records early motoring before good highways: breakdowns, mud, hotels, and the novelty of speed. It is a charming pioneer road book, written when automobiles were still a gamble.
12808-frank-on-a-gun-boat:
Harry Castleman's 1892 boys' novel sends Frank Nelson into the Union Navy during the Civil War. Eager to serve, Frank learns the ropes aboard a gunboat on the western rivers, where guerrillas, spies, and river fighting test green sailors. Capture, escape, and a chase by bloodhounds raise the stakes.

A loyal Black servant and a Union family ashore help Frank through plantation danger and near betrayal. Castleman keeps the action moving from deck to shore and back. The novel offers young readers a stirring, period view of river war, with its hero's pluck as the constant thread.
12810-uncle-sam-s-boys-with-pershing-s-t:
Hancock sends Dick Prescott to France with Pershing's troops in this First World War adventure. Training camp comes first, with German spies, sabotage, and a court-martial threat, before the troopship crossing and the trenches. No Man's Land, a German trench raid, and a prisoner train follow.

Dick's old Gridley grit meets a new kind of war: gas, machine guns, and enemies in camp dress. A spy ring in Camp Berry, unmasked through a false carpenter and a doctor, gives the home chapters their bite. The book is boys' war fiction of its year, brisk, patriotic, and full of close escapes.
1303-the-scapegoat:
Hall Caine sets this novel in Morocco, where Israel ben Oliel, a Jewish merchant, suffers persecution and exile, and his story becomes a parable of suffering and redemption. The tale moves through Moorish courts, prisons, and deserts, with love and faith tested at every turn.

Caine writes with Victorian sentiment and a reformer's zeal against bigotry. The novel was a bestseller in its day and stirred sympathy for Morocco's Jews. It suits readers who like old-style melodrama with a moral purpose. Caine's melodrama still moves readers who like moral tales with force.
13897-the-adventure-club-afloat:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote The Adventure Club Afloat in 1917, a school story of summer sailing. The club begins one June evening in Number 17 Sumner Hall, oldest and most vine-hidden of seven dormitories. Two cruisers chug out of harbour as boys plan a cruise. Mr. Hyatt, Perry, and others debate whether parents will allow the trip.

Barbour mixes boating detail with schoolboy humour and loyalty. Waves threaten a boat, a prize is won, and protests fill a chair scene. The boys learn seamanship and teamwork on the water. Barbour, known for school sports stories, writes with easy pace. The novel suits young readers who love boats and summer adventure.
14092-the-world-s-fair-or-children-s-pri:
Published for young readers around London's Great Exhibition of 1851, this gift book turns inventions and manufactures into stories. Children learn how goods are made, where they come from, and how their makers live at home. Jamaica, Haiti, and Barbados appear in turn, with sugar cane, ginger, rum, and hurricanes described in simple, vivid terms. The tone stays warm and curious throughout.

Picture-book pleasures lead the way. Colored plates, short tales, and accounts of far peoples sit beside lessons on useful things like earthenware and cloth. Later pages advertise companion toy books, from rural tales to alphabets of objects. Read today, the volume charms as a Victorian child's guide to a world fair. It also shows how Britain taught its children to see empire: as a cabinet of wonders, full of work, weather, and distant lives.
14729-a-review-and-exposition-of-the-fal:
An Elector's Review and Exposition, printed at Ballston Spa in March 1816, answers a pamphlet addressed to the Republicans of Saratoga County and signed A Citizen. That pamphlet, generally called The Book, was printed by Ulysses F. Doubleday.

The Elector calls the rival effort the last work of an expiring faction, fit only for contempt and pity, and charges its leaders with a secret political bargain with the Federalists. Certificates test the claims made for Elihu Roe and James Thompson, the twin leaders likened to Castor and Pollux. The pamphlet is a sharp specimen of early American party warfare.
14976-mob-rule-in-new-orleans-robert-cha:
Ida B. Wells-Barnett's 1900 pamphlet Mob Rule in New Orleans tells of Robert Charles and his fight to death, the story of his life, burning human beings alive and other lynching statistics. Its introduction opens immediately after an awful outbreak of mob violence in the city.

Wells-Barnett, who notes variant spellings of names such as Cantrell, Porteous and Ziegel, sets Charles's story beside a wider record of lynching. The pamphlet argues that mob rule was not spontaneous justice but organised terror, with police and press at times complicit. It remains a searing work of investigative reporting, naming victims and demanding accountability.
16320-if-not-silver-what:
John W. Bookwalter, an Ohio maker and landowner, argues the money question from a farmer's point of view in this 1896 tract. He takes up silver coinage, gold, bimetallism, and the silver dumps of Asia, answering each objection to silver in turn. Paper notes backed by silver, he says, weigh less than coin and serve just as well.

The book speaks plainly and with heat, as befits a pamphlet from the free-silver fight of the 1890s. Bookwalter leans on his own travel and trade, not on party slogans, and he ends by asking what system, if not silver, gives a steady standard. It is a clear window on a fierce American money debate.
16426-unknown-mexico-volume-1-of-2-a-rec:
Carl Lumholtz records five years of exploration in Mexico in this first of two volumes, dedicated to Morris K. Jesup of the American Museum of Natural History. His route runs through northern Sonora, the Sierra Madre, and the lands of the Tarascos of Michoacan. Notes on the Yaqui River, the Opata people, and the tierra caliente of Tepic and Jalisco fill out the picture.

Early chapters tell of muleteers, Apache stories, rock carvings, new plants and animals, and a flourishing medical practice among the people he met. Lumholtz writes as a field scientist, keen on detail and daily life. The book gives a vivid first-hand account of Mexico's western tribes at the end of the nineteenth century.
16685-private-peat:
Harold R. Peat, ex-Third Battalion of the First Canadian Contingent, tells his war in this illustrated 1917 memoir, with scenes from the photo-play of the same name. Chapters run from the call to arms and the old country through under fire and the mad major. Vive la France, tears and no cheers, out of it, and the ten commandments of a soldier on active service follow.

Peat writes with humor and grit, still smiling in the frontispiece though his right arm is useless. The book is dedicated to the boys who will never come back. Readers of Canadian war memoirs will find a vivid, humane voice from the trenches.
17054-the-submarine-boys-on-duty-life-on:
Victor G. Durham wrote this 1909 first book of eight in the Submarine Boys series, Life on a Diving Torpedo Boat. Chapters move from two boys who planned to become great into a fighting chance and Josh Owen starting trouble. A flashlight trick, a dumfounded face, and a trail of trouble follow. Thieves falling out, a swift stroke for honor, and a submarine bowing to old ocean appear. Dives, try-outs in the depths, and a high-sea mystery lead to a dive like magic.

Durham writes for boys in brisk, patriotic style, as Jack Benson and his mates learn submarines, honor, and nerve under water. The tale mixes schoolboy rivalry with new naval technology. Young readers get a fast, old-style adventure of early submarines, full of dives, mysteries, and a last-second rescue.
17966-life-history-of-the-kangaroo-rat:
Charles T. Vorhies and Walter P. Taylor wrote this 1922 bulletin on the banner-tailed kangaroo rat, printed by the United States Department of Agriculture. Vorhies worked at the Arizona Experiment Station, and Taylor served with the Bureau of Biological Survey.

The paper covers the rat's marks, range, habits, food stores, burrow systems, foes, and numbers, with notes on its worth or harm to farms. The banner tail, a white brush, sets this form apart from its kin. It is a plain, careful field study, still useful for desert naturalists and a neat look at how early wildlife science was done.
18527-an-assessment-of-the-consequences-:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency issued this report at Washington in November 1980, after President Carter asked for a review of readiness for a huge California quake. Spurred by the Mount St. Helens eruption that May, a National Security Council committee spent the summer of 1980 weighing scenarios, losses, and response plans. Federal, state, and local agencies took part, with help from outside experts.

Chapters cover quake scenarios, loss estimates for chosen events, the current state of readiness, and social effects, with letters between Carter and Governor Brown in an annex. The report is sober and practical, naming gaps as well as steps already taken. It remains a clear record of disaster planning at the time.
18699-the-moving-picture-girls-at-sea-or:
Laura Lee Hope published this girls' adventure at Cleveland in 1915, after a Grosset and Dunlap copyright. Sisters Ruth and Alice DeVere, moving picture actresses, take on a great marine film with a schooner, a sailor's story, and Captain Brisco. Early chapters mix studio mishaps, such as a spoiled hat in a parlor scene, with plans for sea filming.

The pictured shipwreck turns real in later chapters, with a storm, a disabled ship, a vortex, a wreck, mutiny, and help at last. Hope keeps the pace brisk and the heroines plucky. The book is a fun early look at film making plus sea adventure.
19167-billy-whiskers-the-autobiography-o:
Frances Trego Montgomery wrote this 1902 goat autobiography, Billy Whiskers, with pictures by W. H. Fry. Billy tells his own life, from Mr. Wagner buying a goat to trouble at the soda fountain, a ducking in the mill pond, a ride in the police patrol wagon, and a turn in the circus. Nanny and snakes join the fun.

Billy butts his own image in a kitchen looking glass, crashes a marble table of wax fruit, and bites a tasteless peach, still hunting his rival down a dark hall. Each chapter is a fresh scrape. Young readers get a rollicking animal tale told by the goat himself, mischievous and warm.
19333-the-story-of-a-china-cat:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this tale for young children about a toy china cat and the children who play with her. The cat cannot move or speak for herself. Her hopes and fears are told by the narrator as she is carried, dropped, fought over, and nearly broken in busy households.

The charm lies in seeing the world from a toy's low view, where a fall from a chair can feel like a great peril. It belongs to Hope's Make Believe Stories, in which toys come to life in feeling if not in fact, and kindness to small things is the quiet lesson.
19642-lights-and-shadows-of-new-york-lif:
James D. McCabe Jr. wrote this panorama of New York life, describing the great city in all its phases. Marble palaces and dark dens, high life and low, rings and frauds, charities, mysteries, and crimes all appear, with pictures of Grand Central Depot and city views.

One mission tale shows a man hiring five houses for the poor of nearby hovels, finding them needlework and basket making, and paying mission costs from the work's profits. McCabe's book is a Victorian guide to a city of sharp contrasts, still vivid today.
19801-the-drummer-s-coat:
J. W. Fortescue wrote tales of old Devon for young and general readers. The Drummer's Coat opens on an oak-wooded coast of green headlands. Headlands cross each other, fainter and fainter, into distance. They end in a little patch of purple heather. That patch seems the end of all things. Fortescue paints the West Country before his story stirs.

A drummer's coat means a soldier's uniform and a boy's ambitions. Fortescue, historian of the British Army, knew both well. His stories carry military memory into village life. The coast itself acts as a character here. Smuggling-era Devon haunts many of his tales. This one begins with the land, as his readers expected.
20010-the-calico-cat:
Charles Clark Munn wrote The Calico Cat, a story of rural New England life. Mr. Peaslee argues mileage money with masculine scorn in its pages. The state does not waste money that way, he insists. Mileage exists to get a man there and home again after term. Between whiles he is supposed to stay around, Peaslee holds. The talk is court-week talk in a country town. A calico cat threads the human story together.

Munn's novels celebrate Maine and Connecticut valley folk. His humor is dry, local, and affectionate. Animals in his books often judge the humans silently. The Calico Cat belongs to his Uncle Terry period of popularity. Court sessions, farms, and village politics make its world. It preserves New England speech with a phonograph's ear.
2019-the-bat:
Mary Roberts Rinehart and Avery Hopwood turn their hit stage thriller into a novel, set in a rented country house where a master criminal called the Bat is on the loose. Miss Van Gorder, the tenant, refuses to be frightened out of her home. Rinehart and Hopwood first made The Bat a stage hit in 1920, before turning it into this novel.

Hidden rooms, a blackened bag, shots in the dark, and Detective Anderson's questions pile up through twenty-one chapters. The tale is pure stagecraft in prose, built on shocks, suspects, and a final unmasking that rewards close attention. The masked criminal and the hidden room became stage trademarks, copied by many later thrillers.
20335-the-case-of-edith-cavell-a-study-o:
James M. Beck wrote The Case of Edith Cavell, a study of non-combatants' rights. Edith Cavell, a British nurse in Brussels, was shot by Germany in 1915. Beck argues the rights of those who do not fight in war. Baron von der Lancken, he says, may escape some general blame.

His part, Beck writes, was like Pilate washing his hands of blood. Von Bissing, by contrast, will bear ill fame to the last syllable of time. Beck writes as a lawyer stirred by a case that shocked the world. Readers get a legal and moral brief on a wartime execution.
20348-the-moving-picture-girls-in-war-pl:
Laura Lee Hope published The Moving Picture Girls in War Plays in 1916. Alice DeVere hunts through piles of clothing for her scout shoes. She has oceans of things yet to pack into her trunk. She will need those muddy, comfortable shoes for hiking in war scenes.

War plays were films of sham battles staged at places like Oak Farm. The girls act in them while real war rages across the Atlantic. Hope's series shows film work as bright, brave fun for girls. Readers get a peek at early movie making dressed in wartime khaki.
20717-the-girl-on-the-boat:
P. G. Wodehouse's The Girl on the Boat is a comic romance that starts on an Atlantic liner and lands in an English country house. Its hero is Sam Marlowe. Wodehouse's preface defends Sam against a charge of copying another writer's hero, and the defense is a joke in itself.

Both the other hero and my Sam Marlowe, he admits, try to escape a tight corner by hiding in a suit of armor. The scenes sit in the halls of country houses in both books. And yet, Wodehouse calls on Heaven to witness, the likeness is chance. The novel's engagements and mix-ups sail on regardless.
21078-the-tale-of-miss-kitty-cat:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote gentle animal tales for children. Miss Kitty Cat belongs to his Slumber-Town Tales series, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Around Farmer Green's farmhouse, Miss Kitty Cat is politeness itself whenever anyone is watching. Late meals draw only a soft, plaintive mewing as a reminder.

Bailey gives farm animals voices, habits, and small social dramas that young children can follow. The frontispiece shows Miss Kitty Cat chasing Old Dog Spot, a hint of her livelier side. Short chapters and simple scenes made these tales bedtime reading, and this one keeps the farmyard cast Bailey's readers knew.
21399-dick-and-his-cat:
Mary Ellis retells an old folk tale in Dick and His Cat, printed at Philadelphia in 1871. Her hero is Dick Whittington, the poor boy of legend, and his famed cat. The book was first entered for copyright in 1866, in a dress made for new readers.

Ellis uses no word of more than four letters, and none of more than one beat of sound. A sick, hungry boy rests on a step, and a kind girl takes note of him. From such small starts the old tale climbs toward luck and fame. Small children can read the whole story for themselves, word by word.
2152-island-tales-on-the-makaloa-mat:
Jack London gathers Hawaiian stories told on the makaloa mat, a woven mat where islanders shared tales. A woman under a hau tree, the bones of Kahekili, and the tears of Ah Kim open a set of seven stories. London visited Hawaii several times, and his island tales grew from those stays.

London writes of Hawaii with affection for its people, surf, and customs, in his last years. The collection, published in 1920, gives a warmer, gentler London than the Yukon tales, and a vivid picture of island life. The makaloa mat, where stories were told, gives the book its title and its warmth.
21744-the-lifeboat:
London's river slums open this Ballantyne novel, in a street of wharves, warehouses, and smells of tar and tallow. Cranes cling to the walls, and anchors and chains crowd down to the mud of the Thames. From this rough ground Ballantyne builds toward the sea service he praised all his life.

The lifeboat and its crews stand at the heart of the tale. Ballantyne mixes dockside lives with storms and rescues on the coast. Poor homes, hard work, and sudden heroism share the chapters. The book helped make the lifeboat a household word for his young readers. It is London and the sea in one story, grit and courage side by side.
21889-peter-the-great:
Peter the Great of Russia is Jacob Abbott's subject in this volume of his Makers of History series, first issued in 1859. Abbott begins with the fame of the tsar who founded Russian civilization, as the world generally regards him. Young readers knew Peter best for one story. He went to Holland and worked with his own hands in a shipyard at Saardam, learning shipbuilding from the keel up.

The little wooden shop where Peter studied still stood in Abbott's day, much decayed but guarded. Abbott tells the reign as a story of a giant forcing his country toward the sea and the West. His Makers of History books taught generations of American children the lives of rulers. This one remains a clear, lively first life of Peter.
2194-mauprat:
George Sand's Mauprat tells of Bernard de Mauprat, raised among rough, lawless kinsmen in a decaying castle, and of Edmee, the cousin whose love and teaching try to civilize him. Set in pre-revolutionary France, the novel moves between wild woods, a grim fortress, and the courts where Bernard must answer for his past. It is a story of education in the deepest sense.

Sand uses the romance to argue that character is made, not born, and that patience and affection can tame even a brutal upbringing. The plot mixes adventure, trial, and passion with long, thoughtful passages on nature and justice. Readers get a sweeping French classic about love as a force for change.
22043-the-book-of-the-cat:
Frances Simpson edited and largely wrote The Book of the Cat, published in 1903. Simpson was a leading judge and breeder in the young world of cat shows. Her book opens with the cat's wild past, when it won its food by fighting and luck. From there it turns to the pedigree breeds then filling show pens.

Persians, Siamese, and short-haired breeds each receive detailed treatment. Feeding, housing, illness, and judging all come under her practical eye. Other fanciers contributed chapters, and fine plates show champion animals. For years this was the standard English guide to keeping and showing cats, and it still documents the fancy's early days.
22621-the-new-england-magazine-volume-1-:
The New England Magazine opens its run with volume 1, number 1, dated January 1886, the Bay State magazine's first issue. The catalog record names no editor. Regional magazines of the era mixed history, essays, fiction, and verse for a loyal local readership, and this one announced itself as New England's own.

The sample comes from an article on Brown University, tracing its origin to Baptists who wanted an educated ministry free of sectarian tests. The writer notes how Baptist views then ran against the prevailing religious opinions of the colonies. College history, regional pride, and literary matter shared the issue. A first number is a promise as much as a product, and this one shows the editors' ambitions plainly.
22943-the-nebuly-coat:
Heritage watchdogs take fire in The Nebuly Coat, a novel of church restoration and village pride. One speaker unloads on a Society for the Conservation of National Inheritances. Ignoramuses who cannot tell an aumbry from an abacus, charlatans and amateur faddists, he charges, are pledged to abuse the restorers' work, good, bad, or indifferent.

John Meade Falkner set his tale around a great church and the coat of arms, the nebuly coat, at its heart. Secrets in stone, a missing inheritance, and quarrels over the old building drive the plot. The book, issued in 1903, became a quiet classic of the English regional novel. Its anger at careless preservation still sounds strikingly current.
22991-boy-scouts-mysterious-signal-or-pe:
G. Harvey Ralphson imperils his patrol in Boy Scouts' Mysterious Signal, or Perils of the Black Bear Patrol, published in 1916. A calm voice answers a protest in the excerpt. The boys' captor names himself Heinrich von Liebknecht, a captain in the Kaiser's army. His detachment, he says, was sent ahead to seize the city. He has decided the patrol will remain his prisoners.

War had come to the Boy Scouts series. Signals, captures, and escapes replace campfire contests as the patrol faces a German officer on American ground. Ralphson wrote brisk, patriotic adventure for boys who followed the European war in headlines. The book shows how quickly children's fiction mobilized in 1916, a year before America joined the fighting itself.
23048-adrift-in-a-boat:
A beautiful bay gathers a party in Adrift in a Boat. The bay's sands hold shells so tiny and fragile that their whole survival in a rough, boisterous sea seems a small wonder. In one of those bays, many years ago, a large party collected on a bright autumn afternoon.

A pleasure outing supplies the calm before the title's trouble. Tales of boats cast loose at sea were a staple of the improving story paper, mixing peril with providence. The shells in the opening do quiet thematic work, fragile things survive rough water. Readers get a period sea tale built for family reading, with danger enough to quicken the pulse and a shore kept firmly in view.
23124-the-lady-of-the-basement-flat:
A woman announces her own death in The Lady of the Basement Flat. Evelyn Wastneys announces her own death at three that afternoon. She died, she says, on an Irish doorstep, hands full of silly little silver shoes and horseshoes, a Paris hat on her head. A trembling treble voice whispered in my ear as it happened.

Mrs. George de Horne Vaizey, to whom this novel is credited, builds the tale on that figurative death, a woman's old life ending at a door. Silver wedding trinkets in her hands mark the occasion her past chooses to die on. What rises in the basement flat makes the book. Vaizey's domestic fiction specialized in such rebirths, witty, wounded, and practical about money and rooms.
23283-the-youth-of-jefferson-or-a-chroni:
This chronicle of college scrapes follows the youth of Jefferson at Williamsburg, Virginia, in seventeen sixty-four. Student pranks, friendships, and scrapes at the College of William and Mary fill a tale told with fond humor for young readers.

Its Latin motto, sweet it is to play the fool in place, sets the tone: boyish folly in good company, learned and laughed over. The book offers a playful glimpse of colonial college life before revolution claimed its hero. College scrapes and friendships fill the tale with fond humor throughout. Sir Asinus stakes his garters against a pistole and loses, one of the book's named college scrapes.
23385-saved-by-the-lifeboat:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote this tale to show how the lifeboat service worked and how gifts from private folk could pay for a new boat. It opens with a wreck near a small seaside village, as local men rush to the beach to save life in dark, rough weather.

The story then turns to a mean, grasping shipowner who skimps his ships' gear to save money, until shame and sense bring him to give funds for a new lifeboat. A fund raising chapter shows how appeals were made, much as they still are today, though the boats themselves have changed greatly. Young readers get a stirring rescue tale and a plain lesson in how ordinary giving can save strangers at sea.
23861-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
The fifth volume of The Story of the Great War, published by P. F. Collier and Sons, covers Neuve Chapelle, the Battle of Ypres, Przemysl, and the Mazurian Lakes. It is a contemporary history, written while the war was still being fought, with maps and pictures of guns in action near Arras.

Part One follows the Western Front from preparations for an offensive through Neuve Chapelle, Second Ypres, Festubert, and the Argonne. Part Two turns to naval war: the Dardanelles, German raiders, the Emden, and the sinking of the Lusitania. Part Three covers the Eastern Front, from the Carpathians to the fall of Przemysl.
23880-a-new-name-for-the-mexican-red-bat:
E. Raymond Hall published A New Name for the Mexican Red Bat in the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History. It appeared as volume five, number fourteen, pages 223 to 226, dated December 15, 1951. It is a short taxonomic paper, only four pages, but it untangles a name that had stood for half a century.

In 1897, Gerrit S. Miller applied Saussure's 1861 name Atalapha mexicana to the red bat, Lasiurus borealis, known from southern Mexico. Later work showed the hoary bat, Lasiurus cinereus, also lives there: an adult male was taken in Michoacán in 1945. With two species, not one, in the region, Hall argues the old name cannot stay where Miller put it.
24018-the-golfer-s-rubaiyat:
H. W. Boynton published The Golfer's Rubaiyat in Chicago in 1901, a golfing parody of Omar Khayyam's Rubaiyat, with each verse set in a full-page illustration. Its opening quatrain wakes the reader as the sun drives the stars from the tee of night and holes them every one without a miss.

Dawn comes, red marker in hand on the eastern green, summoning her little ones to swap a happy three for each sad thirteen. Those before the first tee murmur that they have just this chance to score, and once departed may return no more. Campbell's fame is past, and old Tom Morris is only a name now. Many a Jamie still blows by the bunker, and many a Willie still rules us just the same.
24199-two-poems-against-pope-one-epistle:
Joseph V. Guerinot introduces this Augustan Reprint Society volume, publication number 114, issued by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at the University of California, Los Angeles, in 1965. It pairs two satiric poems against Alexander Pope: One Epistle to Mr. A. Pope by Leonard Welsted, dated 1730, and The Blatant Beast, anonymous, dated 1740.

Welsted's epistle appeared, according to the Daily Journal, on April 28, 1730, occasioned by two epistles lately published. Pope himself listed it in the appendix to The Dunciad as one of the books, papers, and verses in which he was abused. Readers get two sharp Augustan attacks, with a modern introduction to guide them.
24321-tea-leaves-being-a-collection-of-l:
Francis S. Drake edited this collection of letters and documents on the shipment of tea to the American colonies in 1773 by the East India Tea Company, published in Boston by A. O. Crane in 1884. The papers, now first printed from the original manuscript, carry Drake's introduction, notes, and biographical notices of the Boston Tea Party. They hold information on the tea troubles before the Revolution, much of it new to students of the period.

The collection long lay buried, in the possession of Abel Bowen, engraver and publisher of Boston. He got it from a man who procured it in Halifax, Nova Scotia, where many New England papers were carried when the British and Tories evacuated Boston in March 1776. Bowen's daughters gave leave to publish. Readers get raw material of the Tea Party, in the writers' own words.
24396-the-wesleyan-methodist-pulpit-in-m:
This volume gathers sermons preached at the opening services of the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel at Malvern in 1866, by the Reverends W. M. Punshon, W. Arthur, J. H. James, C. Prest, J. Priestley, G. Smith, and G. Wood. Knowles King wrote the preface, and John Snow and Company of London published the book in 1866. It is dedicated to Ralph Barnes Grindrod of Malvern, in thanks for his healing gift, his large charity, and his high Christian character.

The chapel owes its erection to Punshon's piety and energy: in 1862 he proposed raising a fund by lectures for Wesleyan chapels in summer resorts. Forty thousand pounds have already built chapels at Ilfracombe, Dawlish, the Lizard, Brighton, Weymouth, Eastbourne, Walmer, Folkestone, Bournemouth, Blackpool, Lancing, Rhyl, Saltburn, Bray, Matlock, Malvern, Keswick, Bowness, and the Isle of Wight. Readers get opening sermons, printed nearly as preached.
24616-bell-s-cathedrals-southwark-cathed:
George Worley wrote this volume on Southwark Cathedral, formerly the collegiate church of St. Saviour, with some account of the college and the see. It belongs to Bell's Cathedrals series, the handy illustrated guides to England's great churches. Southwark, on the south bank of the Thames, is London's oldest Gothic church.

Worley traces its history from collegiate church to cathedral, describing its architecture, monuments, and associations with Shakespeare's London. The book is compact, clear, and well illustrated. Visitors to Southwark, and readers who love English churches, will find it a useful and charming guide.
24921-it-s-like-this-cat:
Dave, a New York boy, narrates life with his cat in Emily Neville's 1963 story, illustrated by Emil Weiss. The cat's adventures follow the city's map chapter by chapter: Cat and Kate, Cat and Coney, a turn around Manhattan, and a visit to Brooklyn. Later episodes take in the West Side, a West Side Story outing, and Rosh Hashanah at the Fulton Fish Market.

Hilda and Tom enter the story midway, widening Dave's circle beyond his feline companion. The humor stays gentle and observational, rooted in how a cat treats every street, market stall, and holiday crowd as its own territory. Young readers get a fond tour of New York as seen at cat height, with the city itself playing almost as large a part as the pet.
26084-parks-for-the-people-proceedings-o:
The proceedings of a Boston public meeting held at Faneuil Hall on June 7, 1876, record the campaign for public parks in the city. Called to act on the Park Commissioners' report, the crowded hall heard speeches from Joseph S. Ropes, George B. Chase, Richard H. Dana Jr., Oliver Wendell Holmes, and others, with a letter from Edward H. Clarke.

Speakers argued that Boston, fresh from its Centennial year, should plant large tracts with trees for the health and pleasure of coming generations, rather than rest on past glories. A committee of one hundred was named to carry the cause forward. The volume prints the speeches verbatim from the Boston Morning Journal, giving a full picture of the park movement's public case.
26429-nights-with-uncle-remus-myths-and-:
Joel Chandler Harris's Nights with Uncle Remus returns to the storyteller of the old plantation, who spins animal myths and legends for a listening child. Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox, and their neighbors people the tales. Daddy Jack, a second storyteller, adds his own lore, including a tale of old man Alligator with his bumpy back and tail. The stories are rendered in the dialect Harris recorded.

Each night brings a new telling, framed by the child's requests and Uncle Remus's soothing replies. Miss Meadows and Brother Rabbit grace the frontispiece, and the book stands among Harris's later volumes of plantation tales. Modern readers will note the plantation setting and dialect as features of Harris's time, preserved here as he wrote them.
27469-radio-shack-trs-80-expansion-inter:
Radio Shack, a division of the Tandy Corporation, issued this operator's manual for the TRS-80 Expansion Interface, catalog numbers 26-1140, 26-1141, and 26-1142, custom manufactured in the United States. The interface lets owners add Radio Shack modules to their TRS-80 system.

Those modules are a screen printer, a line printer, a mini-disk system, and a second cassette recorder. The mini-disk gives vast storage and quicker access than tape. It gives about 80,000 bytes free on the first disk and 89,600 on each additional disk, using sequential or random access and several additional Level II commands. The manual warns that the disk controller makes the computer assume a mini-disk is connected. It is a neat record of early home computing.
27472-the-story-of-a-cat:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich translated this charming story from the French of Emile de la Bédollière, with silhouettes by L. Hopkins, published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York, with an 1878 copyright. Aldrich says he turned the tale into English for the entertainment of two small readers at his own fireside.

The translation then found a larger audience in a popular juvenile magazine, and Hopkins's ingenious and spirited silhouettes became Aldrich's plea for putting so slight a performance into book form. The story follows Mother Michel and her cat in Paris under King Louis XV, opening with a very rich old countess. Young readers get a gentle French tale, prettily told.
28119-my-father-the-cat:
Henry Slesar's short tale My Father, the Cat turns a family story into a sly fantasy. The narrator's mother, a delicate woman from the coast of Brittany, loses her father, who feared any coarse suitor for her. After his death a large white Angora cat named Dauphin strays onto the estate and wins her heart.

Dauphin speaks cultured French, English, and Italian, and soon becomes her friend, protector, and confidant. The narrator, telling the tale with a straight face, must admit what he has and has not told his own wife. The story works as a brief, witty joke about class, gentleness, and a most unusual father.
28147-letters-on-the-cholera-morbus-cont:
Letters on the Cholera Morbus, London, 1831 and 1832, by a professional man of thirty years' experience, argues a bold medical claim. The writer holds that cholera morbus, a gut disease then much feared, cannot pass from person to person by touch, by things, or by air. Cordons and quarantine rules, he says, are not merely useless but harmful to the community.

Two sets of letters, ten from 1831 and three with a postscript from 1832, lay out cases and reasons. Modern notes warn that cholera morbus then meant gut diseases like acute gastroenteritis, not epidemic cholera. The book documents an early fight over contagion and public health.
28174-the-private-library-what-we-do-kno:
Arthur L. Humphreys wrote The Private Library, fourth edition, London, 1900, on what we do know, don't know, and ought to know about our books. Humphreys, who inspected collections in country houses, found most private libraries in chaos, with servants untaught in handling books. He argues a library should be a place of amusement, like a billiard room, not a dusty store.

Chapters ask what makes a good edition, a fine copy, and a fair price, with notes on care and display. Humphreys writes with wit for owners who love books but neglect them. The little volume remains a charming guide to building and keeping a home library.
28330-reflections-on-the-operation-of-th:
Christopher C. Andrews, counsellor at law, wrote Reflections on the Operation of the Present System of Education, Boston, 1853, as a revised journal article. Andrews argues that American schools lack moral instruction, a defect he traces to public opinion, not to the system itself. He proposes remedies, and quotes the proverb on training a child in the way he should go. Crosby, Nichols and Company published the pamphlet.

Andrews cites Solon, who excused children from supporting parents who failed to teach them a useful art. His aim is to call attention to a gap, not to condemn schools. The pamphlet offers a mid-century American argument for moral teaching in public education.
28682-minnie-s-pet-cat:
Mrs. Madeline Leslie wrote these short children's stories about a girl named Minnie and her pets, published in Boston in 1864. The volume opens with Minnie's Pet Cat, about Fidelle, a beautiful tortoise-shell cat with black, white, and reddish-orange fur, who comes running the moment she hears Minnie's voice. A companion story about Minnie's pet horse follows in the same book, part of the Minnie and Her Pets series.

Leslie dedicated the little volumes to a young friend, hoping they would grow his love of nature and country life. The stories are simple and affectionate, written to teach kindness to animals through a child's daily pleasures. Young readers meet a gentle world of pets, farms, and careful attention, in the moral children's writing of the 1860s.
29763-alex-the-great:
H. C. Witwer published Alex the Great in Boston in 1919, with Small, Maynard and Company. Arthur William Brown drew the pictures. The frontispiece shows Alex with a dame he seems to have kidnapped from the Follies while Ziegfeld counted receipts. Seven chapters carry titles like Introducing Alex the Great, The Self-Commencer, Play Your Ace, and Don't Give Up the Tip.

Girls are warned to be wary when a husband arrives home touting a plan for turning mud into gold or a losing club into pennant winners. Witwer tells it in slang, with jokes about matches, sweaters, vampires, and languishing glances. Alex is a brash, self-starting comic hero, and the book is a set of tall, funny tales about him.
29863-the-rambles-of-a-rat:
A. L. O. E., author of The Giant-Killer, published The Rambles of a Rat in London, Edinburgh, and New York in 1864, with T. Nelson and Sons. The preface warns readers not to take the book as mere bubbles of fancy for an idle hour. Like glass balls with something solid inside, her bubbles hold facts: she makes rats talk, feel, and reflect, but true rat life runs through the fiction.

Twenty-three chapters follow a rat family from a clap-trap discovery and poorer than rats, where a blind rat holds a stick and a black rat takes the other end. A visit to the Zoological Gardens, a voyage, and a first view of St. Petersburg follow. A Russian kitchen, a storm, and a new kind of watch-dog, with the lost brother Oddity, close a charming, instructive animal tale for young readers.
3036-the-railroad-builders-a-chronicle-o:
John Moody wrote The Railroad Builders, volume thirty-eight of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. The book traces a century of railroad building, from the Commodore and the New York Central through the Pennsylvania system and the Erie. The Appalachian crossing, the linking of oceans, the Santa Fe trail, the Hill lines, and the southern system complete the map. Moody shows railroads as politics as well as engineering.

A passage on Jay Gould in Albany, during a snowstorm winter, has sick legislators suddenly recovering and flocking to the capital on fast trains. By April a bill's fate had changed with the mentality of a majority. The volume explains how rails welded the states into one market and one nation.
30712-combat:
Mack Reynolds wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in October 1960, about first contact seen from the wrong side. Henry Kuran, called Hank, comes back from Peru full of talk about Incas and rival powers, and he reports to his chief, Morton Twombly. The story's framing idea is that an alien landing on Earth might be misled by a one-sided view, and that Earthmen might be misled just as well.

Reynolds keeps the early scenes in offices and talk, not in space battles, as Hank's field work meets head office politics. The title points to a clash that is less about guns than about who understands whom. Readers get a wry, talk-driven tale about bias, first impressions, and how easily each side can read the other wrong.
3169-the-pursuit-of-the-house-boat:
John Kendrick Bangs sends Sherlock Holmes after a stolen house-boat in this sequel. The Associated Shades, the famous dead who dwell on the Styx, lose their floating clubhouse, and Holmes takes the lead in getting it back. Bangs, author of A House-Boat on the Styx, returns to his comic underworld in this Harper edition, here in its fourteenth impression.

The joke is the cast: great names of history and letters, arguing, scheming, and bungling like any club committee. Holmes presides with grave method over proceedings that refuse all method. The afterlife, Bangs suggests, behaves very much like a London club, with committees, quarrels, and minutes.
31704-type-cases-and-composing-room-furn:
A. A. Stewart's 1918 primer, published by the United Typothetae of America for its Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices, explains type cases and composing-room furniture. It covers early type cases, their sizes and structure, cases for various purposes, compositors' work stands, case stands and racks, and the modern type cabinet.

The volume is a working manual for apprentice printers, with illustrations, review questions, and a glossary, part of a series on types, tools, machines, and materials. Readers get a clear record of how a print shop was laid out and worked in the age of hand-set type.
31751-what-bird-is-that:
Frank M. Chapman's What Bird Is That, a pocket museum of the land birds of the eastern United States arranged according to season, was published by D. Appleton-Century Company with copyright in 1920. Chapman, curator of birds at the American Museum of Natural History and editor of Bird-Lore, gives the student a map of a bird's plumage. With it, descriptions of color and markings can be written and understood.

The volume presents 301 birds in color by Edmund J. Sawyer, ordered by the season in which a reader is likely to meet them. Readers get a classic field guide for beginners, built for use outdoors, where a bird's season, shape, and markings matter more than a long scientific account.
31777-why-a-national-literature-cannot-f:
Joseph Rocchietti's 1845 essay, printed in New York by J. W. Kelley, asks why a national literature cannot flourish in the United States of North America. Chapter one contends that Americans are not a fresh people at all: their land may be new, yet they are as old as Europeans.

Rocchietti says the colonies came from the old continent with its laws, religions, learning, languages, prejudices, arts, and literature, so its classical writers belong to America as well. Readers get an early, contrarian piece of American literary criticism, arguing that youth of country is no excuse for a thin literature.
31948-thompson-s-cat:
Robert Moore Williams's short story Thompson's Cat was printed in Planet Stories in September 1952. It opens on a dead world, where Thompson stands on a rooftop with awe and a trace of beginning fear. Beside him, Kurkil whispers the question Thompson did not want to hear: what killed it.

Its sidenote warns that a weird, invisible insect depopulated an entire planet. Now it is felling Thompson's crew as his ship hurtles toward the sun, certain death for all, including the disease carrier. Buster, Thompson's wise cat, is forgotten in the panic. Readers get a tense space story in which a cat may matter more than a crew.
32606-dorothy-on-a-house-boat:
Evelyn Raymond sends Dorothy Calvert and her great-aunt Mrs. Betty Calvert on a new venture when a letter offers Dorothy the gift of a house-boat. The pair, back at the old Calvert home of Bellvieu, take up the offer and plan a cruise of kindness.

In seventeen chapters the cruise meets storms, a mule and melon bargain, visitors, monkeys, and a colonel with a secret to tell. Dorothy's good nature and quick wit carry the party through scrapes, and the tale closes with a promise kept and a cruise well spent.
32630-tiger-cat:
David H. Keller's Tiger Cat, printed in Weird Tales in October 1937, opens with a house sale in Italy. The narrator buys a mountain villa less for its view than for its marble fountain. That spouting Cupid is what he had come to Italy to buy and carry back to America, after a letter from George Seabrook.

The villa commands a valley three and a third miles at its widest, whitewashed cottages set like pearls among grape-vines. Keller builds horror from the purchase itself. A curious piece of marble, a half-ruined stone house, and a valley with no sign of life draw the new owner deeper into the place he has bought.
32735-forsyte-s-retreat:
Winston Marks tells of Sextus Rollo Forsyte, a hotel man seeking a retreat, in this story from IF Worlds of Science Fiction of May 1954, illustrated by Kelly Freas. In forty years Forsyte has managed half a dozen large hotels. Boards of directors fired him for drinking on the job, and his name reached the hotel associations' black list.

Forsyte craves anonymity as other men crave fame, and he takes the general manager's post at the Mahoney-Plaza at six hundred a month. The hotel holds only two hundred and sixty rooms, with two guests to a room. Yet it somehow accommodates five thousand two hundred guests at the same time, and Forsyte must learn how.
33174-the-book-of-this-and-that:
Robert Lynd's Book of This and That, published in London in 1915 and dedicated in memory of William Barkley, gathers short essays on whatever caught the essayist's eye. Its contents run from suspicion and good resolutions through the sin of dancing and thoughts at a tango tea. They go on to the humours of murder, the decline and fall of hell, and cheerful readers, before turning to Shaw and the bishop, stupidity, waste, Christmas, demagogues, and coincidences.

Later essays treat indignation, the heart of Mr. Galsworthy, spring fashions, black cats, being shocked, confessions, the terrors of politics, disasters, and the rights of murder. They go on to hoaxes, Anatole France, the sea, and the futurists, closing with a defence of critics. Lynd writes with humor and a light, humane touch, finding a topic in a small thing and following it out.
33536-a-report-of-major-hart-s-case-of-r:
W. H. Inglis reports Major Hart's case of rice frauds near Seringapatam in this 1818 pamphlet addressed to the proprietors of East India stock. Hart, dismissed from his command, argues that his junior officer, Major-General Macaulay, succeeded to the very regiment Hart would otherwise have commanded and rose to general rank sooner because of that dismissal. Inglis presents Hart's defense with notes and an appendix.

The report quotes India House papers and Macaulay's replies, including a charge that Hart accused his rival of seeking command of a fortress and field forces in Tinnevelly for himself. For readers of East India Company history, the pamphlet preserves a bitter service dispute over supply fraud, promotion, and reputation in early nineteenth-century India.
33987-beautiful-shells-of-new-zealand-an:
E. G. B. Moss, a barrister of Auckland, wrote this illustrated guide for amateur collectors of New Zealand marine shells, published at Auckland in 1908 with photographs by C. Spencer. Chapters cover shells and their inmates, collecting and cleaning, and descriptions of the plates. An index lists kinds from Acmaea to Chione and beyond.

Moss writes for beginners who walk the shore and want names for what they find. His directions on cleaning keep fragile shells safe for a cabinet. The book still serves collectors of New Zealand shells with clear pictures and plain guidance.
34020-the-window-at-the-white-cat:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote this mystery novel, published in New York in September 1940 by Triangle Books, with reprints in December 1940 and February 1941. A criminal lawyer narrates, and his clerk Hawes announces every woman client as a lady, whatever her dress or trade. Clients range from a market poultry seller grown rich on short weight to Mamie Tracy, whose diamonds were stolen on the avenue.

Another client has a husband who ran off with a woman fond of laces. Rinehart builds her mystery from such cases, with sentiment and clues in equal part. The novel offers a brisk, witty tale of crime and society.
34228-the-accomplished-muskrat-trapper-a:
A. E. Schmidt's 1922 booklet The Accomplished Muskrat Trapper speaks to the amateur, not the seasoned pro. Schmidt argues that the muskrat, the most numerous and least wary of fur bearers, had been slighted by other writers on trapping.

The guide teaches how to trap the animal under varied conditions, and how to sort and grade raw furs for sale. The guide rests on the author's wide practice, and it still serves as a plain first manual for trappers starting out on muskrat ground. Schmidt, writing from Chicago, keeps his advice short, plain, and fitted to a beginner's kit.
34268-spinning-tops-the-operatives-lectu:
Professor John Perry gave Spinning Tops as the Operatives Lecture of the British Association meeting at Leeds on September sixth, eighteen ninety. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London issued a reprint of a new revised edition in nineteen ten. An appendix on the use of gyrostats, with plates, adds to the lecture. Perry gave the report to the late Lord Kelvin, his affectionate pupil speaking.

Perry warns that the printed lecture is not the lecture as delivered. For half a minute at a time, he says, the lecturer played with a spinning top or gyrostat for the crowd. Plates show magnetism, light, and molecular spinning tops. Perry shows how tops, gyroscopes, and Earth itself share one set of laws. Working men and students get physics by play, made deep and clear.
34907-the-irish-on-the-somme-being-a-sec:
Michael Macdonagh's The Irish on the Somme forms the second series of The Irish at the Front, issued by Hodder and Stoughton in 1917. John Redmond supplied the introduction, and the book honours Major William Redmond, who died of wounds on June 7, 1917. He fell leading his men in the attack on Wytschaete Wood.

Redmond frames the war as one of liberation, fought for the rights of small nations against German military rule. He recalls urging young Irishmen to enlist once Britain had trusted Ireland with self government. Macdonagh then records how Irish regiments answered that call on the Somme, in a war the Irish Party backed from its first days.
35487-swamp-cat:
Jim Kjelgaard wrote Swamp Cat, a boys animal novel published in New York in 1957 with illustrations by Edward Shenton. Kjelgaard was known for dog books such as Big Red and Irish Red. This one gives the lead to a cat named Frosty, and the first chapter is called Exiled.

The contents follow Frosty through a first planting and a second, a spell marooned, and an intruder in the swamp. A boy named Andy shares the tale, hunting on his own account in one chapter. The war of the owls and deep sand close the book. The opening sound reaches Frosty as a mere vibration humming in the fine hairs of his ears, whiskers tingling. Kjelgaard tells the swamp from the cat height, sense by sense. Animal lovers were the readers, and Frosty carries the story.
36031-proceedings-of-the-second-national:
Proceedings of the Second National Conservation Congress prints the talks and acts of a meet held at Saint Paul, Minnesota, from September 5 to 8, 1910. Bernard Baker of Baltimore led the congress as its head. The book came out at Washington in 1911, under the motto of keeping safe the base of the nation's wealth.

Lists of officers, vice heads, and boards from many states fill the front pages. The meet drew men and women from farms, lumber, mines, and state office who cared about land, woods, and water. The record shows the young movement to save the nation's stores of soil, trees, and streams at a time when waste still ruled.
36182-the-whale-house-of-the-chilkat:
Whale House of the Chilkat is an anthropology paper by George Emmons, issued in 1916. It forms volume nineteen, part one, of the American Museum anthropological papers series. Emmons, a navy lieutenant, gathered his matter from native sources over twenty five years. Close life with the Tlingit of Alaska grounds every page of the study.

The whale house was a great communal clan house of the Chilkat people of the coast. Carved posts, screens, and crest art made such houses treasure stores of lineage pride. Emmons writes before the old villages emptied to mining camps and canneries. Ethnologists gain a record of Tlingit art and clan life from a trusted witness.
36255-the-corner-house-girls-odd-find-wh:
Grace Brooks Hill wrote The Corner House Girls Odd Find, a girls tale printed at New York in 1916 with art by Emmett Owen. A front plate cries that the girls are millionaires. Sister books in the Corner House set send the girls to school, under canvas, and into a play.

Chapter one finds a thing in the garret, as Uncle Rufus takes the fireboard from the great chimney place in the old Corner House at Milton. Winter dusk makes the black pit yawn like an ogre on the festive room. Heads promise a savage Santa Claus, Dorothy burglar, a family album, and treasure trove. A lost Neale O Neil, a diary by Lemuel Aden, and a robber to unmask fill a warm Christmas mystery for young readers.
36719-the-scapegoat:
The Scapegoat, a short tale by Richard Maples with drawings by Weiss, opens on a street beating. A young, husky man of six feet is pounding an old man who can only shield his head and moan. The narrator, a newspaper man who prides himself on calm judgment, cannot stand by and watch.

One punch back of the ear drops the youth, whose glassy eyes show in the street light. The narrator notes his own compact build, his care for health, and his skill in a clinch. The youth, seen now as a college boy in a red sweater and white pants, gropes for words, says nothing, and reels away. Pity shifts as the tale asks who the true victim is.
37025-getting-at-the-inner-man-and-fifty:
Robert Shackleton wrote a life of Russell Conwell under the title Getting at the Inner Man, bound here with Conwell's own Fifty Years on the Lecture Platform, in a 1915 volume. Conwell's lecture Acres of Diamonds is the core of his fame. Shackleton says Conwell was not primarily a minister at all.

He was first, Shackleton argues, a lover of his fellow men, in the line of Abou Ben Adhem. His pastorate of a great church is almost a minor matter beside his educational, lecture, and hospital work. Conwell is set among the old school of American philosophers, with Emerson, Beecher, and Wendell Phillips. Millions of hearers, the running head claims, heard him.
37329-the-domestic-cat:
Gordon Stables writes a handbook in The Domestic Cat, printed in London in 1876. Routledge issued the book. Chapter one takes up classification and its basis, and the argument runs by contrast with the dog.

In the feline world you find no such diversity, he opens, of form, shape, disposition, coat, and size, as you do in the canine kind. Dogs differ from each other in the size and set of the skeleton, and in many other points, almost as much as if they belonged to separate species. Mark how unlike the bulldog is to the greyhound, he bids, or the Scotch toy terrier to the English mastiff. Yet they are all dogs, every one of them. So is the jackal, so is the fox and the wolf. Among the breeds of cats, he holds, no such deep differences exist. The pet cat gets its natural history here.
37826-daisy-the-autobiography-of-a-cat:
Daisy: The Autobiography of a Cat, by Miranda Eliot Swan, was published by Noyes Brothers at Boston, copyright 1900, with Daisy's portrait from the original photograph as frontispiece. Daisy opens by granting that people will wonder at a cat writing a story, since fighting is more in their line.

A learned man's remark, that the pen is mightier than the sword, turned her from claws to brains. Chapters cover her mother's story, Daisy's party, reverses, cat memories, and her first theft. Thanksgiving, religious aspirations, the story of Freida, and eventide close the life.
38050-all-frightfully-unofficial-about-a:
All (Frightfully Unofficial) about an Old Friend of Mine is an illustrated satire on the bank clerk's life, signed only by the Cat. Its dedication addresses the bankers, brokers, and great firms of the city. They rose to wealth, it charges, without owning that success rests partly on the honesty and energy of their servants. The masters took all the honey in the hive and left the workers nothing but the lees.

A string of pictures traces one respectable banker's clerk through his service. In his first year he fancies he has got a good thing. At ten years he has his doubts. At twenty he has none left, knows all about it, and goes home to his dinner. Martin Tupper's line heads the joke: a good master makes a good servant.
38236-shireen-and-her-friends-pages-from:
Shireen and Her Friends, pages from the life of a Persian cat by Gordon Stables, was published by Jarrold and Sons of London, with pictures by Harrison Weir. Stables gives the preface over to the reviewer, in jest. He warns that there is more truth in the tale than a reader might guess at first sight.

Shireen and Tom Brandy, he says, were real cats, and their shipboard adventures happened much as told. A starling, a cockatoo named Cockie, and a chameleon called Chammy were his own pets too. One hard tale, of Stamboul the show cat, tells only half the truth about the dealer trade, he adds. The book is a companion to his Sable and White of the year before. It pleads for a kinder place for cats in the home.
39560-fairy-circles-tales-and-legends-of:
Fairy Circles gathers tales and legends of giants, dwarfs, fairies, water sprites, and hobgoblins, taken from the German of Villamaria. The book was published in London in 1877 with many pictures.

The first tale tells of Barbarossa's youthful dream and his sleep in the Kyffhäuser mountain. King Laurin the dwarf king follows, with his rose garden. Other tales give the dwarf of Venice, the Rhine gold of the Nibelungs, and the friendship of the dwarfs. A flower of Iceland, a sea fairy, and a faithful goblin come later. The closing tales treat a fallen bell and the last home of the giants. Frontispiece and plates show scenes such as Helga in the fairy king's paradise.
39566-curiosities-of-heat:
Curiosities of Heat, by the Reverend Lyman Tefft, is a book of science lessons framed as a Bible class. It was entered at Washington in 1871 and printed at Philadelphia. The contents open with Mr Wilton's Bible class, then bring new thoughts for the scholars. A difficult question follows, and a chapter calls heat a gift of God.

Later chapters explain how heat travels and its varieties, then its management and sources. The tale woven through the lessons tells of Mr Hume, a doubter in the village store. By some impulse he went to church one Sunday, to the surprise of all the Christian people there. Tefft mixes story with plain teaching on fire, warmth, and the sun. Books of this kind taught science to Sunday school readers. They joined natural facts to faith, in a manner common to their age.
40120-the-vampire-cat:
Gerard Van Etten writes a one-act play in The Vampire Cat, number 641 of Sergel's Acting Drama, published at Chicago by the Dramatic Publishing Company in 1918 and priced at twenty-five cents. The play draws on the Japanese legend of the Nabeshima cat, whose soul, a note explains, can enter a human being. The scene is the room of O Toyo in the palace, between ten and midnight.

The cast lists Prince Hizen, lord of Nabeshima, his chief councillor Buzen, the priest Ruiten, the soldier Ito Soda, the maid Kashiku and the prince's wife O Toyo. Stage directions set candles, a shrine and a sleeping mat.
41778-epitome-of-the-pharmacopeia-of-the:
The Epitome of the Pharmacopeia of the United States and the National Formulary condenses the official drug standards for physicians, with comments. It was prepared under the Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry of the American Medical Association, copyrighted in 1921 and printed at Chicago in 1924. The committee included A W Hewlett of Stanford, Torald Sollmann of Western Reserve, M I Wilbert and W A Puckner.

Opening tables set out metric and apothecaries' weights and measures, from the milligram at 0.001 gram to the kilogram at 1000 grams. Permission to comment on the ninth decennial Pharmacopeia and the National Formulary came from their respective governing bodies.
41852-court-beauties-of-old-whitehall-hi:
Trowbridge wrote historiettes of the Restoration court, published at London and New York in 1906 with thirty-two illustrations. Its motto is a sigh of Francis the First: a court without fair women is like a year without a spring. Eight beauties get a life apiece, each under a label that fixes her character in advance.

Hortense Mancini stands first as the adventuress; Barbara Villiers, the courtesan; the Duchess of Richmond, the prude; the Countess of Gramont, the good woman. The Duchess of Tyrconnel is the splendid failure, the Countess of Shrewsbury the Messalina, and Henrietta of Orleans the evil genius. Louise de Kéroual closes the gallery as the spy. Portraits by Lely and the wits of Whitehall people the pages.
42200-the-shadow-of-ashlydyat:
The Shadow of Ashlydyat is a sensation novel by Mrs Henry Wood, author of East Lynne, here in a 1907 Macmillan printing that boasts its one hundred and eightieth thousand. The story is set at Ashlydyat and the nearby town of Prior's Ash, around the Godolphin family. Its long contents map a plot of love, money and disgrace in three parts.

Chapter titles promise sensation machinery: a snake in the grass, a midnight walk, and bonds that keep reappearing. The novel opens at a meet of the hounds on a bright autumn day, with the corn gathered and the sun on the stubble. Against that fair scene the shadow gathers: a family secret tied to the Dark Plain.
42305-all-about-ferrets-and-rats-a-compl:
Isaacsen, who signs Sure Pop, wrote all on ferrets and rats in one book. A second form came out in New York at twenty-five cents. Isaacsen put the book out from 92 Fulton Street in 1890. Its rights were filed that year in his own name. The full title calls it a hand book on the ferret as well.

Kinds, homes, food, and hunts of the ferret fill the front parts. Rats and how to clear them out take the rest of the book. Tales from his own years with the beasts ground each rule. Rat men and ferret keepers of that age used such guides. Plain steps suit shop and farm alike.
42394-stories-of-the-lifeboat:
Stories of the Lifeboat, by Frank Mundell, was published in London, here in a fourth edition. Mundell also wrote tales of the Victoria Cross, the coal mine, and the fire brigade. His lifeboat book starts with how men man the boat, and with lifeboat disasters.

Chapters tell of the Goodwin Sands, the boatmen of the Downs, and a good night of work. Named wrecks include the Bradford, the Benvue, the Eider, and the Northern Belle. Other tales cover a double rescue, a rescue in mid ocean, and the Cornish coast. Pictures show the boat in storm, its launch, and its house. Readers get short, brave tales of sea rescue round the British coast.
43500-graining-and-marbling-a-series-of-:
F Maire wrote Graining and Marbling, a series of practical treatises for painters. Frederick J Drake and Company published it at Chicago, with copyright in 1910. Maire was the author of the Modern Painter's Cyclopedia. Test questions for the student follow each treatise. The book treats materials, tools, and appliances first. General operations, the preparing of oil graining colors, and mixing follow. Rubbing, distemper colors, wiping out, and penciling get their sections.

The graining chapters treat oak, ash, cherry, and satinwood in turn. Mahogany, maple, bird's eye maple, sycamore, and walnut complete the woods. Marbling in all shades closes the volume. The preface calls the book the fourth of the Red series manuals. Graining had shrunk since hardwood replaced white pine finish, Maire owns. Still, the grainer stays employed longer than a plain brush hand.
43539-immortal-songs-of-camp-and-field-t:
Louis Albert Banks, a Methodist minister, tells the tales behind America's war songs in a book issued at Cleveland in 1899. The Burrows Brothers Company published it. Portraits and pictures fill the pages.

The contents march through the national songbook. Drake's American Flag leads. Yankee Doodle and The Star-Spangled Banner follow. Hail Columbia and Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean keep the early years. John Brown's Body and Dixie face each other across the war. The Battle Cry of Freedom and Tenting on the Old Camp Ground come next. The Battle Hymn of the Republic takes its chapter from Julia Ward Howe. Just Before the Battle, Mother and Marching through Georgia close the list. Banks pairs each song with its story and striking anecdotes.
4398-the-tides-of-barnegat:
F. Hopkinson Smith wrote this coastal novel of Barnegat, New Jersey, opening on a lovely spring morning some fifty years before his writing. The contents promise the doctor's gig, spring blossoms, little Tod Fogarty, Ann Gossaway's red cloak, and Captain Nat's decision. A game of cards, an old portrait, and a letter from Paris follow.

The tides of the title govern the story, with high water at Yardley, breakers ahead, and an undertow pulling at lives. Smith, himself a painter and engineer of shore works, knows the bay, its boats, and its people. The novel blends romance with the daily work of a seaside town, in a warm, old-fashioned manner.
44048-legal-chemistry-a-guide-to-the-det:
Legal Chemistry is a handbook of forensic analysis, meant for the chemist whose findings may be read out in court. Its French author, Naquet, was a professor to the Faculty of Medicine of Paris; Battershall translated the book with additions, and Van Nostrand of New York issued this second edition in 1884. The chapters cover ways of destroying organic matter, the detection of poisons, and the examination of stains and other traces.

The second edition adds a chapter on tea and its adulteration, drawn from the translator's work at the United States Laboratory in New York. Lists of works and memoirs close the book. Compact and practical, it treats chemical jurisprudence as a bench skill: exact tests, plainly set down, for cases where a life or a fortune may turn on the result.
44151-perkins-of-portland-perkins-the-gr:
Ellis Parker Butler wrote Perkins of Portland, Perkins the Great, issued at Boston in nineteen hundred and six. The narrator meets Perkins in the office of the Golden Hotel at Cleveland, Ohio. Perkins pokes an envelope under his nose.

On the back runs an ad: Perkins's Patent Porous Plaster makes all pains and aches fly faster. Perkins calls the first line a gem that takes the cake. He boasts of coining ads known from Maine to California. Six million pairs of one kind of shoes, he claims, sold on two lines of his. His shoes have rubber soles and his hat has odd vents. Comic pride in the ad trade drives the tale.
45234-after-prison-what:
Maud Ballington Booth wrote the prison reform plea After Prison, What? Revell published the book at New York in 1903. Booth dedicates it to her boys in prison, as their Little Mother. A plate shows a life prisoner's cell at the front.

Booth opens with gold in the mine: worth hidden where few trouble to look. She tells of the Volunteer Prison League and the power behind its work. Letters from the boys themselves fill a long chapter. Some men come home unwelcomed, and some are welcomed home. Wives and mothers get a chapter of their own. Santa Claus visits a prison in another. Booth closes with prison reform and the question, does it pay? Her answer, from years of work, is yes.
45276-dame-trot-and-her-cat:
Dame Trot and Her Cat is an anonymous children's picture book in verse. Dame Trot goes to a neighbouring fair and buys the prettiest cat ever seen. The cat is gentle, clever, and clean. Her paws are as black as sloes, her fur as white as snow, and her green eyes shine in a meek, pretty face.

The marvel begins at once. Dame Trot goes upstairs to take off her cloak and hat, and comes down to find Pussy busy preparing the tea. The Dame fears for her best china, but the velvet paws are sure and no harm comes. Next morning the kitchen is swept as clean as if Puss were a regular servant. The tea stands to draw and the toast is browned. Such wish-fulfilling picture books, in bouncing rhyme, were the small change of the nursery.
45543-the-paladins-of-edwin-the-great:
The Paladins of Edwin the Great is a tale of old days by Clements Markham. It first came out in eighteen ninety-six and this fresh form in nineteen eight. Plates fill it. The book stands in three parts named home, exile, and work. Its first part opens past a court of an old clan, past a great ash tree hallowed by its size and age.

That ash stands for the world tree of the old faith and has an elf hole no ash past miles can match. Six young ones dance past it on a bright day of the warm half, the first a stout boy of past twelve years. Parts past that tell of a kidnap by sea thieves, of thrall days in the great south town, and of trips to far lands of the east. The kings christen and his end close the book.
45551-aunt-affable-s-story-of-old-mother:
Aunt Affable's Story of Old Mother Bantry and Her Cat is a short picture poem for children, printed without an author's name. It begins in the pantry: Old Mother Bantry goes to get her cat, Grip, some meat, and finds not a morsel in the house.

Verse after verse, the dame returns home to fresh mischief. Grip eats her fish, dances a jig, feeds a dwarf, and eats a tart. Locked up, the cat escapes and jumps beside her in the gig, earning a slap and then forgiveness. One day Grip vanishes, stolen by a man who kept her chained, but she gets loose and comes home. The dame promises her the choicest of mouse and the full run of the pantry.
45990-bobby-blake-on-the-school-nine-or-:
Bobby Blake on the School Nine tells of the champions of the Monatook Lake League. Frank A Warner wrote it, and Barse and Company printed it in New York and Newark under a 1917 copyright. R Emmett Owen drew the plates. Warner wrote Bobby Blake at Rockledge School and Bobby Blake on a Cruise.

A plate shows two men handing over their pocket contents. Chapters open with flying snowballs, a friend interferes, and the coming storm. Held up, the tramps retreat, and heavy odds follow. Paying an old debt, a cowardly trick, and Rockledge School pace the mid tale. Tom Hicksley reappears, a new enemy rises, and the Monatook Lake League is formed. Who was guilty, on the trail, spring practice, and the first game drive to the ball close. Boys of the day got baseball with a mystery.
46219-an-unsinkable-titanic-every-ship-i:
An Unsinkable Titanic, every ship its own lifeboat, is a safety study by Bernard Walker, editor of a science magazine, issued in July 1912. Walker dedicates it to the memory of the chief engineer of the Titanic and his staff. Those thirty three men stood at their posts in the engine and boiler rooms to the very last, the dedication says, and went down with the ship.

The contents state the argument in order. After the ever present dangers of the sea, a chapter gives the book's slogan as its head. Safety lies in subdivision, the next chapter holds. One chapter praises an unsinkable great ship of 1858, and the next calls the Titanic sinkable by contrast. How the great ship went down follows, then warship defence against ram, mine, and torpedo.
46330-the-introduction-to-hegel-s-philos:
Bernard Bosanquet translated The Introduction to Hegel's Philosophy of Fine Art from the German, with notes and a prefatory essay. Kegan Paul, Trench and Company published the book in London in 1886. Bosanquet had been a fellow and tutor at University College, Oxford. Hegel's full Aesthetics runs to some sixteen hundred pages.

In his preface Bosanquet argues that Hegel should speak for himself. He wholly disapproves of analyses and summaries as stand-ins for Hegel's writing, whose force lies in its detail. Short of translating the whole work, the best course is to translate the entire Introduction, including the chapter on the division of the subject. The Introduction, he says, is Hegel in his best manner and tolerably complete in itself. English readers thus met Hegel on art whole, not in paraphrase.
47454-egoists-a-book-of-supermen-stendha:
James Huneker's studies of eleven egoists, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1909, first appeared in magazines including Scribner's Magazine and the Atlantic Monthly. The book is dedicated to Georg Brandes and carries a portrait of Stendhal, an unpublished letter of Flaubert, and an original proof page of Madame Bovary. Its subjects are Stendhal, Baudelaire, Flaubert, Anatole France, Huysmans, Barrès, Nietzsche, Blake, Ibsen, Stirner, and Ernest Hello.

The opening study, A Sentimental Education, takes up Henry Beyle, known as Stendhal, and the mismatch between his fine sensibility and his heavy looks. Berlioz called him a little pot-bellied man with a spiteful smile; Sainte-Beuve fills out the portrait with the turned-up nose, full-blooded neck, and small bright eyes. Huneker uses the clash to open his account of the man's mind.
48084-the-white-cat:
The White Cat, a novel by Gelett Burgess, was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York, the story copyrighted in 1907 by the Bobbs-Merrill Company. Pictures by Will Grefé go with the text. Burgess was a humorist and versifier who also wrote tales of modern manners. The story opens in confusion, with its hero hurt and lost.

The narrator wakes in a strange house, in a broad canopied bed in a guest room he cannot place. His motor car has run off the road after its steering gear failed, in a wooded country far from home. He has a lump on his head, a pain in his side, and no clear memory of how he came there. A breakdown of the senses follows, and then the lady of the house. The white cat of the title moves through the mystery that unfolds.
48229-a-blue-devil-of-france-epic-figure:
Captain Capart wrote A Blue Devil of France from his war diary, translated by Drouillard for Watt at New York. Copyright rests in 1918, and Capart had served on Petain's staff in France. His preface, written June 2, 1918 at the Lawrence Hospital in Bronxville, states his rule. He wrote nothing but what he saw or heard in three years of war.

Born at Brussels in 1881, Capart left Switzerland on August 2, 1914 to enlist. He fought at Antwerp, retreated, then joined the French army in December of that year. Nieuport, marine fusiliers, and Zouaves fill the early stories of the book in turn. Convalescence gave him time to shape true episodes of the poilu. French grit in relief is his one aim.
48430-the-rocky-mountain-goat:
The Rocky Mountain Goat is a natural history monograph by Madison Grant. The New York Zoological Society issued it in 1905. Grant, the society's secretary, reprinted the study from its ninth annual report. Photographs show goat country in northern British Columbia. Other plates compare goat and sheep, mounted heads, skulls, and kids.

Grant calls the white goat the least known game animal in North America. Writers had confused it with white mountain sheep, and even with deer. Its home begins among the highest peaks of the northwestern United States. The range runs north through British Columbia into Alaska. Few hunters or naturalists had ever reached it.
