Only eight young specimens had lived in eastern zoos, Grant counts. Four were then living in the New York Zoological Park. The Stoney Indians, he notes, call the animal Waputehk.
48497-the-silent-watchers-england-s-navy:
The Silent Watchers: England's Navy during the Great War, by Bennet Copplestone, author of The Lost Naval Papers, came from E P Dutton and Company at New York in 1918. It reached a second printing that October. Copplestone contributed the pieces between June 1916 and February 1918.

His prologue holds that the navy is a matter of machines only so far as men achieve material ends by material means. The ships and guns, he writes, are secreted by the men, as a tortoise secretes its shell. Maps from the original articles are included.
48611-fall-and-holiday-trade-season-1900:
Nerlich's illustrated catalogue for the fall and holiday trade season of 1900 and 1901 lists wholesale goods for Canadian stores. Printed muslin flags on sticks come in eight sizes from two and a half inches to eighteen by twenty-seven. Union Jack prices run from fifty-five cents to three dollars twenty-five per gross across the sizes.

Merchants' red ensigns, Canadian flags, and stars and stripes fill the printed flag tables with net prices. Printed cotton flags, unmounted or on sticks, list from forty cents to seven dollars eighty per gross by size. The Canadian flag with coat of arms in correct colours surpasses any other line at similar prices, the catalogue boasts. Trade ephemera collectors get Toronto wholesaling.
48694-musk-ox-bison-sheep-and-goat:
Musk-Ox, Bison, Sheep and Goat was published in New York in 1904, as part of the American Sportsman Library. Three writers share the book. Caspar Whitney writes the musk-ox part, George Bird Grinnell the bison, and Owen Wister the mountain sheep and the white goat.

Whitney opens with his first kill, then turns to food supply, seasons, and gear. He sets out a method of hunting, and only then the beast itself. Pictures show musk-oxen at bay, brought to bay by dogs, and skulls and feet in detail. Wister titles promise the ways of sheep and goat in their high ground. Readers get big game hunting and natural lore from men who hunted in the far north and the west.
49042-american-scenery-vol-1-of-2-or-lan:
American Scenery, volume one, is a picture book of land, lake, and river views of America, printed at London in 1840. The drawings are by W H Bartlett, engraved by Wallis, Cousen, Willmore, and others. N P Willis wrote the letter-press that goes with the plates.

The preface holds that nature has wrought with a bolder hand in America. Its rivers, forests, unshorn mountain sides, and unbridged chasms have a lavish, large-featured grandeur unlike the picturesque of other lands. To compare the New World's vales and waterfalls with the Old World's was once the privilege of the far-wandering traveller alone. Books of this class bring the enjoyment to the fireside of the home-keeping reader. In the letter-press Willis aimed to gather legendary traditions and anecdotes, tales of the Revolution, and Indian history. The volume pairs fine engraving with romantic American story.
49043-american-scenery-vol-2-of-2-or-lan:
American Scenery is a two part work of views of land, lake, and stream in the United States. Book two came out in London in 1840. W H Bartlett drew the scenes, and a team of skilled hands cut them in steel. N P Willis wrote the prose that goes with each plate.

The plates show falls at the Catskills and the great falls at Niagara. Views of Lake George, Boston, and New York from Weehawken follow. One plate shows the house of the chief at the seat of rule, from the stream. Mount Vernon, Harpers Ferry, and Baltimore all appear. White Mountain scenes and a light house in Maine add wild notes. The work sold the young land to British eyes as a place of grand sights.
49162-the-speedwell-boys-and-their-ice-r:
Roy Rockwood wrote The Speedwell Boys and Their Ice Racer, or Lost in the Great Blizzard, published in New York in 1915. The Speedwell Boys had already run motorcycles, a racing auto, a power launch, and a submarine in the series. Rockwood also wrote the Dave Dashaway flying books.

The ice racer is a machine of the frozen lake age, part sled and part car. A picture caption explains her gait: under pressure of wind and claw-wheel, she hit only the high places. Speed on ice turns to peril when the great blizzard of the subtitle swallows the course. Lost boys, white wind, and a machine that must not stop make the tale. Such series books sold speed itself to boys of 1915, one vehicle at a time.
50118-napoleon-s-appeal-to-the-british-n:
Napoleon's Appeal to the British Nation, on his treatment at Saint Helena, was printed for William Hone in London in 1817. The pamphlet, priced at two pence, presents an official memoir dictated by Napoleon and delivered to Hudson Lowe. Santini, an usher of Napoleon's cabinet, brought the account to Portsmouth on February 25th, 1817.

The appeal says Napoleon was moved to Longwood, a former East India Company farm, where his sleeping room barely holds a bed and chairs. Its paper and pitch roof leaks, rats gnaw his linen, and rats run about at dinner. Food, it claims, came short and poor, forcing Napoleon to sell his plate, broken in pieces, to buy basic needs.
50368-king-solomon-s-goat:
King Solomon's Goat is an attack on Bible religion by Willard Bartlett. The Everett Print issued the book at Boston in 1918. Bartlett had written The Origin of Priestcraft and other freethought works. An apology at the front blames careless compiling for missing credits to other authors.

Bartlett argues that the Christian faith was stolen from older sun worship. When the sun entered Taurus, he writes, god was reborn as the bull. That bull was Apis in Egypt and Moloch in Syria. Jacob's wrestling match, on this reading, was a bout with Moloch himself. Hebrew blessing words are pressed into the same scheme. The book heaps quotes from Gerald Massey and like writers. It is a raw specimen of the freethought pamphlet wars of its day.
50715-de-tribus-impostoribus-a-d-1230-th:
An infamous treatise on the three impostors, ascribed to the year 1230, was translated from a French manuscript of 1716 and privately printed for subscribers in 1904. A dissertation on the original treatise accompanies it. A bibliography of the various editions is added. The translator signs himself Alcifribas Nasier the later, an anagram of Rabelais's pen name. An index expurgatorius in verse opens the book.

The verse curses readers who bend pages, keep borrowed books, or hoard them unshared. The treatise itself, denying Moses, Jesus, and Mahomet as impostors, was long Europe's most hunted atheist text. No copy of a 1230 original exists. The edition serves collectors of forbidden books.
5110-the-adventures-of-jerry-muskrat:
Thornton W. Burgess's Adventures of Jerry Muskrat opens with Jerry kicking his heels on the Big Rock, trying to remember what Mother Muskrat said about Farmer Brown's boy and his traps. Jerry had not half heeded, thinking of other things, and considers his mother altogether foolish about a great many things.

Pooh, says Jerry, throwing out his chest: he can take care of himself without being tied to his mother's apron strings, and Farmer Brown's boy cannot fool his Uncle Jerry. The Smiling Pool's traps soon test that boast. Young readers get a muskrat tale about heeding warnings, told with Burgess's woodland humor and gentle moral.
51304-a-touch-of-e-flat:
A Touch of E Flat is a science fiction story by Joe Gibson, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in May 1957. Dick Francis illustrated it. A warning stands at its head: never let anyone point any weapon at you, even a water pistol. It may be a Cooling gun. The narrator writes his account under police surveillance.

He is residing, he says, in the Recuperating Ward of Saint Luke's Memorial Hospital. He had always meant to write the account, but not from there. The police officer who put him there has proved most helpful, with long discussions to aid the tale. That officer is Sergeant Nicolas Falasca of the Ohio State Police. The narrator's discovery of the Cooling Effect came by accident, and twice that accident has almost killed him. Gibson unfolds the story as a confession dictated to the law.
51336-what-is-posat:
Phyllis Sterling Smith wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in September 1951, with pictures by Ed Alexander. A headnote says that coming events cast their shadows before, but this shadow was four hundred years long. The tale opens with an advertisement from the July 1953 issue of several magazines. It promises mastery of all knowledge through the Perpetual Order of Seekers After Truth.

POSAT, the advertisement says, is an ancient secret society, and a free booklet explains it. Most readers passed it by with scarcely a glance, as ads of that same society had run for years. Bill Evans, an unemployed pharmacist, finds the magazine left on a bus seat and mails the coupon with a stubby pencil. He has, literally, nothing to lose. Miss Elizabeth Arnable, who seldom reads magazines, comes on the same ad in another paper.
51510-the-first-regiment-massachusetts-h:
Frye had been a major of the regiment. The book was printed at Boston by the Colonial Company in 1899. It holds the regimental roster and muster rolls and fifteen illustrations. A photograph of Colonel Charles Pfaff, who commanded the regiment, fronts it.

Fifteen chapters tell the regiment's war. They open with the coast defence problem in Massachusetts and the marching orders of April 1898. The regiment goes off for active service and settles at Fort Warren. A period of suspense follows, then the change from state militia to United States Volunteers. The final days in the service close the tale, with a claim to an honourable record. The regiment's war was one of garrison duty on the home coast, and Frye records it in full detail.
51960-the-ancient-stone-implements-weapo:
Sir John Evans catalogues the ancient stone implements, weapons, and ornaments of Great Britain in this second edition, revised, from Longmans in 1897. More than four hundred illustrations fill the work, which began at Nash Mills in 1872 and was revised there in 1897. The first chapter sets the order of treatment, across the Iron, Bronze, and Stone Ages, noting that bronze came before iron and that stone kept a place in religious rites.

The second chapter studies manufacture: flint for striking fire, gun-flint making, modes of producing flakes, and the flint mines at Grime's Graves and Spiennes. Rough-hewing, grinding, sawing, and boring of stone follow. The Neolithic implements then begin with celts, once believed to be thunderbolts fallen from the sky. Chipped and rough-hewn celts, some found at Cissbury and some perhaps tools of husbandry, take the next chapters.
52399-the-125th-regiment-illinois-volunt:
Robert M Rogers, late Second Sergeant of Company B, records his regiment in The 125th Regiment Illinois Volunteer Infantry, printed at Champaign, Illinois, in 1882. The book is dedicated to the officers and men who left home at their country's call and gave their lives in her service. A frontispiece portraits J W Langley, late colonel of the regiment.

Rogers promises a record of marches, battles and bivouacs plus a complete roster. Of the thousand men mustered on September 3, 1862, only 343 answered their names at the muster-out in Chicago. The roster states what became of every man, down to cemetery grave numbers.
52699-the-chinese-coat:
Jennette Lee wrote The Chinese Coat, a novel published by Scribner in New York in 1920 and dedicated to her husband Gerald Stanley Lee. The book opens in Stewart's department store during a sale of coats and suits. Eleanor More drifts through the closing shop. She cannot afford to buy anything, even at a sale, but she has come in all the same.

One garment holds her. A Chinese coat stands alone on its dummy at the end of the glass cases. In the fading light its gold and blue colours gleam like a bit of Oriental flame. Dragons chase each other across it in gold shadow. Eleanor walks away, then turns swiftly back and half reaches out her hand. Lee's novel begins with that small act of longing, a poor woman and a beautiful coat, and builds its story from the meeting.
52978-stem-to-stern-or-building-the-boat:
Oliver Optic wrote a boys' tale of building a boat on Lake Champlain. Lee and Shepard issued Stem to Stern in Boston in 1886, rights from 1885. The book stands fourth in the Boat-Builder Series of six. Optic gives it to his adopted nephew, John S Shriver of Baltimore.

Boys of the Beech Hill Industrial School carry on the tale's action. Plain teaching on shipbuilding runs through the fun, Optic writes in front. Full plans for a yacht would fill a book alone, he warns kindly. Boys gain sound craft lore wrapped in adventure on lake and shore.
53092-the-ancient-bronze-implements-weap:
John Evans wrote The Ancient Bronze Implements, Weapons, and Ornaments of Great Britain and Ireland, printed in London in 1881. Evans held many learned honours and led the Numismatic Society among other bodies. The preface admits the work was unfortunately many years in progress, as private and public occupations left small leisure for writing.

During the slow progress, Continental literature on bronze antiquities grew at an unprecedentedly rapid pace, Evans notes with regret. By reading and travel he kept pace with discoveries and theories broached abroad and at home as best he could. Facts and present information, he hopes, will not be found materially wanting in the volume. Archaeology readers get a Victorian standard.
53582-mammals-of-washington-volume-2-uni:
Mammals of Washington, by Walter Dalquest, forms volume two of the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History. It appeared on April 9, 1948, running to 444 pages with 140 figures in the text. A frontispiece shows Mount Rainier from Indian Henry's Hunting Ground, in a Fish and Wildlife Service photograph.

The contents lay out a state monograph. Introductory chapters cover the physiographic provinces of Washington, its distributional areas, climate and vegetation, life zones and ecology, and the geologic history of the state. Speculation follows on how the mammals arrived and spread. A check list of the state's mammals then gives way to the bulk of the book: accounts of species and subspecies, arranged in order, with a bibliography and index behind them.
53649-horace-walpole-a-memoir-with-an-ap:
Horace Walpole is a life of the great letter writer by Austin Dobson, issued in New York by Dodd, Mead in 1890. An appendix lists the books printed at Walpole's own press at Strawberry Hill. The portrait at the front is after Rosalba.

The contents map a full life. Walpole was born on September 24, 1717, son of the prime minister. He went to Eton in 1727 and to King's College, Cambridge, in 1735. In 1739 he set out on the grand tour with the poet Gray. Paris, Rheims, Florence, and Rome fill the second chapter. The tour ends in a quarrel with Gray and a sick return home. Later chapters treat his father's fall and death, and the means on which the son lived.
53796-life-of-frederick-marryat:
Life of Frederick Marryat, by David Hannay, stands in the Great Writers set shaped by Professor Eric S Robertson. Walter Scott printed it in London in 1889, with a New York and Toronto house. Marryat was the famed sea novelist of Peter Simple and Mr Midshipman Easy.

In a note Hannay says the materials for a life of Marryat are scanty. Mrs Ross Church collected, in 1872, all the surviving knowledge about her father life. The present little book has no pretensions to be founded on new materials. Its aim is a clear use of printed matter and a fair estimate of Marryat work. Chapter one tells that Frederick Marryat was born on July 10, 1792, and ran away to sea. He joined the Imperieuse under Captain Lord Cochrane in September 1806. Life fans get a compact Marryat.
53815-elizabeth-ann-s-houseboat:
Josephine Lawrence wrote Elizabeth Ann's Houseboat, copyrighted in 1929 and printed in New York, with pictures by John Foster. Lawrence had written Adventures of Elizabeth Ann, Linda Lane, and The Two Little Fellows. A front picture shows a polite ghost inviting guests to walk right in. Chapter heads open with A Letter, then About Elizabeth Ann, and All Decided. Sailor Talk and Taken Boys follow.

The Bonnie Susie is named in the heads, then school news, party plans, and seamen's chests. Witches and all, bad news, and a fortune-teller fill the later list before all is straightened out. The tale opens on a road, where Elizabeth Ann wants to stop for a flower in a field. Lex will not stop for once: he promised Cousin Nellie to come right back with the mail, and when he makes a promise, he keeps it.
53907-the-universal-counterfeit-and-alte:
The Universal Counterfeit and Altered Bank Note Detector is a manual for spotting false bank notes at sight. H C Foote of 71 Broadway, New York, arranged and improved the system. Mann and Spear printed the fourth edition in 1853; the work was first entered for copyright in 1848 by Wheeler M Gillett.

The whole method is complete in seven rules. Diagrams and illustrations on steel support self instruction. In an age when hundreds of banks issued their own notes, cashiers faced a daily flood of doubtful paper. Testimonials open the book from bank officers who had examined the method. F W Edmonds, cashier of the Mechanics' Bank of New York, calls it exceedingly serviceable. Foote promised infallible detection, applicable to every bank in the United States. The manual survives as evidence of America's chaotic paper money before the Civil War.
54039-fast-day-cookery-or-meals-without-:
Fast Day Cookery, or Meals Without Meat, is a household cookbook from a London set of cheap home guides. Adverts at the front list hints on cookery, an economical cook for all seasons, and a guide to washing and stain removal. A book on children by Richmond, with a preface by Sarah Tytler, stands in the same list.

Recipes give full fast day dishes without meat for Catholic and frugal tables alike. One soup takes pints of milk and water, the liquor of oysters, twelve cloves, twelve peppercorns, and three bay leaves. Fine flour is stirred in a bowl to thicken. Plain measures and cheap goods make the book a working kitchen tool, not a show piece.
54069-the-boy-inventors-diving-torpedo-b:
The Boy Inventors' Diving Torpedo Boat, by Richard Bonner, was published in New York in 1912 with drawings by Charles Wrenn. Bonner wrote other Boy Inventors tales, on wireless wins and a vanishing gun. The craft at the heart of the book is the White Shark, part boat, part underwater torpedo craft.

The tale opens with a runaway car and Jack Chadwick, a clean-cut lad of about seventeen, leaping up in alarm. His cousin Tom Jesson joins him as trials begin. Chapters promise a wild chase, a fight with a water beast, fog, a British skipper, and the White Shark saving the day. Speed, risk, and boy-made tech drive the plot.
54800-colonization-and-christianity-a-po:
Colonization and Christianity, by William Howitt, is a popular history of the treatment of native peoples by Europeans in all their colonies. Longman and partners published the book in London in 1838. Howitt opens with a verse from Malachi asking why men deal treacherously with their brothers.

Howitt states his object at once: to lay open what he calls the most extensive system of crime the world ever witnessed, one at work for more than three hundred years. He blames English apathy on want of knowledge, noting that single acts of injustice stirred strong feeling while the whole field never came into clear view. The book offers no plans of remedy. Its first business, he says, is to make the facts known, colony by colony, so that the public can no longer plead ignorance of what was done in its name.
54945-all-taut-or-rigging-the-boat:
Oliver Optic wrote All Taut, or Rigging the Boat, for Lee and Shepard at Boston. Rights were held in 1886 by William Adams, the author's own name. The book is the fifth volume of the Boat-Builder series. A plate shows a vessel foundered, named the Thunderer, in its pages. The series runs: All Adrift, Snug Harbor, and Square and Compasses before it.

Stem to Stern, building the boat, stands fourth in that list. All Taut rigs the boat, and Ready About will sail her, the list promises. Cat notes call it the fifth volume, finished in the next book. Nearly all the characters of the earlier books stand present here. The book is given to a young friend of the author at Grand Rapids. Optic gives boys boat craft, work, and adventure in his brisk school.
55228-notes-on-the-new-testament-explana:
Explanatory and practical notes on the book of Revelation fill this commentary volume. The notes were written when many words had not settled into standard spelling, a modern transcriber warns. Page numbers from the original book are shown in braces for reference through the text.

Verse by verse, the commentary reads the seals, trumpets and vials of John's vision. Plain explanation comes first in each note, then practical remarks for the reader's life. Such commentaries stood in farmhouses and manses for a century, giving plain families a learned guide to the most puzzling book of the New Testament in their Sunday reading.
55557-ready-about-or-sailing-the-boat:
Ready About closes Oliver Optic's Boat-Builder set, the sixth book in six years of boys learning boats. The preface brings in the Nautifelers Club to show two sorts of young men: those with high aims, and those who live too fast. Half the club stands at the edge of crime.

The head of the Beech Hill Industrial School works to save the led-astray half, with a glad result. Sailing the boat is a chief part of the tale, taught as an art. Optic, in life William Adams, wrote that courage need not mean rashness, and a principled boy need not be a coward.
55760-ambrose-lavendale-diplomat:
E Phillips Oppenheim wrote Ambrose Lavendale, Diplomat, issued at London in 1920 by Hodder and Stoughton. Ten chapters carry the tale. The first is named The Man Who Could Have Ended the War. A lost formula and a deal with Niko come next.

The tale opens just past one in a packed London bar. Americans, news men, trade men, and Canadians on leave crowd the room. A small, ill dressed man with stained fingers stands at the edge. He holds a glass of vermouth half raised and listens hard. General Matravers, Mr Kessner, and Mr Courlander enter the plot in turn. Plots, indiscreet travellers, and a court sentence close the tale of spies and statecraft.
55826-peggy-goes-straw-hat:
Peggy Goes Straw Hat, by Virginia Hughes, was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York in nineteen sixty-three. Sergio Leone illustrated the volume. The story stands in the Peggy Lane Theater Stories, about a young actress building a career. Its frontispiece shows Chris telling Peggy what fun it is working with her.

Peggy rides a rickety bus eight hours from New York to an Adirondack town. Lake Kenabeek gleams below the pines as she arrives with her make-up kit. She has been hired as resident ingenue for eight weeks of summer stock. Each week means a different part and new backstage lessons. She won the job by reading for the producers, on her own. The chapters run from arrival through a broadcast, opening night, and summer stock intrigues.
56050-castillo-de-san-marcos-a-guide-to-:
A park handbook fills this item: a guide to Castillo de San Marcos National Monument in Florida, handbook number 149, produced by the publications division of the National Park Service at Washington. A note on use says the fort stands in the longest lived town founded by Europeans in the United States. The handbook tells the meeting-of-cultures story of the long effort to build the Castillo.

An aerial view shows the plan's logic: no wall or approach unguarded. A map shows an early attack, English troops firing across the water in 1586. A first chapter on pirates opens on May 28, 1668, when a ship from Veracruz anchored with flour and the town rejoiced at a friendly sail. Unknown to all, pirates had seized her, and the pilot who boarded her was taken at gunpoint.
56144-folk-lore-notes-vol-i-gujarat:
Folk Lore Notes, volume one on Gujarat, was compiled from materials gathered by Jackson of the Indian Civil Service and printed at Bombay in 1914. Jackson was killed at Nasik in December 1909, before he could publish the notes himself. Friends raised a fund in his memory to print his library and papers.

Around 1900 Jackson sent a standard list of folklore questions to schoolmasters across the region. Their replies form the raw notes here, sorted for Gujarat and the Konkan for easy use. Enthoven saw the work through the press without deep re-editing of the replies he received. Students of custom, tale, and belief get rare field replies from local teachers in western India, close to daily village life.
562-the-go-ahead-boys-and-the-racing-mot:
Ross Kay sends four boys racing on the Hudson in this motor-boat tale, largely based on true events. The Black Growler glides from dock with families waving, then faces a missing boy, a lost bag, a tavern row, and a night summons. A bond, a boathouse man, and a collision test the crew.

Kay writes brisk, clean action without sensationalism, praising open-air life and fair play. The boys learn seamanship, pluck, and teamwork at speed. The book charms young readers as a wholesome adventure, where a fast boat and four true friends meet every turn with grit.
56487-an-apology-for-the-true-christian-:
Robert Barclay's Apology for the True Christian Divinity, here in its eighth English edition, was printed by John Baskerville at Birmingham in 1765. Barclay wrote it in Latin and English to explain and vindicate the principles and doctrines of the people called Quakers, and it was translated into Dutch, French, and Spanish.

The argument stands as fifteen propositions, each proved at length: the true foundation of knowledge, immediate revelation, the scriptures, the condition of man in the Fall, and universal redemption by Christ. Later propositions treat the saving light given to every man, justification, perfection, the ministry, worship, baptism, and communion. The last two take up the power of the civil magistrate in matters of conscience, and salutations and recreations. An address to King Charles the Second opens the book.
56653-the-german-fleet-being-the-compani:
Archibald Hurd wrote a study of the German navy, printed in London in 1915 as a companion to his Fleets at War. He traces sea power from the Hanseatic League, whose towns once ruled trade in north and west Europe. Chapters cover a first German fleet, growth in the last century, and British sway over that growth. He also treats the German Navy Acts in depth.

Later pages deal with ships, officers, and men, and with William II and his naval minister. Two added parts set out German naval policy and compare British and German shipbuilding plans. The book is a wartime British view of a rival fleet.
56928-history-of-frederick-the-second-ca:
History of Frederick the Second, called Frederick the Great, is a life of the famed Prussian king by Abbott. He had writ past tales of the great French captain, of that lands revolt, and of the exiles isle. Its form holds pictures through the text.

It came out at New York in the early eighteen seventies, and its rights were set in law that same year. A front print shows the king at age seventy three. Its first words own a plain truth of its craft. Men who know not the wild past, it says, may judge that true tales of it must be made up tales. Yet the mind can scarce invent scenes more strange than those found in the annals of days gone by. The tale of the soldier king then makes the case.
57401-the-king-s-scapegoat:
The King's Scapegoat is a novel by Hamilton Drummond, published in Toronto by Copp Clark in 1905, with a frontispiece by Cyrus Cuneo. Drummond had written The Seven Houses and A Man's Fear. The tale is set in France under Louis the Eleventh, the spider king, whose court at Plessis-les-Tours fills the background.

Contents follow the narrator's claim to be heard for truth's sake. Fire and sack, Babette, and Paris in eighty-three open the intrigue. The muse in draggled skirts and France's shrewdest brain follow. The doors of the Louvre, opening only inwards, mark the court's trap-like ways. The plot of four nations meets the king's counterplot. Commines explains, and a lesson in diplomacy is given. A mission of peace, a rose of promise, and the justice hall at Morsigny follow. The cunning king's scapegoat narrates his own bruisings.
57469-doctor-rabbit-and-tom-wildcat:
Thomas Clark Hinkle wrote a tale for children about a wise beast doctor. The book came out in Chicago in 1918. It sits in the Greenwoods series of wood tales. Doctor Rabbit lives among the small folk of the Big Green Woods. The book is given to all children who love those woods.

Tom Wildcat comes as an unwelcome caller at the start. Doctor Rabbit finds a secret and holds his peace to learn more. Wit, not claws, is the doctor's chief tool in the woods. Each short part brings a fresh trick or scare. Young readers learn to out-think a foe with a cool head.
57773-theism-and-humanism-being-the-giff:
Theism and Humanism, the Gifford Lectures of Arthur James Balfour, were given at Glasgow in 1914. Hodder and Stoughton published them at London in 1915 from those lectures. Balfour dedicates the volume to the professors and students of the university. They gave so kind a reception to the lectures in the Bute Hall, he writes.

The dedication is dated May 24, 1915, from his London house in Carlton Gardens. Part one opens with an introduction to the whole argument of the course. A statesman philosopher asks whether science alone can hold a world view together. Naturalism leaves beauty, reason, and morals homeless, his lectures argue at length. The case for theism is built as the ground that makes knowledge itself sane.
57933-angels-of-the-battlefield-a-histor:
George Barton wrote this history of Catholic sisterhoods in the American Civil War. It was first entered for copyright in 1897. The copy here is a revised second edition. Barton says many books had told of other women's war work. Apart from stray newspaper pieces, he argues, nothing had been published on the self-sacrificing labor of these sisters.

His aim is a full, ordered account of that service. Nuns who nursed the wounded and sick on both sides stand at the center of the book. The Philadelphia edition of 1898 gathers their hospital and field work into one record. Faith and care run through the stories of wards, camps and battlefields alike.
58028-she-blows-and-sparm-at-that:
William John Hopkins wrote a tale of whaling told by an old man looking back on his life. The book came out in Boston and New York in 1922. Clifford Ashley, who knew whaling well, read the proof and made fixes and hints. His paintings give the book its pictures, from lancing a whale to lowering boats.

The narrator owns that age has made him prone to dwell on the past. He tells of fitting out, cutting in, bailing oil, and harpoon work on porpoise. A Nantucket sleigh ride, the wild ride when a harpooned whale drags a boat, gives the book one of its best known scenes. Salt air, hard work, and risk fill the tale.
58113-an-act-to-provide-for-the-paving-g:
The Act for Brompton Square, printed by George Eyre and Andrew Strahan in 1825, provides for paving, gravelling, lighting, and watching the footways and carriageways in and near the square. Brompton Square lies in the parish of Saint Mary Abbotts Kensington. The Act also provides for keeping up a garden and shrubbery in the square. An alphabetical index of its provisions fills the front of the volume. Accounts books must lie open to the free inspection of trustees and rated persons.

The index shows the machinery of such local acts: rates on occupiers, appeals by persons aggrieved to the trustees and then to quarter sessions, and penalties for annoyances. Houses occupied by ambassadors are rated on their landlords instead. Money may be raised by annuity, limited to the lives of two persons under thirty-five. Actions must begin within six months of the fact complained of.
58263-the-candle-and-the-cat:
Mary Leonard wrote The Candle and the Cat, a story for young readers published in New York in 1901. Leonard dedicated the book to the memory of Trolley, and the cat shares the stage with a girl named Caro from the first chapter on. The tale came out in the Sunshine Library, a line of books for children.

Twelve chapters follow Caro and Trolley through a silver candlestick, a gate in the orchard, and a visit by the cat. A local snow storm comes next, then a shock for Miss Elizabeth and time in the garden. Christmas candles glow near the close, and the final chapter is a simple goodbye. Readers get a gentle home story in which a pet counts as a true member of the family.
58394-anatomy-of-the-cat:
Jacob Reighard and H S Jennings wrote Anatomy of the Cat, published by Henry Holt at New York in 1901. Both men taught zoology at the University of Michigan. Louise Burridge Jennings drew the book's one hundred and seventy-three figures. The preface owns a gap: the cat has long served for the practical study of mammalian anatomy. Yet no clear, correct, and not too bulky account of its structure stood ready for laboratory students.

The authors list the books that came before. Strauss-Durckheim's two volumes of 1845 treat muscles and bones only, and are not open to American students. Mivart's Cat of 1881 and Wilder and Gage's Anatomical Technology of 1882 follow. A laboratory guide of 1895 and Jayne's Mammalian Anatomy of 1898 complete the list. Reighard and Jennings set out to give the dissecting room one exact, usable cat.
58584-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger built an index to the Project Gutenberg works of Frédéric Bastiat. Bastiat was a French voice for free trade and sound wealth laws. The index lists his chief books and their full part lists. The Law and Harmonies of Political Economy stand in the set. Essays on Political Economy leads the list here.

Inside that book, the famed broken window tale makes its case. What is seen and what is not seen is its core thought. Corn sacks, houses, and planes show how wealth in tools works. Free trade pleas and taunts at trade curbs fill the rest. New readers get a map of a clear, bold mind.
58664-my-rubaiyat:
Sadakichi Hartmann wrote his own rubaiyat of quatrains in a proud third form. The book came out in San Francisco in 1916. He gave it to Dunbar Wright, a guest among men in his words. That man courts the sun and makes Arcadia of winds, Hartmann writes. A note in place of a front talk drops his mask in full.

His verse is rough and half done, he grants to a St Louis judge. A poem of this scope is never done, he holds as his plea. William Marion Reedy of the Mirror is that judge he quotes there. Themes of wine, fate, love, and brief life fill the quatrains. Each four line bit stands on its own for the eye. East forms wear west dress.
5868-nothing-to-eat:
Horatio Alger and Thomas Chandler Haliburton offer Nothing to Eat, an illustrated humorous work that plays on the famous Nothing to Wear. Its verses nibble at appetite itself, with a speaker pampering a delicate thing, confessing an appetite none of the best, and claiming the least mite will suffice. The joke lies in making a little do, and in making hunger itself comic.

You get a short, light piece of Victorian humor, where food, fashion, and appetite become subjects for verse and satire. The collaboration of two popular writers gives the work a double comic voice. It suits readers who enjoy literary parody and period humor, and it offers a brief, amusing glimpse of how Victorians laughed at their own appetites.
58796-through-the-wheat:
Through the Wheat is a Great War novel by Thomas Boyd of the Marines. Scribner of New York and London issued the book in April nineteen twenty three. Young William Hicks leans by a French canteen wall at dusk in it. Nine months in France had shunted him from place to place in rear work.

Hicks had served as military police and stevedore and built camps for new men. He was supposed to be a soldier, yet had never yet seen real action. A Cincinnati sergeant had promised him real action with the Marines at enlistment. His heart had flown to the rich promise of battle back then in Ohio. The wheat fields of France give the bitter war tale its title.
5948-the-bobbsey-twins-on-a-houseboat:
Laura Lee Hope sends the Bobbsey children aboard a houseboat for a family holiday afloat. The early chapters promise good news, a rescue in which Snap saves Freddie, and household upset from Dinah. Flossie and Freddie, the younger twins, join their older brother and sister in the fun.

Life on the water gives the story its shape, with days spent close together and small mishaps turning into adventures. The tale stays warm and plain, built for young readers who enjoy a large family, a lively dog, and a summer spent somewhere new.
59577-the-life-of-charlemagne-charles-th:
The Life of Charlemagne is a tight past of the great Frank king by Thomas Hodgkin. Henry Ketcham added notes to this form, out from Burt in nineteen two. A Durer paint of the king heads the book as its front plate. Hodgkin grants the squeeze of so vast a reign in so small a book. He spends eighty pages on the kings who came ere Charles for cause.

Charles was the last term of a rise line, he holds in the front words. Lords, house chiefs, then kings make that line in its climb. Old proof for the first span rests on the Fredegarius tale in rude Latin. House town annals kept at great monk homes serve the reign span. Ranke held those annals a state work, not a lone monk craft.
59693-the-old-goat:
Charles Fontenay wrote this science fiction story for Worlds of If, where it ran in February 1957. The head note plays on an old saying: the soul is the form that makes the body. That may just explain what happened on a fatal day at Ivy College.

Doctor Angstrom is known to his students as the Old Goat, and the name fits. He has a goat's cold blue eyes, a goat's waggling whiskers, and the temper of a goat with a stomach ache. The college, the narrator says, keeps a goat as mascot in his memory. On the day of the tale, six top scientists gather to watch Angstrom test his matter transmitter on a live animal. The subject is a real goat, straining at its rope among the jars and glassware. Readers get a campus tale where the joke turns deadly serious.
59846-a-comparative-view-of-the-mortalit:
A Comparative View of the Mortality of the Human Species, by William Black, appeared in 1788. Dilly printed it at London in the Poultry in that year. Charts and tables illustrate the view of death at all ages in the work. It was published at the unanimous request of the Medical Society of London.

Black was a doctor of the Royal College of Physicians in London then. A dedication addresses George, Prince of Wales, at the front of the book. Diseases and casualties by which men are destroyed or annoyed fill his tables. Bills of mortality and parish counts stand behind such early medical statistics. A founder of medical arithmetic counts how London died in the age of reason.
59950-junior-park-ranger-program-montezu:
The Junior Park Ranger Program is a work book for young guests at two old sites. Montezuma Castle and Tuzigoot, in the south west, are kept by the Park Service. The book sets the pledge of a young ranger at its front. Keep the parks clean, learn their lore, and hold to the rules and signs. Stay on the trails, it warns, for your own safe state and the sites.

Tasks in the book teach who lived at the sites in old days. Plants those folk used and beasts that live there now fill the tasks. Young ones pick two tasks from pages marked for their age band. Grown bands take harder tasks from cactus marked pages as they rise. A true Junior Park Ranger badge pays the work at the end.
60182-a-young-macedonian-in-the-army-of-:
Alfred Church wrote this tale of a young Macedonian, published by Seeley in London in 1890. Sixteen illustrations dress the story of Alexander's army for young readers. Church defends Alexander's visit to Jerusalem, told by Josephus only, in a note at the front.

Westcott thought that narrative may be true, and Church rests his use of it there. A wrong opens the contents, and a revenge follows in the second chapter. Preparations, Troy, the Granicus, Halicarnassus and Memnon march the boy soldier through Alexander's conquest of Persia, in a classic of the schoolroom shelf by a Latin professor.
609-america-through-the-spectacles-of-an:
Wu Tingfang, a Chinese diplomat, looks at America in 1914 through an outsider's eyes in this volume. He weighs presidents, courts, schools, and daily manners, sometimes praising, sometimes scolding, and once even suggesting the president be called emperor. An editor's introduction warns that some views are odd, some wrong, and some keenly right.

Wu writes with calm, well-considered prose, comparing Chinese and American ways without flattery. His hopes for peace, written on the eve of war, now read as poignant. The book serves as a rare mirror: America seen by a thoughtful visitor who loved neither praise nor blame for its own sake.
60923-the-rainbow-cat:
Rose Fyleman tells fairy tales in The Rainbow Cat, from George H Doran Company of New York, copyrighted in 1923, with pictures by Thelma Cudlipp Grosvenor. Fyleman had written the verse books Fairies and Chimneys and The Fairy Flute. The contents hold fifteen tales, four of them the Rainbow Cat's own adventures.

The first tale introduces the cat itself: violet nose, indigo eyes, pale blue ears, green front legs, a yellow body, orange back legs, and a red tail. It lives in Fairyland and, bored one sunny day, sets out on a voyage of adventure. A princess who could not cry follows.
60984-the-sportsman-s-club-afloat:
The Sportsman's Club Afloat is a boys' adventure novel by Harry Castlemon, published at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates. The copyright was entered in 1874. It is one of the three books in his Sportsman's Club series, and the title page lists his many other series for boys.

The story opens on the Gulf, with chapters named A Surprise, Outwitted, and Fairly Afloat. The young sportsmen meet deserters, a man called Don Casper, and a foe named Pierre, shown in the front picture. Castlemon wrote fast, plain tales of shooting, boating, and camp life. Books like this one taught a generation of American boys to dream of the outdoors.
61063-negroes-and-negro-slavery-the-firs:
J H Van Evrie writes a defence of slavery as a natural state in a New York volume entered in 1861 at 162 Nassau Street. Van Evrie held a medical degree, and his own house, Van Evrie, Horton and Co, issued the work. A long quote from Thomas Jefferson's Notes on Virginia heads the title page as proof text.

Four figures of skulls and heads stand at the front, tied to pages 135 and 136 of the text. A preface states that disunion and civil war have come since the first edition of the work. Van Evrie blames a party fed on British abolition writing for that fall into war in his account. The book stands as a period piece of pro-slavery thought at the war's outbreak in 1861.
61165-the-roman-index-of-forbidden-books:
Francis Betten, a Jesuit, told in brief how Rome's ban list of books works. A second form came out in Saint Louis in 1909. A sum of the Index stands in the book for quick use. Church leave to print dates to November of 1908 in its front. The brief first ran in a Buffalo church sheet of that age.

It then ran in the Catholic Mind set of Fordham in 1907. Those too busy for deep study are its named guests in the note. Rules, bans, and how to hold a banned book fill its parts. Lists of banned names and works stand in its back sum. Church folk and book men share its plain, brief aid. Each rule is set short.
61235-peter-and-alexis-the-romance-of-pe:
Dmitri Merejkowski closed his famed trilogy of novels with Peter and Alexis, in an authorized English version from Putnam. The two books before it treated the Emperor Julian and Leonardo da Vinci. The note at the front calls this novel a study of the mind, not a tale made to please the young. Its theme is the most moving stretch in the life of Peter the Great.

The book shows Russia at the start of the 1700s, learning from the West through its Tsar. It draws court, town, peasants, and wild folk faith in that age. At its heart stands the clash between Peter and his son Alexis. The note claims Russia had changed but little in the bulk of her people since that time. Readers get a grave, rich picture of a land torn between old ways and new.
61853-frank-merriwell-s-false-friend-or-:
Frank Merriwell's False Friend, or An Investment in Human Nature, is one of the Merriwell tales of sport and school life by Burt Standish. The host print is one of the cheap week tales of the set, sold for a few cents a copy. The front pages of the print give the bill of the whole set. That bill boasts of a half a mint of keen young fans of the two Merriwell lads.

The tales, says that bill, are rich in fun and thrills in all kinds of sport and games. They are of a high tone of right and wrong, and can not fail to do good to each boy who reads them. They fire a boy's will to be a fine man of sport, that he may grow to a strong, straight, right thought man.
62255-stellar-showboat:
Malcolm Jameson wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1942. Special Investigator Billy Neville serves with the Interplanetary Police among the settled worlds. Fresh from hard duty on Venus and Mars, he is sent to Pallas, chief world of the Asteroid Confederation.

A wave of blackmail and extortion has swept the System for two years. Rich and trusted people vanish, and prized secrets leak out for sale. Colonel Frawley gives Neville the thick case file and sends him after the hidden ring. Behind it all waits the Showboat of Space, a stage where a strange plot is set to play out.
62407-the-measure-of-value-stated-and-il:
Malthus states his measure of value in this essay, published by Murray in London in 1823. He was professor of history and political economy at the East India College then. His application runs to the alterations in the value of English currency since 1790, the title promises in full.

The word value has two meanings in common language, Malthus begins at the start. Value in use is usefulness in supplying man's most important wants, he writes. Value in exchange is the power of commanding other objects, and finding one steady measure for that power is the puzzle he argues against Ricardo and Smith.
62526-let-us-have-peace-remarks-of-logan:
Let Us Have Peace is a speech by Logan Roots in the House of Representatives. It was delivered at Washington on Friday, January 22, 1869. Its subject is the assassination of James Hinds, a fellow member from Arkansas. Roots opens by saying the sad subject bears on his mind with peculiar force.

He was personally acquainted with James Hinds in a busy part of his life, he states. Hinds met his death by political assassination in the district Roots represents, he adds. His life, though short, endeared him to hundreds who wished it longer, the speech holds. A child of poverty grown into an honored man is the lesson Roots draws from it. Reconstruction violence in Arkansas stands behind this House memorial of 1869.
62829-frank-merriwell-s-setback-or-true-: Frank Merriwell's Setback, or True Pluck Welcomes Defeat, is a story in the Merriwell series of books for young men, sold at fifteen cents. The series pages praise Frank and Dick Merriwell as lads of high ideals who play fair in sports and in life. Athletics, fun, and a strong moral tone are promised to boy readers, with the hope that the tales will fire a boy to become a strong and right thinking man.
63140-a-lost-chapter-in-the-history-of-t:
J. H. B. Latrobe wrote this lost chapter in the tale of the steamboat. It was read to the Maryland Historical Society in 1844 and printed in 1871. The tale opens in the spring of 1828. Latrobe had a law office in a hall in Baltimore, and his work was scant. He had but just been let into the bar, and sat in thought on his hopes. Then the door was opened and a man came in.

The guest was a fine old man of great air, with a rich Irish tongue. He asked if the young man was Latrobe, and if he knew him. The face and the voice were known, but Latrobe could not place them. The guest gave his name in full pride: John Devereux Delacy. He had known the boy in his father's house, when the boy was a small child.
63483-frank-merriwell-s-chase-or-excitin:
Frank Merriwell's Chase is a boys' tale of a cruise on the coast. Burt Standish wrote the long run of tales of the Yale sports star. This book came out in New York in the year 1898. Frank is at the wheel of his yacht White Wings as it starts.

Four of his college mates sail with him on the Maine coast cruise. A Dutch lad's broad speech gives the first laughs of the book. The yacht makes port at Belfast, a town of fair fame in the tale. A big sign board in the port tells of a famed tonic drink. The boys look to meet the town's fair girls at their land fall. The chase of the title then takes the crew out on the waves. Sport, jest, and risk are the stock of the whole Merriwell run.
63571-exploits-and-adventures-of-a-soldi:
William Llewellyn Adams wrote Exploits and Adventures of a Soldier Ashore and Afloat, published at Philadelphia in 1911. He inscribes the book to his bunkies and shipmates of the army and navy. A signed portrait of Adams in uniform stands at the front.

The chapters march around the world. The Governor's Troop of Pennsylvania cavalry opens the service, then a man-of-war carries him from New York to Morocco. A thrilling adventure with Moors in the kasbah of Algiers follows. From the pyramids of Egypt he sails to Singapore, Hong Kong and its underworld, and Japan under war orders. Life among hostile Moros in the jungles of Mindanao fills a long chapter. The Marine guard of honor at the Saint Louis world fair of 1904 brings him home in ceremony. One man's wars make a whole atlas.
63808-space-bat:
Carl Selwyn wrote a tale first printed in Planet Stories in winter 1946. A huge bat from the caves of space stands at its heart, worth a million dollars. Lou Flint, a trapper on a small planetoid, guards feathered deer from hide hunters. The girl at his side shares the stakes of the hunt.

Hunters drive the deer into a hid corral and lift clubs to kill them. Flint steps from shade and fires an ice-ray pistol that freezes a man's arm mid-swing. He orders the gang off the planetoid at gunpoint. Pulp readers get fast action, strange beasts, and a lone hero with nerve.
63952-the-pneumatic-despatch-tube-system:
The Pneumatic Despatch Tube System of the Batcheller Pneumatic Tube Company is a technical book by Batcheller, a mechanical engineer. It was printed at Philadelphia in 1897. A view of the main post office of that city stands at the front. The first chapter gives a brief history of the art. Early records and the London pneumatic telegraph open the tale. The Siemens circuit system and late London improvements follow. An underground pneumatic railway for transport is treated as well.

The heart of the book is the Batcheller system itself. Senders, receivers, time locks, and carriers are each described and drawn. Lines of two stations and of many stations are laid out. Air supply, blowers, and compressors get their chapters. The book sells a system that then sped mail through the great cities of America. It is an engineer's catalogue and history in one.
64595-animat:
Animat, by Basil Wells, is a science fiction story from Planet Stories, Spring 1949. The starship Sun Maiden, beaten by meteors, falls burning into the clouds of Venus and crashes in a wet meadow. Among the survivors stands Jay Forsix, called J46, a square jawed redhead who looks and talks like a man.

Jay is no man but an animat, a cheap living robot of flesh and bone bred by Animats Incorporated for the uranium mines of Jupiter's moons. The teaser asks whether he is man or android as he fights Venus slime and frog apes. Pulp fiction rarely put its question so plainly.
64624-lady-into-hell-cat:
Lady Into Hell-Cat, by Stanley Mullen, first appeared in Planet Stories in spring 1949. Tracking the lady across black space-lanes and snapping magnetic bracelets on her was duck soup for Space Patrol agent Heydrick. Only then did he learn what a planet-load of trouble he had bought.

Lee Heydrick reports to the security police at 9 Ganymede, a slime-hole frontier town. His fugitive is a red Martian girl who killed Feyjak, third man in the Red Council, in his laboratory. Heydrick, foster son of Tyko, head man of the Blue, suspects the assignment is politics aimed at his foster father.
64716-a-farewell-sermon-delivered-on-sun:
Archdeacon Pott preached this farewell sermon at the parish church of St Mary Abbots, Kensington, on Sunday, the twenty-third of October 1842. Rivington printed it at London the same year, at the request of the parishioners. Pott inscribes it to them with fervent prayer.

His text is Ecclesiastes, third chapter, first verse: to every thing there is a season. Pott warns against saving the whole work of life for its last portion, which comes only by daily progress. Hezekiah's lament and David's pleas for longer days serve as examples. Life's loan, he argues, always suffices for its proper end where grace is not blocked.
64870-st-clair-s-defeat:
Saint Clair's Defeat is a historical pamphlet prepared by the Fort Wayne public library staff in 1954. It belongs to a series issued under the library boards' direction. The battle it treats was the army's disaster of 1791 in the old Northwest. Major Jacob Fowler's own narrative anchors the account. Charles Cist printed Fowler's story in his Advertiser in 1844. Cist praised the old soldier's undimmed eye and vigorous memory.

Fowler could still pick off a squirrel at a hundred yards at eighty. His story charges that Saint Clair kept out almost no scouting parties. Volunteer militia scouts alone warned the army the night before. Rifle fire through the night gave further warning of the attack. The pamphlet preserves a participant's case against his general. Local history publishing kept such testimony in print.
66318-ten-years-in-washington-or-inside-:
Mary Clemmer wrote Ten Years in Washington, a big illustrated account of the national capital as a woman saw it, printed in Hartford in 1882. The book promises the marvels and sights of Washington and daily life at the White House, past and present. Forty-eight wood engravings and a portrait of the author fill its pages.

Clemmer takes readers inside the government departments and shows how each one works. She describes every phase of political, public, and social life at the capital. Added at the end is a full account of the life and death of President James Garfield, written by Shipley. The volume preserves the Washington of the early 1880s in close, lively detail.
66467-rev-t-connellan-to-his-dearly-belo:
Connellan addressed a letter to his dearly beloved brethren, the Roman Catholics of the diocese of Elphin, printed at Dublin about 1889. For seven years and three months he laboured among them, he writes. Thousands knew him in the confessional, almost all heard his pulpit voice, and he baptized not a few of the flock.

He worked in Sligo, Strokestown, Roscommon, and Athlone, the four most populous centres, without a word of disagreement. Wasn't he drowned in Lough Ree a couple of years ago, they will ask: is it his ghost coming among us? He left the diocese, put off clerical garb, and worked on the London press for eighteen months. Converts' literature readers get his reasons.
66732-mystery-at-mesa-flat:
Mystery at Mesa Flat is a science fiction story by Ivar Jorgensen, printed in the magazine Imagination in June 1956. Its blurb sets the puzzle. A desert town did not seem a likely place for murder, especially a murder planned on a world light years away.

The murder, the story begins, was committed ten minutes before the Otarkian ship lifted for the trip back to the mother planet. It was discovered ten minutes after blast-off. The killer, a lout of an upper-hillman signed on at the last moment, bragged of the kill to his sergeant, grinning. The victim had crouched behind a rock, peeking out at the ship. The killer came behind him quietly and broke his neck. The guard is rushed before the Commander, whose eyes are terrible and whose voice stays soft. Secrecy, he reminds the man, has been the key to the invasion plan.
67050-the-perilous-seat:
Caroline Dale Snedeker wrote The Perilous Seat, a tale of old Greece, for Doubleday, Page in 1923. Snedeker had written Seth Way and The Spartan before this work. She gives the book to her son Karl, whose Greek scholarship aided her task. A verse at the front tells the peril of the title. The untaught maid who mounts the high seat can speak wisdom kings will seek, yet the god will soon destroy her.

Book one opens at the Pythian festival, where Dryas wins the prize. Book two tells a childhood in Delphi, with Theria at age seven. Guests, gifts, a robber taken, laurel from Tempe, and a boy called Sophocles fill its chapters. Book three goes within the oracle, to the place of golden tripods.
67123-show-boat:
Edna Ferber wrote Show Boat, for Grosset and Dunlap in 1926. Ferber was the author of So Big, the title page notes. Kim Ravenal always said she was thankful for her name. It had been no worse, by a breath, she knew. She escaped being called Mississippi by that breath, the tale opens.

Imagine Mississippi Ravenal, she often said. They would have cut it to Missy, or even Sippy, she feared. No one would see an actress named Sippy seriously. Kim itself is the first letters of three states joined. Kentucky, Illinois, and Missouri spell her name between them. In all of them she was, incredibly, born, the book jokes. Her mother insists she was born in no state. Winthrop Ames first said show boat to Ferber, the dedication owns. Ferber gives the river stage three generations of players.
67215-a-united-states-midshipman-afloat:
A United States Midshipman Afloat is a naval adventure for boys by Lieutenant Commander Yates Stirling, printed at Philadelphia by the Penn Publishing Company in 1908. Ralph Boyer illustrated it. A frontispiece shows a boat heading up to a buoy. The heroes are fresh from Annapolis, their four years' course filling their minds with a store of wisdom.

The contents promise a full cruise. Enemy or friend, under arrest, and a track meet open the tale. The face in the locket and hurried orders bring the secret service in. Prisoners and a terrible predicament lead to a naval engagement. Captain Garcia's strategy and Lazar's cunning fill the middle. A house on La Mesa is defended and assaulted, an accusation follows, and a court martial hears an important witness. Stirling wrote from the service itself, and his midshipmen carry real naval drill into their adventures.
67785-the-cat:
Violet Hunt wrote a life of a cat told by the cat herself, issued in London in 1905 among a set of animal autobiographies. Companion volumes gave the dog, the black bear, and the rat the same treatment. The narrator is Loki, a blue smoke Persian, pictured at the front.

She was born blind, as kittens are, on the twenty-third of April, one of five, three boys and two girls. Her father, Blue Boy the Second, has taken prizes at cat shows all over the country. Chapters cover the nursery, the schoolroom, a first mouse, and a man who hated her. The joke and the charm rest on a cat's cool view of her owners.
67989-the-rambler-club-afloat:
The Rambler Club Afloat is a boys boat tale by Crispin Sheppard, out in nineteen nine. A Penn house of Philadelphia holds that right claim in its front leaves. Sheppard wrote A Knight of the West Side in a past book of his. Part one, The New Club, heads the scheme of the book at front. Dave Brandon, a stout boy, lounges in willow shade by a brook at start.

No school for two months, no dry books, no scold talks, he hymns in joy. Boat days, fish days, and sport of all kinds lie in wait that year. Part names run through the boat, Nat wrath, and a trial trip in rank. Tom cook craft, fix work, camp out, and Hackett shots fill mid parts. Squall, man lost, wreck, and jail scare crowd the late scheme ranks.
6853-betty-gordon-in-washington-or-stran:
Alice Emerson sends Betty Gordon to Washington for strange adventures in a great city, opening with a gored cow and a chipmunk on a fence rail. Betty, lacking a better listener, talks to the saucy little creature staring at her from the old worn fence. Hospitality under difficulties, Bob's great news, a vendue, and consequences follow, with a runaway missed and a belated letter.

Goodbye to Bramble Farm leads to new friends, fellow travelers, a serious mix-up, and the Washington Monument. Libbie grows romantic, Betty investigates, and Bob is cleared at last. Betty Gordon in Washington is a bright, friendly girls' adventure in the capital.
68727-the-emerald-of-catherine-the-great:
Hilaire Belloc's The Emerald of Catherine the Great was published by Harper & Brothers in 1926, with drawings by Chesterton. Belloc gives the book to Maurice Baring, the fourth he has given him, and explains why in a letter at the front. Emeralds are green, and Catherine, he says, founded the fortunes of them all.

Baring had long urged him to write a detective story, since such books sell hugely. Belloc promised he would, on one condition: there must be nothing to find out. Chapter one then opens on William Bones, a stalwart of thirty-five, master of a brig out of Boston in Lincolnshire. Bones traded with the Baltic when George the Third was young, and knew the Russian trade at St Petersburg well.
6879-the-gold-bat:
Wodehouse sets this school tale at a house where cricket pride runs high and a small gold bat trophy stands for honor. Trevor and his mates open the term with a match, and the chapters soon turn to a secret League, warnings left for the boys, and a mayor's statue caught in the mischief. Ferrets, vaults, and night watchers add to the fun as the bat goes missing.

O'Hara takes up the hunt, Renford sees more than he should, and the League is at last unmasked in a dress rehearsal of its tricks. Through house matches, a sprained player, and a vacant place filled, the story keeps its light schoolboy tone, and it ends with the bat found and the plotters known.
69117-the-jumping-kangaroo-and-the-apple:
The Jumping Kangaroo and the Apple Butter Cat is a children's animal book by John Harrington, printed at New York in 1900. Condé drew its pictures. Harrington dedicates the book to his daughter Ruth, for whose entertainment the pages were originally written. A plate shows a carrier pigeon being asked to read aloud.

Chapter One, Jumping Jehosophat, introduces Kerchug the leap frog, who was always jumping. Each morning he stood on the edge of his pond and addressed the birds in the trees above. Yellow Lion and Hedge Hog's scribbling, the Ant's Aunt's picnic, and White Rabbit's cheese scruple follow. The Apple Butter Cat arrives in Chapter Six. Gray Mouse's rich brother, the Church Mouse's circus, and Hoot Owl inventing golf fill the rest. When Carrier Pigeon had gone, Kerchug packed his goods in a red bandana. The book is nonsense-animal fun of the picture-book age.
69158-doomsday-on-ajiat:
Doomsday on Ajiat is a science fiction story by Neil Jones, first printed in Astonishing Stories in October 1942, from his long-running Professor Jameson series. It opens with the professor's strange solution to the problem of lasting forever: not embalming, which only makes caricatures, but a body cast into space, where no change can touch it. He builds a radium-driven rocket to carry his dead body into an orbit sixty-five thousand miles out.

That scheme, laid down in the earlier tales, made Jameson the machine-bodied wanderer of the series, and the Ajiat adventure grows out of his long afterlife among the stars. Jones wrote space fiction of the old school, full of earnest reasoning about atoms, distance, and time. The story keeps the professor's cold logic at its center while the peril turns planetary.
69346-dishes-made-without-meat:
Dishes Made Without Meat is a cook book by Peel, put out at London in nineteen hundred and seven. It stands in a set of small cook books for the home. Her past books are list at the front. They treat the books of the house, the lone hand cook, and the keep of a house. One treats the new home and its dress on a mid purse.

A note at the front sorts the bounds of the book. Fish dishes are not treat of here, it says. They stand in the book of the set made for fish. These small books are made first for homes where time and coin must both be kept in mind. The first words own a growth of taste in the land.
69398-don-sturdy-in-the-tombs-of-gold-or:
Don Sturdy in the Tombs of Gold, a boys’ adventure book by Victor Appleton, was issued at New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1925. Pictures by Walter Rogers go with the tale. The full title promises the old Egyptian’s great secret as the prize of the hunt. A front plate shows a captain calling for rifles to be made ready.

The book belongs to the Don Sturdy series of travel adventures. Companion volumes take the hero to a desert of mystery and across the North Pole. Appleton also wrote the Tom Swift books, as the title page notes. In this volume the trail leads to Egypt and its buried tombs of gold. Boys of the day got danger, travel, and lost treasure in one package. The series form promised a new land in every book.
69400-gay-life-in-paris-how-life-is-enjo:
Gay Life in Paris is a number of the Multum in Parvo Library, dated June 1895 at Boston. The series boasted itself the smallest magazine in the world, at fifty cents a year. Courtney published it from Milk Street. Its subtitle asks how life is enjoyed by the people of that great metropolis.

An illustration shows the Queen of the Mabille, the dance garden. The preface takes up the old proverb, see Naples and die, and the French turn of it: see Paris and pray to live there till the end of the world. Life in the metropolis, it says, differs far from the sober living of American cities. Men and women plunge into the lovely city, a quoted journalist says, as into a bath of pleasure. The little book deals with the women of Paris and its masked balls.
69706-proceedings-of-the-fourth-national:
The Proceedings of the Fourth National Conservation Congress record a meeting held at Indianapolis from October 1 to 4, 1912. A portrait of President Woodrow Wilson fronts the volume, and its motto is the governors' 1908 declaration: let us conserve the foundations of our prosperity. The congress printed its own volume that year.

Sessions open with welcomes from Indiana and the city, a message from the President, and an address by the Secretary of War as his personal representative. Later talks ask what the states are doing, plead for federal protection of migratory birds, and turn to the conservation of man himself. Public health, land frauds, and human life as a national asset fill the middle sessions.
70034-the-stainless-steel-rat:
Harry Harrison wrote The Stainless Steel Rat, printed in Astounding Science Fiction in August 1957 and illustrated by Freas. When the office door opened suddenly, the narrator says, I knew the game was up. A cop walks in as he sits back with a happy grin.

James Bolivar diGriz, the cop begins, I arrest you on the charge. DiGriz was waiting for the word charge. As it lands, he presses a button that fires black powder in the ceiling. The crossbeam buckles and a three-ton safe drops on the cop's head. One crumpled hand twitches beneath it, still pointing, and the muffled voice repeats the arrest. Readers get the first adventure of science fiction's favourite gentleman thief.
70182-tom-swift-and-his-flying-boat:
Victor Appleton wrote a boys' adventure in the Tom Swift series, printed in 1923. A front picture shows the giant flying boat heading in between tall pinnacles of ice. The subtitle names the stakes at once: the castaways of the giant iceberg.

Early chapters give Tom an idea and a fortune, a treasure chest, and the laying of a keel. Trials follow, with bad luck and peril before the boat takes the air. Later chapters cross the Atlantic on the wings of the wind, then reach the giant berg and a desert of ice. The crew lies imprisoned in the ice, wins back to the flying boat, and fights home still crippled. Readers get the series formula at full stretch: invention, daring, and the Arctic, in one fast tale for boys.
70249-uncle-jo-s-old-coat:
Uncle Jo's Old Coat is a children's story by Eleanora Stooke, printed in London by Partridge, with five illustrations. Stooke also wrote Salome's Burden and Mousey. Chapter one is titled Unexpected News, and it breaks at a September breakfast table.

The family belongs to a country doctor, his wife, and their three children: Edwin, eleven, Claude, nine, and Poppy, eight. A letter says the wife's brother is marrying again and asks them to keep his son Freddy, a boy of nine, for a few months. Freddy is the spoiled only child of Marldon Court in Devonshire, motherless since infancy and humoured in every whim. Edwin, who has visited, is not charmed. Contents promise Freddy's arrival, an impulsive act, a kept silence, and a happy Christmas.
70383-combat-lessons-no-1-rank-and-file-:
Combat Lessons Number 1 is an official United States Army booklet of the Second World War, subtitled rank and file in combat: what they are doing and how they do it. It collects short, practical reports from the fighting fronts and prints them for the troops, with a portrait of the Chief of Staff, General Marshall, at the front.

The contents are organised by arm. Infantry lessons cover battle leadership, night attack, knocking out pillboxes and jungle patrolling, drawn from Sicily, Attu and the South Pacific. Sections follow on field artillery, on booby traps and strafing, on the Japanese enemy under the heading Notes on the Nips, and on German tactics as Hints on the Heinie. Named episodes do the teaching: the bazooka worked at Salerno, massed fires, an opportunity lost and a lesson learned. It is doctrine written as front-line anecdote.
7050-the-swoop-or-how-clarence-saved-eng:
Wodehouse's Swoop, or How Clarence Saved England, tells of a great invasion in a spirit of mock patriotism. His preface warns some may think he paints the horrors of invasion in too lurid colors, and that realism in art can go too far. He prefers to trust most readers will acquit him of undue sensationalism, since England must be roused to her peril.

Only a frank account of invasion's probable results, he argues, can do that rousing work. The story, he claims, was written purely from patriotism and duty, though he jokes that a financial success would jar his publisher's sensitive soul and his own. Clarence, the unlikely savior of the title, drives the comic tale.
70622-the-stainless-steel-rat:
Harry Harrison's The Stainless Steel Rat appears here in its book edition, published at New York in this printing of 1970 from the 1961 copyright. Portions first appeared in Astounding in August 1957 and in Analog in April 1960. The novel is dedicated to Hans Stefan Santesson. Chapter one opens as the office door flies open.

James Bolivar diGriz knows the game is up. It had been a money-maker, but it is all over. As the cop walks in, he sits back and puts on a happy grin, noting the somber expression and heavy foot they all have. Readers get the expanded first adventure of the galaxy's slipperiest thief, the magazine caper grown into the book that launched a series.
70739-burning-truths-from-billy-s-bat:
Joseph Pallen compiled Burning Truths from Billy's Bat for the Diamond Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1914. The subject is the conversion of the Reverend Billy Sunday, billed as the world's famous evangelist. Portraits show Sunday, his wife, his pianist, and his choir master.

The contents promise his early life and conversion, then beacon lights on his trail. Anecdotes follow: honor your wife, two pictures of American homes, and kind words to children. A tribute to his wife and a scoring of the smart set come next. Sunday had been a professional baseball player before the pulpit. The bat of the title is his old trade turned sermon.
71913-the-green-hat:
The Green Hat, by Michael Arlen, was published in New York in 1924. Eleven chapters carry the tale, from The Green Hat to The Fall of the Emerald. The last chapter is called St George for England. The narrator names the book for a hat worn by its heroine. A bright green felt hat was the first thing he saw of her. In a way, he says, it was also the last.

He begins on the eve of a move within London. His old rooms sat above a mean lane in Shepherd's Market. He catalogues the lane's wonders: arrests, fights, and a pickpocket who beat a constable. Butlers fought there, and an old nobleman wooed a flower girl. The bright, brittle world of the tale grows from that lane.
72363-launch-the-lifeboat:
Walton, author of Peep Behind the Scenes, wrote Launch the Lifeboat, a poem with illustrations published in London by the Religious Tract Society. Rhodes drew the pictures. The contents page lists the plates like a picture sermon: launching the lifeboat, summer days on the beach, beacon lights, the rocket apparatus, and the rescue.

The plates tell the whole shore story. A bell rings, the crew hastes to the rescue, and a steam tug tows the boat out. Rockets fire, and the life line flies to the wreck. The breeches buoy saves its passenger, and a baby comes ashore in a blanket. One plate shows a rescue by a dog. The poem begins with a boy's memory of August at the sea-side. Sunday-school children got the lifeboat service as a hymn of pictures.
72439-the-road-to-sinharat:
The Road to Sinharat, by Leigh Brackett, appeared in Amazing Stories for May 1963, illustrated by Finlay. Its headnote sets Mars against Earth: the Martians do not want the proffered gift of rich land, much water, and new power, and they fight Rehabilitation.

With them fights Carey, an Earthman who wants only the secret at the end of the road. The story opens at night by the Jekkara Low-Canal, where the town is shut tight and silent, though Carey knows he has not taken a single step unwatched. He knocks at a low door sunk in a thick wall and claims the guest-right in the antique High Martian. Derech, who owes him blood, bars the door behind him.
72607-uncle-wiggily-s-silk-hat:
Howard Garis's picture book gives three stories about Uncle Wiggily, the bunny rabbit gentleman, pictured by Lang Campbell. In the title story the tall silk hat proves both stylish and useful.

Uncle Butter the goat mocks the fancy hat and asks the use of being so stylish. When Susie Littletail's milk runs out of a leaky pail, Uncle Wiggily pours it into his hat instead. He carries the milk home for her with only a little lost. The other stories tell how he brought home company without telling Nurse Jane. A third tells how he tried to make salt water taffy.
72766-the-rambler-club-s-house-boat:
Sheppard's The Rambler Club's House-boat was published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1912, with the author's own drawings. The half-title lists the club's earlier outings: afloat, in winter camp, in the mountains, on Circle T Ranch, among the lumberjacks, at a gold mine, and in an aeroplane. This cruise takes the boys up the Hudson.

The house-boat Gray Gull, Jack Lyons master, is near Yonkers when Bob Somers aids a young man in distress. He had tutored a boy at Nyack and lost the place through no discredit of his own. The Nyack boy joins the trip with enthusiasm, and misunderstandings threaten the cruise for a while. In the end right prevails. Twenty-two chapters run from the engine and all aboard to a battle for the boat, a collision, a midnight tow, and a push-boat.
73346-the-adventures-of-a-black-coat:
A black coat tells its own adventures in a tale printed in Dublin in 1762. The coat was witness to many strange events as it passed through London and Westminster on the backs of varied folk. A Latin line from Horace stands at the front. The preface is kept short, the coat owns, since readers of tales hate long prefaces.

To stir virtue, crush vice, and mock folly is the novelist's business as much as the playwright's, the coat argues. A coat can go where a man cannot boast of going, into closets, taverns, and courts. Passed from owner to owner, pawned, sold, and stolen, it sees high life and low. Its small tale shows Georgian manners with a smile.
73674-space-brat:
Space Brat is a science fiction story by O H Leslie, taken from Fantastic for January 1958. A blurb lays out the alien plan in verse, to conquer man they start with baby and work up. The tale opens in a flat where a baby will not stop crying.

Mr Gertz slaps his forehead and begs his wife Emma for sleep. She says it is only a baby and asks what he expects. He expects a little peace and quiet. Next door the brat cries on. The scene cuts to Athra, chairman of the War Council of Nahrla, on a blood red cushion. His eyeless, plastic face twists with contempt as the council argues. Seven orbits of war planning stand behind the move on Earth. Readers get a sly tale of invasion by cradle.
74010-the-boy-me-and-the-cat:
The Boy, Me and the Cat, subtitled Cruise of the Mascot, 1912 to 1913, is by Henry Plummer. It was copyright 1961 at Rye, New Hampshire, and reached a fourth printing in 1986. A publishers prologue tells how the book was found.

We first heard of it when asked if we had read it, the publishers say. When they said they had not, their questioner shook his head with pity. It is the greatest cruising story ever written, he stated flatly. Their curiosity was piqued. It first appeared in a paper covered, mimeographed edition of a few hundred copies, now prized and scarce. Borrowing one, a yachting editor said, is about as simple as borrowing a man favourite wife. Readers get a legendary sailing narrative of a father, a boy, and a cat.
74535-all-in-the-same-boat:
All in the Same Boat, by Earle and Barbara Reynolds, tells of a family voyage around the world. David McKay published it at New York in 1962 under the subtitle The Forbidden Voyage. The yacht Phoenix carried the family on that long circuit of the seas. For simplicity, the tale is told from the point of view of the skipper.

A dedication speaks to all those men who want to go to sea and never do. Their long suffering wives share that dedication in the front of the book. The rise of the Phoenix opens the contents, with a line on dream and deed. Between a dream and a deed lie the doldrums, that chapter motto observes. Blue water sailing with children aboard fills this family log in book form.
75099-the-red-hot-dollar-and-other-stori:
Umbstaetter's The Red-Hot Dollar and Other Stories gathers tales from The Black Cat, the short-story magazine he ran. Page of Boston issued the book in 1911, with copyrights running back to 1895. Jack London wrote the introduction, and he makes a bold claim for the editor: Umbstaetter made the Black Cat story a kind apart, and made many a writer.
