London says the man saved his own writing life, and perhaps his life outright. Starved, sick, and with all he owned in pawn, London had got nothing back but his own scripts for months. Then a thin letter came holding his tale To the Man on Trail, at ten dollars a thousand words. That sale is the ground of his thanks.
75149-american-boys-afloat:
American Boys Afloat, or Cruising in the Orient, by Oliver Optic, was copyrighted in Boston in 1893 in the All-Over-the-World set. Optic wrote the Army and Navy, Boat-Club, and Lake Shore tales, among many more. He dedicates the book to William Leavitt, a fellow traveler in foreign lands. Chapters follow the Big Four on a yacht cruise.

The tale opens with the Salihe alongside the Guardian-Mother, then plans an outing and weighs the dangers of the voyage. Gibraltar Bay, the Palmones River, and a battle on deck follow. The Big Four are taken prisoner in the cabin, hatch a scheme, and lasso a Scotsman. Smugglers, a Spanish court, and the Rock of Gibraltar fill a brisk tour of the western Mediterranean.
75512-the-life-and-adventures-of-a-cat:
The Life and Adventures of a Cat was printed in London in 1760. The spelling and stops of the day are kept in this copy. Chapter one praises the wisdom of cats above all other beasts. The owl, sacred to Minerva, is mocked as a rival. The ass is dismissed for daring to compete. A cat by the fireside, grave and still, shows true prudence in the writer's eyes.

Old wives, he notes, call cats witches who can foretell the weather. A cat washing her face is said to promise fair days. In her frolics she is said to call up wind. The tale that follows gives the cat a human style life of turns and talk. It is an early beast tale told with dry wit.
76311-the-book-of-the-cat:
The Book of the Cat, a handbook by Frances Simpson, was published by Cassell and Company in 1903. Twelve coloured plates and near three hundred fifty pictures from photographs and drawings fill the volume. A black Persian, painted by Madame Henriette Ronner, stands at the front.

Early chapters trace cats of the past and of the day, then care, housing, and the rules of exhibiting. The points of a cat lead into long sections on Persian cats, colour by colour: black, white, blue, silver, smoke, orange, cream, and tortoiseshell. Notable catteries get a chapter of their own. Manx and Siamese cats, short haired cats, and foreign cats follow. A closing part treats the diseases of cats and their cure.
76440-the-history-of-tabby-a-favourite-c:
The History of Tabby, a Favourite Cat, is a children tale told by a cat. Smyth wrote it; Didier and Tebbett issued it at London in 1809. Tabby relates her own life to her youngest kitten in the frame. She sits in an old tree watching her kitten chase fallen leaves.

Play is over for her; counsel for her children is her task now. As a kitten she chased her own tail for young masters delight in fun. The kitten begs the long promised tale of how she joined the family. Age, gratitude, and household adventure shape the moral animal story here. Juvenile Library readers of 1809 met few books like it then.
76551-alfred-the-great:
Alfred Bowker, mayor of Winchester, gathered a book on Alfred the Great, printed at London in 1899 and given to the Queen by her leave. Many hands wrote the chapters. Walter Besant adds a first word, and a poem by the poet laureate Alfred Austin sings the spotless king.

Frederic Harrison treats Alfred as king. The Bishop of Bristol treats him as a man of faith and a teacher of his people. Charles Oman takes the warrior, and Clements Markham the map maker. John Earle writes on Alfred as a writer, and Frederick Pollock on English law before the Norman conquest. Alfred's own words head the book: he sought to live worthily while he lived.
76815-a-devil-of-a-fellow-and-the-yellow:
A Devil of a Fellow and the Yellow Cat is a tale pair by Wilbur Daniel Steele. It stands as small blue book nine hundred six in the Haldeman line. First right claim bears eighteen by Harper, with a reprint by grant. Va Di, a spoiled Cape sea man, comes back from the dead in tale one. He and Stiff Peter were held lost for more than half a year.

He steps off a fruit ship at Boston in cream duds and a Panama hat. Dark skin, neat face, and black spur whiskers mark his bold look. A cane grace learned at Port au Prince tops his shore strut. Peter bears the new straw case in his old wreck rags at his back. A home note sent ere they land mars the shock of their rise.
76911-good-bye-to-all-that:
Robert Graves wrote Good-Bye to All That, his life story, first printed in nineteen twenty-nine. Graves was a poet who had served as an officer in the Great War. The book carries maps of the trench lines where he fought in nineteen fifteen and sixteen. Photos show brick stacks at Cuinchy, the Somme fields, and Graves in later years.

Graves tells of school, home, and his time with the Second Battalion of the Royal Welch Fusiliers. He shows the front line, the mud, and the cost of the war in plain terms. A court of inquiry, code names, and diary leaves fill out the record. The title bids farewell to the world the war had ended, and to the self he had been in it.
76982-folk-tales-of-sind-and-guzarat:
Folk Tales of Sind and Guzarat was written by C A Kincaid, an officer in the Indian Civil Service, and printed at Karachi in 1925. Most of the pieces first ran in the Daily Gazette or the Times of India. Kincaid says he claims no great merit for them beyond a first touch.

In his preface he hopes the tales will lead others to dig into the rich folk store of Sind, a land most guests see only as heat and dust. Four tales from Guzarat join the Sind set. A verse from Shah Latif stands near the front of the book. Readers get local tales told in English by a man who lived and worked in the region. The book keeps lore that might else have stayed in speech alone.
76985-sally-in-her-fur-coat:
Eliza Orne White wrote Sally in Her Fur Coat, a book about cats published in nineteen twenty-nine. Lisl Hummel made the pictures from scissor-cuts. White had earlier written Brothers in Fur, and she gave this book to two true friends of cats.

A long poem opens the book, praising the keen senses of kittens. Kittens, it says, hear each tiny sound and climb the tallest tree. Even a child, close to the ground, may miss the wonders cats catch. The first tale, The Orphans, tells of two motherless kittens in tiger gray coats. Sally's own races through the garden set the tone.
77133-catherine-the-great:
Katharine Anthony wrote Catherine the Great, a biography published in 1925. The contents begin with a nickname: Fike of Zerbst is born. Fike is the small German princess Sophia, and the chapters educate her, send her to Russia, and rename her.

Fike becomes Catherine, becomes a mother, and takes lovers whose names head the middle chapters: Poniatovsky, Orlov, and Potemkin. Catherine the Great gets a chapter of her own at the center, between the men and the grandmother years. The book opens in Stettin, a grim frontier post of Pomerania, repeatedly devastated by Russian and Prussian marching. Anthony wrote lives of strong women for the general reader, with a plain style and a feminist eye. Her Catherine is neither saint nor monster but an able girl who outplayed an empire. The reign follows in twelve brisk chapters.
77687-jerry-todd-and-the-rose-colored-ca:
Leo Edwards wrote Jerry Todd and the Rose-Colored Cat, held in 1921 and reissued at New York in 1924. Jerry Todd tells the tale in his own voice at the front. A letter from Mrs Kepple starts the fun. She says she will ship her famed rose cat, Lady Victoria, to the boys.

Professor Stoner says at once that no such cat can be. The boys go in a group to the depot to meet the box. What they see in the box gives them a great shock. Folk in Tutter treat the cat woes as a joke. Jerry names his past books and the pals Scoop and Red. The tale is a light boy's romp with a pet at its heart.
78034-in-a-lifeboat:
Jeffery Farnol wrote In a Lifeboat, a short tale with a picture by Rico Tomaso. Farnol was known for The Broad Highway. The tale opens on a becalmed boat under a pitiless sun.

Two men crouch in the boat, watching each other over a still, shrouded form. Trasker, a big sailor, growls that he is parched and in agony. Farrant, the slim man in tweeds, holds the water back by the clock. They may drift for days, and a woman, Miss Wellerby, lies with them. Farrant rules that when they drink, they drink together. Thirst and duty fight it out.
78124-1066-and-all-that:
1066 and All That is a comic history of England by Sellar and Yeatman, illustrated by John Reynolds and published in London by Methuen. Its subtitle promises all the parts you can remember, including 103 good things, five bad kings, and two genuine dates. First printed in 1930, it had been reprinted thirty-four times by the 1951 edition shown here.

The compulsory preface explains the method. Histories, the authors say, were written to exalt their authors. This one aims to console the reader. History is not what you thought; it is what you can remember, and all other history defeats itself. The book grew from years of research in golf clubs, gun rooms, and green rooms. Of four dates first included, two were thrown out as not memorable enough. The result is the schoolroom's revenge: English history as every pupil half-remembers it.
78428-the-tortoiseshell-cat:
The Tortoiseshell Cat is a novel by Naomi Royde-Smith. The hosted text opens with pages of praise from London papers rather than the story itself. Reviewers call the book sunlit in humour, gentle, and shrewd. One paper names it the best novel its critic had read that year. The tale follows a charming girl who is grown in body but still young in mind.

Critics praised the people of the story, above all two leading figures. They found the talk sparkling and the scenes clever and daring. Several papers stress the author's sure, candid touch with life. The novel is set in a world where all strangers are delightful and all events are nice. That quaint, lovely air is part of its design. The praise pages serve as the book's introduction in this edition.
78677-magpie-diplomat:
Magpie Diplomat is a western story by Tuttle, the writer of many tales of Hashknife Hartley and his pard. It is told in dialect by Ike, partner to Magpie Simpkins. The pair stop their jackasses on the road at the sight of three men sitting on a pile of boulders. The near one stands six feet six in his boots, with a face any Roman nosed horse might envy.

The next is built like a bureau, with a tobacco stained mattress of beard. The far one is a runt of five feet, whose redeeming part is his feet, big as a church foundation. Holy mackerel, says Magpie: in Alaska he would call them totem poles, but here they are a sad trio. The three prove to be the mayor of Pinto, his chief of police, and his treasurer.
79156-tomina-in-retreat:
Amy Le Feuvre wrote a tale of a worn-out society girl sent to rest. The Religious Tract Society issued Tomina in Retreat in London. Le Feuvre had written A Daughter of the Sea and The Mender before. Twenty-two chapters run from a doctor's order to a wedding at the close.

Dr Carisbrooke tells Tomina her pace would kill a strong man outright. Shattered nerves and sleepless nights are her harvest, he says plainly. She spurns rest cures and the Riviera alike in her Harley Street talk. Readers gain a gentle tale of quiet, work, and a life rebuilt.
79435-the-brat:
Henry Slesar wrote The Brat, a tale of a mutant child. What a man does not understand he hates, it says. Turesco felt that way about mutants, it adds. So he asked Remington to help destroy the brat. The tale opens as the child comes flying out of a doorway.

A heavy farmer's boot has just missed him at the door. He scrambles down wooden steps and is up in a flash. The farmer follows in a plodding run, waving a blunt shovel. The brat drops under the raised house into shadow and safety. Boots thrash through high grass past his hiding place. Trusting everybody, the farmer shouts inside. He might have been a thief, for all you know, he rages. He was just a little boy who was lost, she answers. Slesar gives a hunted child with a grasshopper near.
79637-what-the-butler-winked-at:
What the Butler Winked At is the life story of Eric Horne, butler. Horne wrote the tale himself after fifty-seven years in service. Thomas Seltzer brought the book out in New York in 1924. He served the nobility and gentry of England through that long span. His foreword owns that names and places stand changed in the telling.

The publishers kept his words just as they came from his pen. Chapter one recalls the big house fifty years before his writing. Matched footmen, swells in copious chairs, and slavey markets fill that world. A well thought out plan of robbery shows the house's dark side. Bread at a shilling a loaf marks his poor but proud parents. He went to work for a printer, then as odd boy to a doctor. Page boy days and a gallon of beer fill his early service years.
8386-ptomaine-street-the-tale-of-warble-:
Carolyn Wells opens this foolish book, as she calls it in her foreword, with a poet's excuse: life is earnest, but some prefer cap and bells. Warble Petticoat, the heroine of Ptomaine Street, leads a tale of nonsense, wordplay, and light satire, in the vein of Wells's popular humorous verse and children's stories. The title itself warns readers not to expect a solemn novel.

Wells, best known for her children's books and mysteries, wrote here for pure fun, and the book's charm lies in its refusal to be serious. Readers looking for a light, old-fashioned comedy of manners and mischief will find it here, best taken as an evening's amusement rather than a literary monument.
a-review-and-exposition-of-the-falsehood: An Elector answers a pamphlet signed A Citizen in this review from Ballston Spa, dated March 1816, addressed to the Republicans of Saratoga County. The pamphlet, generally known as The Book, defended a faction the Elector calls expiring, and he promises detection and exposure of its falsehoods. Comparing its concealment to Iago in the play, he treats contempt and pity as the only fit answers to treachery and detraction.
america-through-the-spectacles-of-an-ori:
Wu Tingfang, a Chinese diplomat who served in Washington, wrote this book of observations on the United States. The introduction supplied with the text describes it as a look at the America of 1914 through an outsider's eyes, on the eve of the First World War. Seventeen chapters, listed in the contents, cover the importance of names, American prosperity, government, education, business methods, and freedom and equality.

Later chapters take up manners, women, costumes, dinners, theaters, opera, circuses, and sports, with two long chapters comparing American and Chinese civilization. Wu praises much and questions some things — he even suggests the title of President might give way to Emperor. The introduction warns of his misunderstandings as well as his insights, and that double view is the book's value.
an-assessment-of-the-consequences-and-pr: The Federal Emergency Management Agency weighs what a huge California quake would do, and how ready the state is, in a report of findings and acts taken. It looks at harm to homes, roads, and lives, and at what aid teams must do first. The report lists steps for towns, firms, and homes, so that a feared quake finds people less unready than before.
betty-gordon-in-washington-or-strange-ad:
Alice B. Emerson's Betty Gordon in Washington sends its heroine from Bramble Farm to strange adventures in a great city. Betty begins by talking to a saucy chipmunk on a fence, sorting grasses and flowers and admiring a vase of heavy old colonial glass.

Chapters follow a gored cow, hospitality under difficulties, Bob's great news, a vendue, a runaway, a belated letter, and new friends on the journey. In Washington itself Betty sees the Monument, investigates a mystery, survives an accident and a rescue, and helps clear Bob's name. The book offers young readers a cheerful blend of country life, city sightseeing and mild detective excitement.
billie-bradley-and-her-inheritance-or-th:
Janet D. Wheeler wrote this first Billie Bradley volume in 1920, launching a girls' series in the Stratemeyer manner. Billie, her brother Chet, and her friends Laura and Violet face an accident, a hundred dollars, and a last hope in the opening chapters. The inheritance of the title is a queer homestead at Cherry Corners, complete with old furniture, weird tales, and ghosts and things.

On the train to Cherry Corners, Violet pushes Mrs. Gilligan ahead of her through the door, first in case of ghosts. Laura chuckles that Vi reminds her of a relative who always pushes her escort in front when she meets a strange dog. Later chapters add a noise in the dark — only a bat — a wrecked aeroplane, and a thrilling discovery of coins and postage stamps. Wheeler writes the haunted-house mystery for girls, with the haunting strictly negotiable.
billy-whiskers-the-autobiography-of-a-go:
Frances Trego Montgomery published this goat's autobiography with Saalfield of Akron in 1902, illustrated by W. H. Fry. Billy narrates his own life from the day Mr. Wagner buys a goat. The contents promise trouble on a rising scale. First the soda fountain and a ducking for the boys in the mill pond. Then a ride in the police patrol wagon, the fire patrol, marriage to Nanny, and a circus career.

In the ring, Billy earns his fame among trained animals. A monkey's tongue is matched only by the parrot's; the two sit and sauce each other by the hour. A bugle calls the procession, and the elephants stand decked in scarlet while Billy cools down from his fuss. Montgomery's week of Billy — what he did from Sunday to Friday — made the goat a durable nursery rogue.
britannica-1911-acrobat:
Acrobat comes from a Greek verb meaning to walk on tiptoe. It first named a rope-dancer. The word now covers a whole trade. Trapeze performers fall under it. So do contortionists, balancers, and tumblers. The 1911 Britannica entry notes the art is ancient. Skilful tight-rope performers existed among the Romans. Their Latin name was funambuli.

Balance is the modern performer's problem. Rope-walkers like Blondin use a long pole. The pole is loaded at both ends. Shifting it lets the walker keep equilibrium. It also lets him recover balance quickly. The entry is brief, but it fixes the essentials. An acrobat earns his living by controlled balance. Height and risk make the skill a spectacle.
britannica-1911-agordat:
Agordat is a town of Eritrea in north-east Africa. It stands on the route between Massawa and Kassala. A strong fort protects the town today. The 1911 Britannica entry is built around one battle. Italian troops under Colonel Arimondi fought there in 1893. On the twenty-first of December they inflicted a severe defeat. Their foes were followers of the khalifa. Readers are sent to the Eritrea and Sudan articles for context.

Few facts crowd the short entry. Route, fort, and battle are its whole substance. Agordat mattered as a point on the Massawa road. Italian colonial power in Eritrea rested on such points. The khalifa's men threatened that hold from Sudan. Arimondi's victory secured the route westward then.
britannica-1911-algae-habitat:
Where an alga can live turns on how much drying it can bear. Habitat, a part of the Algae article, maps that test. Most algae, the brown and red groups above all, pass their whole life cycle sunk in water. Fresh kinds of the green and blue-green groups bend that rule: their seed cells can stand long dry spells and ride far in that state.

The shore between tide marks sets a sterner trial. Scores of sea algae there take air twice a day unharmed, and kinds sort into bands by how much dry time each can stand. Laminaria digitata, the mark of the lowest band, is barely left bare at all. Pelvetia canaliculata, at the top belt, may go days with no wash of water at neap tides. Fine kinds hold their own there by trapping water in their mesh or crouching in the knots of bigger seaweeds.
britannica-1911-animal-heat:
Animal heat is the physiology of body temperature. Higher animals hold inner sources of heat. They also regulate heat production and loss. Their mean temperature stays constant across seasons. That fact proves the regulation exists. Exact data waited for thermometers, though. Local differences appear across the body. Heat production varies by region. Blood circulation evens the internal average out.

Measurement site therefore matters greatly. The rectum best reflects internal temperature. Mouth, armpit, and groin serve more usually. Comparable results require the same situation. Warm-blooded and cold-blooded animals form a key division. The long article develops that contrast in detail. It surveys fever, hibernation, and human heat limits. Boycott and Haldane's work on high temperatures appears. Journal references close this substantial physiology survey. Readers get both theory and measurement practice.
britannica-1911-armstrong-john-diplomat:
John Armstrong is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Carlisle, Pennsylvania, on the twenty fifth of November 1758, he was a soldier, envoy, and public leader of the United States. His father, an Irish born general, had fought in the war for freedom.

The article follows the son's bold and mixed career. As a young major he wrote the famed Newburgh Addresses of 1783, issued with no name attached. He sat in the Senate in the first years of the new century. From 1804 to 1810 he served as envoy to France. In the war of 1812 he rose to secretary of war under President Madison. Blame for the war's course forced him out in 1814.
britannica-1911-baccarat:
Baccarat is a gambling card game of unknown name origin, said to have reached France from Italy under Charles VIII. Two forms are accepted: chemin de fer, the railway game, and banque, played against two tableaus. The entry sets out the chemin de fer rules in full.

Six full packs are shuffled by croupier and players. The banker stakes a sum; punters match it, or one cries Banco to play against the whole bank. Cards come face down, two to punters and two to banker; court cards and tens count nothing, others their pips. A hand of eight or nine ends the play at once. On lower counts, fixed rules govern drawing a third card: six or seven stands, five is the player's choice, and four or less must draw.
britannica-1911-balaghat:
Balaghat is a district of British India. Its name means above the passes, the highlands. It sits in the Nagpur division. The Central Provinces contain it there. Burha town holds its headquarters. Its area covers 3,132 square miles.

The district forms the plateau's eastern portion. That plateau divides the province across. The land was desolate until 1866. Balaghat district formed in that year. Wainganga valley peasants opened the country. Three parts divide it geographically. Southern lowlands are well cultivated plains. The Mau valley runs narrow between hills. A lofty plateau carries the Raigarh Bichhia tract. Hills there reach about 3,000 feet. The Wainganga is the principal river. Population fell 15 per cent in a decade. Famine caused that sharp drop. The 1901 count was 326,521.
britannica-1911-banat:
The Banat is a district in the south-east of Hungary, made up of the counties of Torontál, Temes, and Krasso-Szörény. The word in Hungarian means a frontier province ruled by a ban, much like the German Mark. Hungary once had several banats, in Dalmatia, Slavonia, Bosnia, and Croatia, lost during the Turkish wars.

Used alone, the name means the Temesvár banat, which oddly took the title after the peace of Passarowitz in 1718 though no ban ever ruled it. The 1911 Britannica entry bounds it by the Transylvanian Alps, the Danube, the Theiss, and the Maros, at 11,260 square miles. Mountains fill the south, flat marshy ground the north and west, and the soil ranks among Hungary's most fertile.
britannica-1911-bandicoot-rat:
Bandicoot-rat is the Anglo-Indian name for a large rat, Nesocia bandicota, found in India and Ceylon. The body measures twelve to fifteen inches to the root of the tail, and the tail itself runs eleven to thirteen inches more. The name is said to be a corruption of the Telugu pandi-koku.

The animal parts from common rats of the genus Mus in its broader front teeth and in the blunter cusps on its molars. Other kinds of the genus range from Palestine to Formosa and across central Asia. The 1911 Britannica entry says the typical kind haunts villages, towns, and farmed ground all over India and Ceylon, and is most common in the south of the peninsula.
britannica-1911-barlaam-and-josaphat:
Barlaam and Josaphat is one of the most popular religious romances of the middle ages, spread across the whole medieval world. Its importance, the entry states plainly, is that it is a Christianized version of the story of Gautama Siddhartha, the Buddha, matching it not only in broad outline but in essential details.

In the Greek form, traced among the works of John of Damascus in the early 700s, St Thomas has converted India, then a pagan king, Abenner, persecutes the Christians and their ascetics. His long-desired son Josaphat is born, and astrologers foretell the boy glory beyond all his forefathers. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, unfolds the tale of the prince, the hermit Barlaam, and the faith that follows.
britannica-1911-bertat:
Bertat is the name of a people of the Shangalla group, living by farming. They occupy the valleys of the Yabus and Tumat rivers. Both streams feed the Blue Nile. The 1911 Britannica entry describes their dress, marks, and homes in plain terms. Their huts are round, with floors raised on short poles. Salt blocks serve as their favourite currency. Gold washing is also practised among them.

Their weapons include the spear, throwing-club, sword, and dagger. The kulbeda, a throwing-knife, is also named. Nature worship still held out against Islam when the entry was written. The Bertat numbered about 80,000 around 1880. Dervish rule from 1884 to 1898 nearly destroyed them, the entry states. Arab settlements among them kept their own sheiks.
britannica-1911-buckwheat:
Buckwheat is the seed-like fruit of Fagopyrum esculentum. The plant is a herb, native to central Asia. This 1911 Britannica article describes the crop and its uses. The fruit has a dark brown, tough rind. It is three-sided, with sharp angles. Its shape recalls beech mast. The German name Buchweizen, beech-wheat, comes from that likeness.

In Britain buckwheat feeds pheasants and poultry only. Elsewhere it is a food for people. Northern Europe bakes it into thin cakes. Dutch children eat its meal as crumpets. Russian soldiers get buckwheat groats in their rations. In the United States, buckwheat cakes are a national dish. Hindus eat it on fast days as a lawful food. The article compares its food value with true cereals. It is poor in nitrogen and in fat. Still, it grows fast on poor land. Bees love its flowers, and Russia gathers much honey from it.
britannica-1911-carat:
The carat is a small weight used for gems and gold. This 1911 Britannica entry explains the measure and its history. The word comes from an Arabic term for a weight of four grains. Behind it stands a Greek word for the carob fruit. The carat began as a seed used as a weight. Its exact weight now varies a little from place to place.

In 1877 jewellers of three cities fixed a standard. London, Paris and Amsterdam set it at 205 milligrammes. That equals 3.163 troy grains by the entry's reckoning. The South African carat is slightly heavier, at 3.174 grains. Gold fineness is also measured in carats. Pure gold counts as 24 carats in that scale. Two parts of alloy in the mix make 22-carat gold. The entry gives both uses of the one word.
britannica-1911-cattegat: Cattegat, also spelled Kattegat, is named in a 1911 Britannica article as a strait between Sweden and Denmark. The Scandinavian name means cat's-throat. The strait forms part of the link between the Baltic Sea and the North Sea. It runs north and south. To the north it joins the Skagerrack. To the south it joins the Baltic through the Sound, the Great Belt, and the Little Belt. Its length is about a hundred and fifty miles. Its greatest breadth is about ninety miles.
britannica-1911-cherat:
Cherat is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a hill cantonment and sanatorium in the Peshawar district of India's North West Frontier Province. It stands 34 miles south east of Peshawar. Its elevation is 4500 feet. It sits west of the Khattak range, which divides the Peshawar district from the Kohat district. Height and air are the whole reason for the place.

Cherat was first used in 1861. Since then it has served in the hot weather as a health station for the British troops of Peshawar. The vale below is hot and malarious, so the men were sent up to Cherat to recover and to escape the worst season. The entry is short. It gives the site, the height, the range, the date of first use, and the purpose. A few facts fix a mountain refuge built into the routine of a frontier garrison.
britannica-1911-cinq-mars-d-effiat:
Henri Coiffier Ruzé d'Effiat, marquis de Cinq-Mars (1620-1642), was a French courtier destroyed by a plot against Richelieu, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells his story. He was the second son of a marshal of France. Richelieu brought him to the court of Louis the Thirteenth. His good looks and easy manners soon made him a favourite of the king.

He rose fast, becoming master of the wardrobe and then master of the horse. After standing out at the siege of Arras in 1640, he asked for a high command in the army. Richelieu blocked the claim, and the favourite began to talk wildly of bringing the minister down. In 1642 he formed a plot with the duke of Bouillon and others, under the nominal lead of the king's brother Gaston, to overthrow Richelieu.
britannica-1911-cleat:
Cleat is a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a plain piece of ship gear and the word behind it. The word runs through many tongues of the Teutonic group in the sense of a wedge or lump. It sits close to the English words clod and clot.

The article gives the main uses in turn. On ships, a cleat is a wedge shaped piece of wood fixed to masts and other spots. It stops a rope or collar from slipping, or serves as a step. A horned piece of wood or metal serves for tying off ropes. A further wedge guards a ship's side in a launch cradle or dry dock. Miners use the word for the upright split planes in coal.
britannica-1911-cole-vicat:
Vicat Cole, who lived from 1833 to 1893, was an English painter of country scenes. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Portsmouth on the seventeenth of April 1833. His father, George Cole, painted scenes of the same kind. The son took the same path with marked success. He showed work at the British Institution at the age of nineteen. His first Royal Academy show came in 1853.

Cole joined the Academy as an associate in 1870 and as a full member ten years later. The article gives two grounds for his wide fame. His brush work was plain and direct, and he chose fair and pleasing scenes. Most of his subjects lay in Surrey and Sussex or on the banks of the Thames. His large Pool of London was bought in 1888 and hangs in the Tate Gallery.
britannica-1911-commissariat: Commissariat is the part of an army charged with the supply of food and forage for the troops. Its work does not cover war stores such as shot and shell, which lie outside its charge. In almost every army, the same body of troops handles both the move of goods and their supply. The term thus names a supply arm, not a fighting arm, and its scope is set by food, forage, transport, and the men who run them.
britannica-1911-conduction-of-heat:
Conduction of heat is the passing of heat by contact, from body to body or between parts of one body. Fourier and other men built its maths early in the 1800s. They brought that maths to such a height that little was left to add. For a time, theory of heat meant that maths and little else. The entry sets that maths aside on purpose.

Fresh tests showed its base to be too simple. It took the rates of conduction and emission as fixed. Real matter does not hold those rates steady. The article thus turns to new lab work. It treats the snags of measurement and the means to beat them. One stress falls on spread rate, called diffusivity in the text. Odd cases show that rate shifting in ways the old maths did not catch.
britannica-1911-cravat:
A cravat is a form of scarf or neckcloth that takes its name from the Croats. The word runs through French, where cravate is a corruption of Croat. Frenchmen of the reign of Louis XIV gave the name to the scarf of the Croatian soldiers. Those men served in the royal Croatian regiment of the French army. Their scarf was made of linen or muslin with broad lace edges.

That scarf caught the fancy of the court and town at once. The name then spread to neckcloths of many forms in England and France alike. One form hung in long, loose lace ends. Men called it a Steinkirk, from the battle of that name in 1692. A late form was folded with great care and lightly starched. Beau Brummell set that style in his day. Linen or cambric formed its stuff in that age.
britannica-1911-cross-roads-burial-at:
Burial at cross-roads was the former way of disposing of executed criminals and suicides. A rude cross usually stood at such a crossing. That sight fed a belief that cross-roads were chosen as the next best ground to a churchyard. The entry gives a deeper reason. The ancient Teutonic peoples often built their altars at cross-roads, and human sacrifices, above all of criminals, formed part of the rite there.

Such spots thus came to be seen as execution grounds. After Christianity arrived, criminals and suicides were buried at cross-roads by night, to keep their funerals close to the pagan pattern. The famous Tyburn in London serves as the entry's example. It stood where the Oxford, Edgware, and London roads met. A gallows ground at a road junction thus closes a custom that joined altar, sacrifice, and dishonoured burial in one place.
britannica-1911-epee-de-combat:
Épée-de-Combat is the duelling sword still used in France, and in blunted form for fencing practice everywhere, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes. Its blade runs about 35 inches, sharp at the point but with no cutting edge. A bowl-shaped guard turns its round side toward the point.

The épée is the modern form of the small-sword, the light dress sword gentlemen wore through the 1700s, far shorter and lighter than the old rapier. Fencing long went on with bare faces, since wire masks came only near 1780 and spread slowly. To spare the eyes, strict custom kept points low and counted hits on the breast alone. That made practice unreal, and more than one fine fencer died in a true duel by the habit. The article holds that the base of modern foil work was laid with the épée alone.
britannica-1911-escheat:
Escheat is a term of English law for the fall of lands back to the next lord when heirs fail. The word comes from Old French roots that mean to fall to one's share. When a tenant of an estate in fee simple dies with no sale or will, and with no heirs, his lands escheat. They fall to the lord from whom he held them.

That rule is made clear by the thought of a freehold estate as a stake in land held from some lord. The king stands as lord paramount over all. The man who grants the estate keeps a stake in the land like that of a man who grants it for a life term. When the life term ends, the land falls back to him.
britannica-1911-etretat:
Étretat, a French watering place in the department of Seine-Inférieure, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the coast of the English Channel, on the road north of Havre. The count in 1906 was 1982 people. Fine cliffs frame the town on both sides.

The sea has worn archways, pinnacles, and other odd forms in those cliffs. A small stream runs under ground for part of its course and rises on the beach. A Roman road, an aqueduct, and other old remains have been found there. The church of Notre-Dame has an eleventh century nave in the Romanesque style. Fishing goes on without a port, and old hulks serve as sheds and even homes.
britannica-1911-fat:
Fat names oily solids found in animals and plants at ordinary temperatures. Chemically, fats are glyceryl esters of fatty acids, chiefly stearic, palmitic and oleic, and they contain no nitrogen. In animals, fat forms part of living tissue and gathers in connective tissue under the skin, in the abdomen and between muscles. In plants, it occurs mainly in seeds and fruits, and sometimes in roots.

Fats resemble the fixed oils in chemistry, but oils are liquid where fats stay solid. Every fat has some industrial use. The fats of sheep, cattle and calves matter most, taken from bones and skins in glue making. They supply the raw material for the soap, candle and glycerin trades.
britannica-1911-flat:
Flat comes from an old Teutonic word for the ground beneath the feet. As an adjective it means level in surface, and by transfer fallen, dull or downright, or in music below the true pitch. As a noun in geography it names a level tract. Its chief modern use is for a self-contained dwelling. That is a suite of rooms forming part of a larger tenement house. It is reached by a hall and stair shared with other residents.

England had much special law on flats, and the entry sets out its main points. Occupants are tenants, not lodgers. An upper owner's right to support from the lower storey, duties for stairs and common parts, and what happens to rent when fire destroys a flat all get attention. The American term apartment-house, the Scots flatted house, and French code rules on divided storeys round out the survey.
britannica-1911-float:
Float is the subject of a word entry in the 1911 Britannica. The entry traces the word to old English and Teutonic roots. Those roots link it to flow and to fleet. At its core the word means to move on water. It can also mean to move through the air. The same word names a wave or a flood tide. It names things that rest on water as well.

Long lists of uses fill the rest of the entry. A float can be a raft or a flat boat. In fishing it is the cork that holds a baited line. In tanks it is the ball that gauges the water line. Stage footlights and wheel boards bear the name too. In mines and looms the word has trade senses. In the United States a voter with no fixed party was called a float.
britannica-1911-ghat: Ghat is a short place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry calls Ghat an oasis and town in the Turkish vilayet of Tripoli. It names the place a key hub of the caravan trade of the desert. That trade linked the Nigerian states with the seaports of the Mediterranean Sea. The entry sends readers to the article on Tripoli for the wider tale of that trade.
britannica-1911-goat:
The goat is the subject of an animal entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is a common Teutonic word, linked to the Latin word for a kid. It properly names the well known domestic European animal. In lore the goat stood as a sign of evil, set against the sheep as a sign of purity.

The entry notes how hard goats and sheep are to tell apart as groups. In both wild and tame forms there is an almost full scale from one to the other. That makes a clean definition of either group hard to give. The text then sets out where the goat group sits among its kin.
britannica-1911-groat:
The groat, its name adapted from the Dutch groot, meaning great or thick, was a name used from the 13th century on the European continent for any large or thick coin. It was almost always a silver coin, though its value varied widely between countries and periods. Scotland and Ireland struck their own versions in imitation.

The English groat was first coined in 1351 at a value somewhat above a penny. Steady debasement of both penny and groat left it finally worth four pennies. Issue stopped after 1662, a fourpenny piece returned in 1836 without any official name but groat in common speech, and that too was discontinued in 1856. David II struck the Scottish groat in 1358, and Edward IV the Irish one in 1460.
britannica-1911-herat:
Herat is a city and province of Afghanistan, set at 2,500 ft. above sea-level, with about 10,000 people. Great routes radiate from it: the Russian railway ends 66 m. north, Kandahar lies 360 m. to the south-east, and Kabul 550 m. east. Roads west lead into Persia. Its old trade importance is gone, but its weight in history and strategy is stressed.

The city forms a rough square of about 1,600 by 1,500 yards. Its main defence is a huge earthwork, some 250 ft. wide at the base and 50 ft. high. A wall 25 ft. high with about 150 towers crowns it, fronted by a ditch. Inside the north face stands the Ark, a citadel of sun-dried brick on a high mound. Royal engineers with the Boundary Commission in 1885 found the works in poor repair, the ditch choked and the gates unguarded. In 1863 Herat was brought into the Afghan monarchy by Dost Mahomed Khan.
britannica-1911-jehoshaphat:
Jehoshaphat, son of Asa and king of Judah in the ninth century before Christ, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. His name in Hebrew means Yahweh judges. In his time Israel and Judah stood in close relations. The two royal houses were joined by marriage. They also undertook joint ventures in war and in trade.

Jehoshaphat aided Ahab against Benhadad at Ramoth-Gilead, where Ahab was slain. His fleet joined in trading voyages toward Ophir. The article weighs the chronicler's account of his war against Moab, Ammon, and Edom. It traces that tale to an older tradition behind the earlier source. A disaster to the ships at Ezion-Geber came before the great revolt under his son. His legal measures are also noted. A closing part treats the valley that bears his name.
britannica-1911-jurat:
Jurat, from the medieval Latin juratus, one sworn, is a name for the sworn holders of certain offices. Under the old order in France, the jurats of towns in the southwest, such as Rochelle and Bordeaux, were members of the town body. The title was also borne by officers like aldermen in the Cinque Ports.

The word now lives chiefly in the Channel Islands. Jersey and the bailiwick of Guernsey each have a body of twelve jurats. They are chosen for life, in Jersey by the ratepayers and in Guernsey by the elective states. With the bailiff as their judge they form the royal court, and they sit as part of the law making bodies. In English law the same word names a part of an affidavit. That part gives the names of those who swear it, the person before whom it was sworn, and the date and place.
britannica-1911-kalat:
Kalat is the capital of Baluchistan, set at 29° 2′ north and 66° 35′ east, about 6780 feet above the sea and 88 miles from Quetta. The town gives its name to a native state which, with Makran and Kharan, covered 71,593 square miles and held 470,336 people in 1901. The word Kalat comes from kala, a fortress, and the town is held the most scenic fortress in the Baluch highlands.

It crowns a low hill, with the close built mass of flat roofed mud houses round its base. A citadel with a strong face rules the town and holds the palace of the khan within its walls. In an upper room of that palace Mehrab Khan, ruler of Baluchistan, was killed when British troops stormed the place at the close of the first Afghan War in 1839. The town itself held only 2000 people in 1901. The valleys round it are well tilled and thickly peopled.
britannica-1911-la-ciotat:
La Ciotat is a coast town of south-eastern France, in the department of Bouches-du-Rhône. It stands on the west shore of the Bay of La Ciotat, 26 miles S.E. of Marseilles by rail. In 1906 it held 10,562 people. Its port is easy to reach and well sheltered.

The great shipbuilding yards and repair docks of the Messageries Maritimes Company employ between 2000 and 3000 workmen. Fishing and a lively coasting trade go on, and the town is visited for sea-bathing. In ancient times La Ciotat was the port of the neighbouring town of Citharista, now the village of Ceyreste.
britannica-1911-maximilian-i-the-great:
Maximilian the First, called the Great, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Maximilian was elector and duke of Bavaria, born at Munich in 1573. The Jesuits educated him at the university of Ingolstadt. He began to share in government in 1591, while still a youth.

In 1597 his father's abdication made him duke of Bavaria. For ten years he kept clear of wider German politics. In 1607 he was charged with enforcing the imperial ban on Donauworth. That free city was a Protestant stronghold, and his troops occupied it in December. Stern steps followed to restore the older faith there. Alarmed Protestant princes formed a union in reply. A Catholic league answered it in 1609, and the entry shows the lines of a great conflict being drawn.
britannica-1911-meat:
Meat is a word first used for food in general. It is so still used in the phrase meat and drink. Now, save as an old use, it means the flesh of tame beasts slain for food. That is butchers meat. It is set apart from game, the flesh of wild beasts, and from fish and fowl.

The 1911 Britannica entry traces the word through kin tongues of the north. Its far root is in dispute. A great word book holds it most likely tied to a root that means to be fat. That root is seen in words of the east, and in a Latin verb for to be wet. The piece is a short signpost. It sends readers to heads on food, health law, and farming for the full tale.
britannica-1911-moffat:
Moffat is a small burgh in Upper Annandale in Scotland, described in a 1911 Britannica town entry. It had just over two thousand people in 1901 and sits north of Dumfries on the road. A branch rail line ends here, two miles from the main line at Beattock. The town has been famed since the mid 1700s for its sulphur and salt springs.

Guests come for the spa waters and for rest in fine hill country near the town. Hills rise close by, from Gallow Hill to the high peak of Hartfell. Streams such as the Annan and the Evan add to the charm of the vale. The burgh bought the main spa in 1898 for town control.
britannica-1911-mole-rat:
Mole-rat is the name of a group of blind burrowing rodents, covered in this 1911 Britannica article. The type is the large grey Spalax typhlus of eastern Europe and Egypt, of the Old World family Spalacidae. All mole-rats of the genus Spalax lack a clear neck, and have small or unformed ears and eyes and short limbs with strong digging claws.

Their flat heads, with tiny eyes covered by skin, wart-like ears, and a stub of a tail, make them easy to know. They burrow in sandy soil and feed on bulbs and roots. The article sets them beside the bamboo-rats of India, Burma, and East Africa. Those differ in having eyes not covered by skin, short ears, and a short tail with sparse hair, and they burrow among tall grass or at the roots of trees.
britannica-1911-morat:
Morat, a small Swiss town on the east shore of the Lake of Morat, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the canton of Fribourg, 14 miles north of the town of Fribourg. In 1900 it held 2,263 souls, most of them German in speech. Old walls with watch towers still ring the town, and a castle looks down on it.

The town was a free town of the empire from 1218, then passed to Savoy in 1264. Swiss troops took it in 1475 in their war with Charles the Bold of Burgundy. Charles laid siege to it in 1476 but was crushed by the Swiss host on the 22nd of June. Bern and Fribourg then ruled it in joint form until 1798.
britannica-1911-nagyszombat: Nagyszombat, called Tyrnau in German, is a town of Hungary in the county of Pozsony, on the Trnava river. Its people numbered twelve thousand four hundred twenty two in nineteen hundred. The town has played a large role in the church history of Hungary. It rose after fifteen forty three, when the archbishop of Esztergom made it his home. Churches and convents were built, and the town won the name Little Rome. A university founded there in sixteen thirty five later moved to Budapest.
britannica-1911-paine-robert-treat:
Robert Treat Paine was an American leader who lived from seventeen thirty-one to eighteen fourteen. He was born in Boston and went to Harvard. He joined the bar and led the case against the troops in the Boston Massacre trial. He signed the great pledge of freedom from Britain.

The entry lists his posts year by year. He sat in state and national groups, helped frame the state frame of rule, and served as chief law officer. He then sat as a judge on the high court for fourteen years. A short close deals with his son, a poet whose songs were once well known.
britannica-1911-palghat: Palghat, a town of British India in the Malabar district of Madras, is described in this short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on the Madras railway, and its people numbered 44,177 in 1901. As the key to Travancore and Malabar from the east, it once held great strategic weight. Its fort fell into British hands in 1768 and later served as a base for operations against Tippoo. The Palghat Pass gives the great route from the west coast to the interior. The municipality runs the Victoria college.
britannica-1911-peat:
Peat is a mass of decayed plant matter found in bogs round the world. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica links the word to old Celtic terms for a portion. Europe alone was thought to hold vast tracts of bog land. Reeds, rushes, sedges, and mosses form most of the source growth.

Still water in hollows lets plant tissue break down and sink. Lower layers are pressed and darkened over long time spans. Cool, wet air favors the process above all else, it says. Peat ranges from pale fibrous stuff to dense dark matter like clay. It holds much water and must be dried before use as fuel.
britannica-1911-rabat:
Rabat, a city on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It stands at the mouth of the Bu Ragrag River, which splits it from Salli on the far bank. Its people number near twenty six to thirty thousand. The town sits on a rock shelf ringed by stout but worn walls.

A plain square tower, left unfinished, is the chief mark seen from the sea. It rises 145 feet on a height west of the walled town. A bar at the river mouth makes shipping hard and slows trade growth. Rabat trades with Fez, the coast towns, and ports in Europe. It is called the greatest work center in Morocco. It was founded in 1184.
britannica-1911-rat:
Rat is a beast entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It deals with the larger kinds of the mouse clan found in Britain. Two kinds hold the name in its strict sense in that land. One is the black rat, and the other is the brown or Norway rat.

The entry warns that no sharp line parts rats from mice in loose speech. In that loose use rats are just the larger mice of the clan. Tail scale rows give one rough test to tell the two apart. Rats bear more rows of scales on the tail than true mice do. Full marks of the clan are left to a long entry on gnawing beasts.
britannica-1911-surat:
Surat is a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a city and district in British India, in the Bombay region. The city holds a famed place in the tale of empire. It is the site where the English first set up a trading post on the mainland of India.

The article dates the modern city to the close of the 1400s. Under the great Mogul kings it rose to be the chief trading city of India. In 1612 English sea captains broke the sea power of Portugal off its coast. Surat then became the seat of an English presidency. Its trade was dealt a fatal blow when Bombay passed to the Company in 1668. The city count fell from a peak guess of 800,000 to 80,000. By 1901 it had climbed back to 119,306.
britannica-1911-symond-s-yat:
Symond Yat is a famed viewpoint on the river Wye in England, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It stands nine miles above Monmouth and twelve miles below Ross by water. At that point the Wye makes a sweep of near five miles round a peninsula. The neck of that loop is just some 600 yards across at its narrowest.

The peninsula is the limestone rise of Huntsham Hill, with caverns in the limestone on both steep banks. The Yat, or Gate, sits on the west side of the neck at over 500 feet. A road drops from the east to a ferry that was of early weight as a highway between England and Wales. The border of Herefordshire and Gloucestershire crosses the neck at that point. Groups of cottages and inns stand on both banks, with the hamlet of New Weir across from the Yat itself.
britannica-1911-tiger-cat: Tiger-cat is a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a wild cat of America. In its strict sense it names a small spotted kind that ranges from Mexico to Paraguay, east of the Andes. Head and body run to just over thirty inches, and the tail makes a third of that. Its fur is a grizzled grey with black spots that form no chains. The name is also used for the ocelot, and in loose use for any small spotted wild cat.
britannica-1911-turner-nat:
Nat Turner, who lived from 1800 to 1831, led a slave rising in Virginia known as the Southampton Insurrection. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his story in a short life. Born in Southampton County, he claimed from childhood to see visions and hear voices. He became a Baptist preacher with great sway among the enslaved.

In 1828 Turner told a few companions that a voice from heaven had said the last shall be first, read as a sign that the slaves should rule. A solar eclipse and strange skies in 1831 were taken as the signal. On the night of the twenty first of August, Turner and seven companions entered his master's house and killed those inside. The band grew to about sixty and struck house after house. White forces scattered them by noon the next day, after fifty five people had been killed.
britannica-1911-tyler-wat:
Wat Tyler, an English rebel who died in 1381, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a man of obscure birth, from Kent or from Essex. Tyler is a trade name, for a tiler, and not a true surname. Froissart says he had served as a soldier in the French war. Hard times for farm hands and poor town craftsmen lay behind his rise.

Want had grown since the Black Death, and the Statute of Labourers of 1351 bore hard on the poor. A poll tax laid in 1379 and again in 1381 brought the anger to a head. Riots broke out in Essex in late May 1381 and in Kent in early June. A mob seized Rochester castle and marched to Maidstone, where the rebels chose Tyler as their leader. In the next days the rising spread over Kent, with much theft and harm to goods.
britannica-1911-wheat:
Wheat is a botany article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, with a labelled figure of the plant. The entry calls wheat the most important and most widely spread of the cereal grasses. It is a yearly plant with hollow, upright, jointed stems. From its base it sends out extra roots and extra shoots, called tillers.

The article describes each part in turn. Each leaf has a long sheath that wraps the stem, with a small white growth where blade meets sheath. The ear stands on a central stalk bent in a zigzag, forming notches. A flattened spikelet grows from each notch, pressed against the stalk. At the base of each spikelet sit two empty boat shaped scales, the glumes. Such detail suits a reader who wants to know the plant's build.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfred-the-gr:
Alfred the Great, also Ælfred, King of the West Saxons, was born at Wantage in 849 and died in 899. Fifth son of Ethelwulf of Wessex and Osburh of the Jutes of Wight, he went to Rome at four. Legend, without foundation, has him anointed king by Leo IV, though his 855 pilgrimage with his father, in Asser, is authentic. After Ethelbald, Ethelbert, and Ethelred ruled in turn from 858, Alfred took the throne in 871 amid the Danish war, buying peace that year.

Peace held a few years, then Danes attacked again in 875, 876, and 877. After fifteen peaceful years a 903 onslaught lasted four. He gathered what seemed good in old English laws, daring to add little of his own, and encouraged learning, translating the Consolation of Philosophy into Anglo-Saxon himself. Popular fancy credits him with more than his military record, but lawgiver and scholar stand beside warrior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anne-madelein:
Anne-Madeleine Remuzat, born at Marseilles in 1696, died in 1730. At nine she entered the Visitation convent. From 1708 she bore sufferings patiently for souls. Withdrawn in 1709, she re-entered and professed in 1713. She applied herself to prayer, and her Spiritual Retreat proves it. In 1713 she experienced a revelation of Jesus concerning his Sacred Heart's glory. As her sanctity became known, many consulted her.

She suffered keenly, inflicting mortifications on her body in reparation. When superiors interdicted these austerities, she begged our Lord to mortify her himself, and she went into a painful decline, her soul abandoned to temptations. In 1720, during the Marseilles plague, Our Lord enjoined a Sacred Heart feast, which Mgr de Belsunce established that October. From 1722 Sacred Heart veneration spread through Provence, Lyons, Rouen, Constantinople, Cairo, Spain, Louisiana, Persia, Syria, and the Indies. In 1888 her cause was submitted, favourably voted in 1890, and Leo XIII signed its introduction in 1891.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-and-g:
Father and son share this entry, two French churchmen separated by a generation. Antoine Duprat, born at Issoire in 1463, rose from law to become chancellor of France under Francis the First, then archbishop of Sens and cardinal. Guillaume, his son, became bishop of Clermont in 1529 and carried the family name into the age of the Council of Trent.

Antoine used royal power to curb great lords, rebuild royal finances, and sign the Concordat of 1516 with Rome. Guillaume backed the Council of Trent and welcomed Jesuits into his diocese, helping them found the College of Clermont in Paris despite strong opposition. Together the two lives show how one family shaped church and state in France through the Reformation century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnaud-d-ossa:
French cardinal, diplomat, and writer Arnaud d'Ossat, born at Larroque-Magnoac in Gascony on 20 July 1537 and dead at Rome on 13 March 1604, was a blacksmith's son. Sent to Auch's college as tutor to a nobleman's sons, then to Paris, he became pupil and friend of the famous Ramus. He defended Ramus in two tracts against Charpentier, rector of the university. He studied law at Bourges under Cujas and turned advocate before the Paris parliament, tutoring Jean de la Barrière, future reformer of the Feuillants.

In 1572 d'Ossat joined the retinue of Paul de Foix, archbishop designate of Toulouse, accompanying him to Rome. When de Foix died in 1584, d'Ossat stayed at Rome, running the French embassy for a year, then serving Cardinals d'Este and Joyeuse. In 1588 he refused Henry III's offer of foreign minister, and later, driven from Rome by broken ties, he pressed on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aurora-lucis-:
Aurora Lucis Rutilat is one of the Ambrosian hymns, though its author is unknown. It has been revised and split into three hymns for the Roman Breviary, the prayer book of the daily office. The first sixteen lines form the hymn for Lauds, morning prayer, from Low Sunday to the Ascension, beginning in revised form as Aurora Caelum Purpurat. Many English versions circulate among Protestants, and Dr J. M. Neale's rendering opens with the line about dawn purpling the east with light.

Lines seventeen to thirty-two form Tristes Erant Apostoli, sung in the Common of Apostles and Evangelists in paschal time at Vespers and Matins. The rest of the ancient hymn forms Paschale Mundo Gaudium, the Lauds hymn for the same Common. Its Gregorian melody runs in the third mode and appears in the Vesperale Romanum. Other English versions include Johnston's, Caswall's, and Chambers's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ballarat:
Ballarat is a suffragan diocese of Melbourne, covering western Victoria from the Murray River to the Southern Ocean. Victoria was first permanently colonized in 1835, and Ballarat's rich pastures were taken up in 1838. On 29 June 1851, Irish miner James W. Esmond found Victoria's first profitable goldfield at Clunes. Rich gold followed at Ballarat that August, and forty thousand people soon camped on the field.

Ballarat swiftly became the world's richest goldfield, drawing a great rush of population. The diocese grew with the colony, and even its remote corners gained resident priests and schools. By March 1907 it counted twenty-nine districts, 145 churches, and 59,488 Catholics. Its clergy numbered sixty-two secular and ten regular priests, with seventeen brothers and 230 nuns. Catholic schools then taught 4,900 children across fifty-seven primary schools and other institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barlaam-and-j:
Barlaam and Josaphat are the heroes of a legend beloved by medieval writers. In India, converted by St Thomas, King Abenner persecuted the Church in the third or fourth century. Astrologers foretold that his son Josaphat would become Christian, so the prince was kept in close confinement. Yet Barlaam, a hermit of Senaar, reached him and brought him to the true Faith.

Abenner failed to pervert his son, shared the government with him, then himself became Christian and abdicated as a hermit. Josaphat later resigned, found Barlaam in the desert, and spent his remaining years in holiness with him. The tale is a Christianized version of a Buddha legend: Josaphat corrupts Joasaph, from middle Persian Budasif, meaning Bodhisattva. It spread through nearly every European language and into Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Armenian, and Hebrew versions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-freder:
Claude-Frederic Bastiat, a French economist, was born at Mugron on 29 June 1801 and died at Rome on 24 December 1850. Pierre Bastiat's son, whose father founded a Bayonne business house. It prospered under the franchise the Treaty of Versailles gave that port, then declined under the Empire's prohibitory regime. The contrast shaped his free-trade opinions. Orphaned at nine and raised by his grandfather, he worked in the Bayonne business. He returned to Mugron in 1825 on inheriting an estate.

After the Revolution of 1830 he became Mugron's justice of the peace and championed commercial liberty. He joined Cobden's free-trade movement in England. An 1844 article in the Journal des Economistes made his fame, followed by Economic Sophisms and pamphlets, including the candle merchants' petition against the sun. Elected to the assemblies of 1848, he fought socialism in treatises on property, capital, and protectionism. His Economic Harmonies appeared in 1849.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concordat:
This long entry defines a concordat as an agreement, or union of wills, between Church and State. Canonists and publicists dispute its exact nature, so the entry premises only a nominal definition. A concordat stands as a law, ecclesiastical and civil, for one country on matters touching both powers, with treaty force. Its purpose is to end or avert dissension between Church and civil power. Two extremes on its necessity are set aside.

Matter divides into spiritual, mixed, and temporal kinds. Spiritual matters touch the spiritual order, such as liturgy. Mixed matters, like education and marriage, fall under both authorities in different aspects. Temporal matters belong to the temporal order alone. Contracting parties must hold treaty power in their spheres: rulers for states, and competent church authorities for the Church. Three theories of its nature are then weighed, with a vast list of agreements appended.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Francesca Steele's entry follows the Congregation of Christian Retreat, in two branches: Fathers and Sisters. Father Antoine-Silvestre Receveur founded it on 19 November 1789 at Fontenelle in Doubs, France. Declared Venerable in 1883 by Leo XIII, he loved the Cross, fond of saying it was a cross to be without one. Revolution raged at the society's birth, bringing privation and sacrifice. For three years seventy sisters faced persecution, then a mob drove them from their convent.

Offered death or separation from Receveur, the sisters unanimously chose death over giving up vocation. By 1902 the congregation held seventeen houses, thirteen in France and four in England, with over a thousand members. Government rests under a mother-general. English convents stood at Shepherd's Bush near London, Clapham, Redhill, Cannock, and three new foundations. Dress includes a white serge cap and cross on the forehead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantine-t:
The entry follows Constantine the Great, named on coins M. or C. Flavius Valerius Constantinus. Born at Naissus, son of Constantius and Saint Helena, his birth date ranges from 274 to 288. After his father's rise to Caesar he lived at Diocletian's court, then fought under Galerius. When Constantius became Augustus, he asked Galerius to release Constantine.

During Maxentius's wars, Constantine stayed inactive, defending his German frontier. Licinius alone survived Diocletian's tetrarchs, leaving Constantine sole master of the Empire. He earned the title Great, turning world history and raising long-persecuted Christianity toward triumph. Raised under his father's ideas, he chose Christianity partly from conscience, moved by Christian example. Tolerance ruled for a time, though the age could not sustain it as equality. He aided children, slaves, and women, first prohibiting girls' abduction. Successors persecuted heretics and pagans, their laws shaping the Middle Ages and the Inquisition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmond-jeaura:
Edmond Jeaurat, also called Edme Jeaurat, was a French engraver born at Vermenton in 1688 and dead at Paris in 1738. Son of a metal worker, he learned his trade under Bernard Picart in Paris, then spent years in Holland copying Dutch pictures in print. Back in Paris he cut plates after the paintings of his younger brother Etienne, and soon won praise for speed and truth to the source.

He worked for the collector Crozat and cut many plates after his brother-in-law Le Clerc. Sets of his prints survive in the British Museum and the Paris National Library. His best-known plate, dated 1713, shows Achilles found among the daughters of Lycomedes, and he also copied Poussin, Veronese, and Watteau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florence-marr:
Florence Marryat was a novelist and actress born at Brighton in 1838 and dead in 1899. Sixth daughter of Captain Frederick Marryat the novelist, she married before sixteen. She travelled much of India with her first husband and bore him eight children. Nursing children through scarlet fever, she turned to novels, publishing her first three in 1865.

In thirty-four years she produced some ninety novels, many reprinted abroad and translated. She edited London Society from 1872 to 1876 and wrote her father's life and letters. She also acted, sang in opera, lectured, and ran a school of journalism. A Catholic convert for years, her faith first showed in the R.I.P. on her obituaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-anna:
Francois Annat, born at Rodes on 5 January 1590 and dead at Paris on 14 June 1670, was a French Jesuit theologian and one of the leading opponents of Jansenism. He entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1607. He taught philosophy for six years and theology for seven at Toulouse, where he became rector, then rector at Montpellier, assistant to the General at Rome, and provincial of Paris. In 1654 he became confessor to Louis XIV.

He discharged that delicate office faithfully and unselfishly until he felt compelled to resign over the king's illicit attachment to the Duchess de la Valliere. As a writer he defended Jesuit teaching on divine grace against the Oratorian Gibieuf in 1632 and entered the controversy over freedom and efficacious grace in 1644. He defended orthodoxy against the Port Royal theologians, earning the notice of Pascal, who aimed his Provincial Letter at Pere Annat. His complete works appeared at Paris in 1666 in three volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-gobat:
George Gobat, a moral theologian born at Charmoilles in 1600, taught casuistry across the German lands for decades. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1618. He held chairs of sacred science and moral theology at Fribourg, Halle, Munich, Ratisbon, and Constance. He also served as rector at Halle and Fribourg and held the Constance cathedral penitentiary until his death in 1679.

Gobat's practical cases on the sacraments, gathered as the Alphabetum and later as Experiential Theology, were reissued as Moral Works at Douai in 1701 and Venice in 1749. His clear, learned handling of live German cases leaned lenient, and several doctrines were condemned by Innocent XI in the year of his death. The Douai edition drew the Arras bishop's censure of thirty-two propositions, sparking attacks on Jesuit morals and published defenses in reply.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-coat:
The Holy Coat is the seamless garment of Christ, for which soldiers cast lots at the Crucifixion, claimed by both Trier cathedral and the church of Argenteuil. Trier tradition says Empress St. Helena sent the relic to that city. Holders of that view once relied on the Sylvester Diploma, a document said to come from Pope Sylvester, but in its present form it cannot count as genuine.

Yet documents prove beyond doubt that since about 1100 the people of Trier believed they held the seamless garment from Helena. A life of St. Agritius, written before 1072, mentions relics Helena sent to Trier and a garment of the Lord kept in the cathedral treasury. The entry weighs both claims and the long history of devotion at Trier and Argenteuil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Labat, a French Dominican missionary born in Paris in 1664 and dead there in 1738, joined the Preachers at twenty and taught philosophy at Nancy before turning to missions. He preached across France, then in 1693 sailed for the French West Indies, where he laboured among Indigenous peoples for thirteen years.

Kept in Rome after a chapter at Bologna, Labat used the delay to write his great history of the West Indies. Paris printers issued it in six volumes in 1722, with drawings of his own. A noted mathematician and naturalist, he packed the work with scientific notes on plants, crafts, and island life. It remains a first-hand window on the early French Caribbean.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-friedr:
Johann Friedrich Schannat, a German historian born at Luxemburg in 1683 and died at Heidelberg in 1739. He studied at Louvain, practised law at twenty-two, then turned wholly to history and priesthood. Fulda's prince-abbot made him historiographer and librarian for the abbey's history, and Trier's archbishop gave like commissions.

In 1735 Prague's archbishop sent Schannat to Italy for council history, with rich finds at Milan's Ambrosian Library and Rome's Vatican Library. His books run from Literary Gleanings and Fulda traditions to Worms's bishopric history and a short Palatine house history. Greatest of all is Concilia Germaniae, edited from his papers by Hartzheim in eleven folio volumes from 1759 to 1790.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josaphat:
Josaphat was the fourth king of Judah after the schism of the ten tribes. Asa's son and successor, he strove to keep the good traditions of his father's virtuous reign, he came to the throne at thirty-five and reigned twenty-three years. His reign is dated 914 to 889 before Christ, or 877 to 853 by Assyrian chronology.

His zeal against the idolatrous high places is commended, though only partly successful. In his third year he sent a missionary expedition through the country to teach the Law. He is reproached for allying with Ahab of Israel and nearly losing his life at Ramoth-Gilead in his eighteenth year. He later joined Ahab's son Ochozias in a failed fleet at Ezion-Geber. He reformed justice with a tribunal of priests, Levites, and elders at Jerusalem. About his twentieth year he repelled a Moabite and Ammonite army more by prayer than by arms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magnificat:
Magnificat is the name for Mary's song in Luke 1:46-55. It comes from its first Latin word, meaning my soul magnifies the Lord. Old antiphonaries also called it the Gospel of Mary. The Roman Breviary lists it among canticles sung at Sunday Vespers.

It stands with two companions from Luke's Gospel. They are the Benedictus of Zachary and the Nunc Dimittis of Simeon. Together they count as evangelical canticles. Commentators split the song into three or four stanzas. A recent debate on its authorship turns on three ancient manuscripts. In worship it takes an antiphon that shifts with feast or weekday. It is sung to the eight modes of plain chant, opening with the sign of the cross. Musical settings close the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-barat:
French scholar Nicolas Barat, born at Bourges early in the seventeenth century, worked in Hebrew and biblical learning in Paris. He studied at Sens and Paris, taught at the Mazarin College, and fell under the sway of the orientalist Richard Simon.

Much of Barat's output came through teamwork: with Père Bordes he edited Thomassin's Hebrew glossary, and he helped Duhamel publish his Bible. At his death in 1706 he was translating a rabbinical library into French, and his critical notes appeared posthumously in 1714. His posthumous New Selected Library of 1714 gathers his critical opinions and curious literary learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-i-the-gr:
Otto I the Great, Roman emperor and German king, was born in 912 and died at Memleben on 7 May 973, son of Henry I and Mathilda. He wed Edith, daughter of King Athelstan of England, in 929, and took the crown on his father's death in 936. His Aachen coronation kept Carolingian empire traditions alive. He aimed at strong central power, against the German love of local freedom, and first had to crush revolts led by his own brother Henry.

Otto bent the duchies to the crown, filled the Church with fresh life, and freed himself from lay lords by leaning on bishops. Crowned emperor at Rome, he pressed claims in Italy and saw his son Otto crowned emperor by John XIII. He dropped his southern Italian war in the end, and the entry weighs his church policy, his justice toward unruly nobles, and his place as founder of the medieval empire's German shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-leo-i:
Leo I reigned from 440 to 461 and died on 10 November 461. His pontificate ranks next to Gregory I's as the most significant in Christian antiquity. As the Western Empire crumbled and the East churned over doctrine, Leo guided Rome's church with far-seeing sagacity. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Tuscan, son of Quintianus. He first appears certainly as a deacon under Celestine I.

Cassian wrote his work against Nestorius at Leo's suggestion in 430 or 431. Valentinian III sent him to Gaul to reconcile the commander Aetius with the magistrate Albinus, a mark of high trust. As pope he guarded the vicariates of Arles and Thessalonica. The Thessalonica vicar consecrated metropolitans, summoned Illyria's bishops in synod, and oversaw their work, while the weightiest matters went to Rome. Anastasius abused that office so despotically that Leo rebuked him sharply. The entry presents a pope who steered the church through imperial collapse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-basil-the-:
St. Basil the Great was bishop of Caesarea and one of the most distinguished Doctors of the Church. This entry follows a man born probably in 329 and dead on 1 January 379. He ranks after Athanasius as a defender of the Eastern Church against fourth-century heresies. He forms, with his friend Gregory of Nazianzus and his brother Gregory of Nyssa, the trio called the Three Cappadocians. 

His father, Basil the Elder, was the son of a Christian of good birth and his wife Macrina. Both suffered for the faith during the persecution of Maximinus Galerius from 305 to 314, spending several years of hardship in the wild mountains of Pontus. Basil the Elder was noted for virtue and won considerable reputation as a teacher in Caesarea, though he was not a priest. He married Emmelia, and the entry follows their famous family.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gertrude-t:
Gertrude the Great, Benedictine mystic of Helfta, entered the monastery at five and became its brightest glory. Born in Germany on 6 January 1256 to unknown parents, she was received into Helfta's alumnate under Abbess Gertrude of Hackerborn. There monastic observance joined the intellectual life passed down from Lioba's Anglo-Saxon nuns, with the Divine Office at the centre. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates her death at Helfta to 17 November 1301 or 1302.

Entrusted to Mechtilde's care, she studied with ardour until, at twenty-six, visions began that lasted for life. Turning from grammarian to theologian, she abandoned profane study for Scripture, fathers, and theology, copying, translating, and writing for others' spiritual good. Her Legatus records a soul condemning its own past negligence in the language of high sanctity. The entry follows learning ripening into mysticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gregory-th:
Gregory the Great, pope from 590 to 604, shaped medieval Christianity's doctrine, organization, and discipline more than any single pope. Born at Rome about 540 to the wealthy patrician Gordianus, he gave the Church principles later Catholicism would develop, as even the non-Catholic scholar Dudden grants in the entry's opening praise. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death to 12 March 604.

After three happy years retired in St. Andrew's monastery, austerities that likely broke his health, he was drawn into public service. His Dialogues picture his age vividly, and his Scripture lectures, on Heptateuch, Kings, Prophets, Proverbs, and Canticles, were noted by a student named Claudius. Meeting Angles in Rome fixed him with desire to convert them, a longing that points toward England. The entry presents a pope who was father to the Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hugh-the-g:
Hugh the Great, abbot of Cluny from 1049 to 1109, led the monastery at the height of Gregorian reform. Born at Semur in 1024, eldest son of Count Dalmatius and Aremberge of Vergy, he was destined by his war-loving father for knighthood and estates. His mother, moved by a priest's vision, wished him for God's service, and his own earnest piety settled the matter. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Cluny to 28 April 1109.

Entrusted to his grand-uncle Hugh of Auxerre, he studied at St. Marcellus's priory school and entered Cluny's novitiate at fourteen, making vows with such fervour that his promise showed early. Under Hugh, Cluny's monks supplied popes Urban II and Paschal II, and Urban consecrated Cluny's new high altar in 1095. With Gregory VII he sought to free the Church from state control and restore discipline. The entry follows an abbot at reform's centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vladimir-t:
