Vladimir the Great, ruler of Kiev and all Russia, became the first Russian ruler to embrace the Christian faith. Born in 956, grandson of Olga, he was the third son of Sviatoslav by Olga Malusha, while Yaropolk and Oleg were legitimate sons. Sviatoslav gave Kiev to Yaropolk, the Drevlanian land to Oleg, and Novgorod, which threatened rebellion, to young Vladimir.

War between his brothers drove Vladimir to flee to the Varangians across the sea. Returning with a large force, he retook Novgorod, overcame Yaropolk, and united Russia. After weighing faiths, tradition says, he chose the faith of Constantinople, was baptised, and ordered his people's conversion. He built churches, schools, and towns, and died at Berestova on 15 July 1015, honoured as baptiser of Russia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thaddeus-amat:
Thaddeus Amat, second Bishop of Monterey and Los Angeles, was born at Barcelona in 1810 and died at Los Angeles in 1878. He joined the Lazarists and was ordained in Paris in 1838. He came to the United States that year for Louisiana missions. He served as novice master in Missouri and Philadelphia from 1841 to 1847. When Bishop Alemany of Monterey became Archbishop of San Francisco, Amat succeeded him, consecrated at Rome in 1854.

Seventeen priests served a mixed, largely Spanish population. The mining era brought settlers, and Amat, visiting Europe, returned with Lazarist priests and Sisters of Charity. In 1859 Rome allowed him the Los Angeles title, and he moved there. Under him Lazarists opened St Vincent's College, Franciscans ran schools, and Sisters of the Immaculate Heart came. Illness forced him to seek a coadjutor, Francis Mora, consecrated in 1873. He began a cathedral, dedicated in 1876, and died with 51 priests, 32 churches, and schools and asylums.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodoric-the:
Ostrogoth king Theodoric the Great, hostage turned ruler of Italy, is the statesman portrayed here. Born about 454, dying 26 August 526, illegitimate son of Theodomir of the royal Amali house, he spent boyhood from eight as a hostage at Constantinople's court, absorbing ancient civilisation's education. At eighteen he returned home to lead a growing horde seeking new lands.

Ally and enemy by turns to emperors, his policy tangled with rival Theodoric Strabo, squint-eyed namesake able to sway Constantinople against him. Strabo's death in 481 brought patricius and magister militum titles from Zeno and consulship in 484. Zeno then set him to expel Odoacer from Italy, a conquest that founded his kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valley-of-jos:
The Valley of Josaphat, or Jehoshaphat, appears in only one Bible passage, Joel 3. There God says he will gather all nations and bring them down into the valley of Josaphat. There he will plead for his people and his inheritance Israel, whom they scattered among the nations. A widely held reading takes the prophet's scene of judgment on the Gentiles as the valley where, before King Josaphat of Judah, God destroyed the coalition of Moab, Ammon, and Edom.

That valley of the desert of Tekoa, called by Jews emek Berakah, valley of blessing, lies near Khirbet Berekut, some distance west of Khirbet Tekoa, about eleven miles from Jerusalem. The entry weighs this reading against others that take the name as symbolic, and traces how pilgrims and writers fixed the valley's site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-joseph-pa:
Joseph Passerat was born on 30 April 1772 at Joinville in France and died on 30 October 1858. Great difficulties blocked his path to the priesthood: driven from the seminary, jailed, and forced to serve in the army from 1788 to 1792. His lofty stature made him drum-major, and later quartermaster. At the first chance he left the service and joined the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer in Warsaw.

Blessed Clement Hofbauer trained him for religious life and priesthood, and Passerat in turn trained newcomers. Later, with great difficulty amid the times, he founded houses outside Poland. After Clement's death, Passerat succeeded him as vicar-general over all the transalpine communities. While in that office from 1820 to 1848 he founded houses in the United States and elsewhere, spreading the Redemptorists beyond the Alps.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-madeleine:
Madeleine Sophie Barat founded the Society of the Sacred Heart, born at Joigny in Burgundy on 12 December 1779, who died in Paris on 24 May 1865. Youngest child of Jacques Barat, a vine-dresser and cooper, and Madeleine Foufé, she was baptized the morning after her birth, with her brother Louis, aged eleven, as godfather. To that brother she owed the exceptional schooling that fitted her for her life's work.

While her mother found her apt in practical matters, Louis saw her singular gifts of mind and heart. When at twenty-two he returned as professor to Joigny's seminary, he taught his sister Latin, Greek, history, natural science, Spanish, and Italian. Soon she read the classics in the original and outshone her brother's pupils. The entry follows her founding of the society and its schools across the world.
doe-osti-17027929-generation-impact-asse:
Argonne National Laboratory assessment ANL-26/69 weighs what a summer 2026 fish experiment at Glen Canyon Dam would cost in lost power. Cooling river water below the dam can slow smallmouth bass, a harmful invader, but bypassing turbines cuts generation. The study checks that trade against a compliance rule named RM15.

Energy losses proved highly predictable in the modeling, while capacity losses were far less certain. Penstock water temperature governed when bypass was needed, and price swings drove most cost doubt. The authors also warn that the reported season understates the full compliance cost. Advice includes sizing firm capacity promises at a cautious level in August and September and watching penstock temperature weekly.
doe-osti-17032787-gpu-accelerated-spectr:
Nadish Saini and R. Balakrishnan of Argonne National Laboratory tested a fluid simulation method on graphics processors in report ANL/NSE-26/74. Their NekRS based method tracks two fluids at once in fully developed turbulence, where the boundary between fluids stretches, breaks, and merges again and again. Earlier checks had covered only calm or weak flows.

A single phase turbulent flow was first built and held steady, then a round blob of second fluid was added. The forcing held turbulence energy near its target, with a Reynolds number near the goal value of 87. Results track interface growth, surface energy, and volume error, then follow the decay phase after forcing stops and blobs merge.
doe-osti-17076814-smart-ops-data-curatio:
Status report on data curation for SMART-OPS, an Oak Ridge project building AI help for accelerator operation, came from Pradeep Ramuhalli and colleagues in September 2026. SMART-OPS aims to steady particle beams and cut beam trips in accelerator driven systems, a tool with uses in nuclear waste transmutation. Its first target is trips caused by radio frequency cavity detuning.

Milestone M2.1 covered gathering and digitizing the raw material the learning system needs. Operator logs, sensor streams, and beam trip reports at the Spallation Neutron Source were reviewed with site experts. Progress was scored by how many trips the data sets captured and how fast each sensor sampled, since sparse data can hide the cause of a trip.
doe-osti-17084211-demonstrating-novelty-:
Dylan Anderson, Susan Caskey, Patrick Lopez, and colleagues at Sandia demonstrate a data discovery method for finding novelty in big record sets, in report SAND2026-26782 printed September 2026. The loop pulls records from a source, scores them with a reward, and lets a decision tree policy choose what to fetch next. The aim is surfacing the odd or telling record, not the average one.

Two vignettes test the loop. In OpenStreetMap data, a search for restaurants, run blind to the kind field, uncovered how restaurant names shift with latitude across North America. In Wikipedia data, a blind search for album articles revealed the articles through other fields. A fitted tree in each case exposed the hidden pattern in plain form.
doe-osti-2570873-sesame-ascii2-file-form:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-25-26256, by David A. Pimentel and Daniel G. Sheppard and issued in July 2025, defines ASCII2, a new text file format for SESAME equation-of-state data. The forty-year-old legacy ASCII format forced data into FORTRAN-style fixed columns. It also capped material and table numbers at six digits and limited the size and precision of stored numbers.

ASCII2 relaxes the fixed layout into a plainer whitespace-separated style that is easier to read and parse. Integer identifiers may run past six digits, and floating point values keep the precision of the equivalent 64-bit binary file. The new format was needed once SESAME added tables for multiphase material representations. The report supersedes an earlier format note, LA-UR-21-23834, whose details had turned out to be wrong or incomplete. Limited support for the legacy formats is promised going forward.
doe-osti-2570985-compressed-sensing-meth:
An internship report dated July 17, 2025, by Cassidy Campbell of Florida Polytechnic University, done at Savannah River National Laboratory under advisor Steve Chiswell, takes on a slow laboratory chore. The laboratory's air samplers collect emissions on sorbent tubes at set locations. Hourly collection adds up to nearly 9,000 tubes a year, and each tube's one-dimensional signal takes real time to analyze.

Campbell applies compressed sensing, a signal method that rebuilds a full signal from far fewer measurements when the signal is mostly empty, or sparse. Random sampling picks which tubes to run, sidestepping the classic rule that a signal must be sampled at twice its highest frequency. An L1 minimization routine, of the LASSO family, then finds the sparsest signal that fits the measurements. The report checks the method's core assumptions, sparsity and matrix incoherence, against the sampling program's real data.
doe-osti-2573046-yes-no-maybe-so-human-f:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Brandon D. Dreslin and Jessica A. Baweja, dated July 2025, examines how people should trust foundation models that admit uncertainty. Such models increasingly support real decisions, yet their confidence statements can mislead. Trust that is too high invites error; trust that is too low wastes the tool. The human factors question is how to land users in between, at calibrated trust.

The report first reviews four literatures: foundation models in decision support, trust in AI systems, how uncertainty information is presented, and how people perform when AI supplies it. It then lays out a study design, with participants, measures, and procedure spelled out in advance. Sections on research objectives and limitations frame what the planned work can show. The aim is practical guidance for designers choosing how a model should say yes, no, or maybe so.
doe-osti-2583457-solarapp-enhancements-a:
Final technical report NREL/TP-6A20-93843 closes the SolarAPP+ enhancement project, led by Emily Dalecki at NREL from March 2021 to December 2024. SolarAPP+ is free software that checks rooftop solar designs against code and issues permits instantly, replacing weeks of back-and-forth at the permit counter. Slow permitting is a quiet tax on every home solar installation.

By the project's end, 256 permitting authorities in thirteen states had adopted the platform. It had issued permits for more than 36,500 rooftop solar projects and another 28,500 solar-plus-storage projects, over 65,000 in total. Adopting towns saw shorter timelines, simpler processes, and lower installation costs. In December 2024 the software moved from NREL to the SolarAPP Foundation, a nonprofit created to run it under a license agreement. The handoff marks the project's last milestone: a federal tool becoming permanent civic infrastructure.
doe-osti-2584661-geochemical-and-hydrome:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-28549, by Wenfeng Li with New Mexico Tech partners, reports the GeoHydRA project's push to make rocks produce hydrogen faster. Serpentinization, water reacting with olivine-rich rock, generates natural hydrogen underground, but slowly. The ARPA-E project attacked the rate problem three ways. Batch reactors sought the best conditions for the reactions. Flow-through tests hunted what limits generation underground. Triaxial shear tests cracked rock open and kept it cracked.

Samples came from four American localities. They were San Carlos olivine in Arizona and Kilbourne Hole olivine in New Mexico. Dunites came from Twin Sisters, Washington and Balsam Gap, North Carolina. The concept joins chemistry and mechanics. A hierarchical crack network exposes fresh surface, while tuned fluids address the factors that stall the reaction. In situ hydrogen, made in the ground rather than a plant, is the long game this work serves.
doe-osti-2587259-hardware-based-demonstr:
Josephine Baiden wrote this summer internship report, INL/RPT-25-86960, at Idaho National Laboratory in July 2025. Palash Bhowmik and Piyush Sabharwall supervised the work. Both men belong to the lab's Thermal Fluid Systems group. Baiden, from Loyola Marymount University, built a hardware demonstration of temperature control functions for reactor systems. Her bench box senses temperature and acts on it, the way a reactor control loop would.

The report follows an engineering design process from start to finish. Housing candidates for the electronics are compared side by side. Cost is held inside a fixed budget throughout. A design matrix weighs temperature sensing options. Thermocouples are measured against a component used in an earlier version of the box. The result is a working, student-built testbed. It lets engineers try control ideas in hardware before those ideas ever touch a reactor system model.
doe-osti-2587441-pfas-waste-management-f:
Subodh Chaudhari, Naushita Sharma, and Robert Bruce Lung wrote this August 2025 guidance article for the Waste Reduction Network's Tip of the Month series. Its topic is managing waste contaminated with PFAS, the per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances that include PFOS and PFOA. These water- and oil-repelling chemicals degrade very slowly, build up in living things, and pass through ordinary water treatment largely untouched.

The article sorts PFAS waste into two families. Primary waste comes straight from making or using the chemicals: process wastewater, sludges, and tars. Secondary waste is born during cleanup: spent activated carbon, used ion exchange resins, membrane reject streams, and landfill leachate. A table maps typical streams by industry, covering solid, liquid, and gas forms. Strategies run from PFAS-free substitutes in manufacturing to treatment plants working with industrial customers on pollution prevention and on-site treatment.
doe-osti-2589170-residential-building-st:
Noah Sandoval of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this characterization study, NREL/TP-5500-92494, dated September 2025, of the residential building stock of Palm Beach County, Florida. It applies ResStock, the laboratory's statistical model of American homes, to one county, so local program planners can see the housing they actually serve: ages, types, systems, and energy burdens.

The work proceeds in tasks. The stock characterization comes first, built from ResStock's sampled representation of the county's homes. Later tasks model energy consumption, utility bills, and emissions impacts for low-income households under program scenarios. An appendix carries data ResStock itself does not report: figures on cost-burdened households and households of color. Those data did not drive the rest of the analysis. They were included because they matter to program decisions, a candid note on what the model can and cannot see.
doe-osti-2589838-non-destructive-structu:
Paul Geimer and Andrew Delorey pair sound measurements with machine learning to inspect graphite reactor parts without cutting them open, in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-29538, issued 25 September 2025. Microreactors under 20 megawatts electric could cut building time and cost, but their small output leaves little room for costly upkeep. Many designs use graphite both to slow neutrons and as structure.

The method rings a graphite part, records its vibration signature, and trains models to link that signature to inner condition. Earlier vibration data sets were reprocessed first to confirm the workflow had improved. Tests then probed how much of the frequency spectrum the model truly needs, finding useful markers spread throughout it. Built-in monitoring could warn operators early, trimming inspection labor that graphite parts have long required.
doe-osti-2589843-design-document-summary:
Los Alamos National Laboratory design summary LA-UR-25-29625, by Richard Fiorella, issued 27 September 2025, documents a change to how a land model treats snow-covered shrubs. The work sits in the IM3 project and the ELM land model, which computes how vegetation and snow trade light and heat. How much leaf area snow buries changes both the surface brightness and the energy balance.

Two new shrub parameters were added. Bendresist, running from 0 to 1, captures how stiffly a shrub resists bending under snow weight; 1 means no bending. Vegshape, with suggested values 1 or 2, captures whether leaf area sits in a parabolic or rounded crown. Both feed a revised buried-fraction formula, and a version note corrects the formula's meaning from exposed to buried fraction. Defaults keep old results unchanged.
doe-osti-2997457-one-turn-delay-feedback:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229013-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-147, by Arshdeep Singh, S. Mai, K. Mernick, and co-authors, documents building a one-turn delay feedback system for the Electron-Ion Collider. Radio cavities in a storage ring fight the beam's own wake; direct feedback calms the cavity at its working frequency. This system extends the calm to the sidebands around each revolution harmonic, where instabilities grow.

The heart is a comb filter held in on-chip memory. Its delay matches one turn of the ring: at a revolution frequency near 78.125 kilohertz and a 20 megahertz clock, the delay line length follows directly. A bandwidth coefficient near 1 narrows the filter's notches. Chapters move from building blocks through simulation tests to hardware validation, using the running RHIC collider's numbers as the working example.
doe-osti-2998379-refining-the-representa:
University of Michigan final project report on award DE-SC0022117, led by Xianglei Huang, covers work from August 2021 to August 2025 on a blind spot in climate models. The E3SM model, the Department's flagship climate simulator, handles the exchange of longwave radiation between the Arctic surface and its atmosphere too crudely. That coupling steers sea ice, so errors there bend the whole polar forecast.

The project published seven peer-reviewed papers and contributed to an eighth, with one more manuscript in progress. One thread showed that letting clouds scatter longwave light, a process models usually skip, warms the surface and cuts outgoing radiation in the model. Other threads tackled three-dimensional radiation effects in mixed-phase Arctic clouds and the surface's own spectral emissivity. Findings were presented at the major climate and radiation meetings across the project years.
doe-osti-2998715-ncsp-outlook-and-intere:
Theresa Cutler of Los Alamos and Catherine Percher of Lawrence Livermore presented these slides at a safety board meeting held at Idaho National Laboratory. The subject is the Nuclear Criticality Safety Program, the Energy Department effort that keeps work with uranium and plutonium safe from accidental chain reactions. Slides trace the program's history, its five-year plan, and how it is organised.

Most program money goes to integral experiments, real test assemblies that produce data for safety handbooks and benchmarks. Such tests run at Sandia and at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center in Nevada, on machines such as Godiva IV and Flattop. Current needs centre mostly on highly enriched uranium and plutonium systems. Funding follows proposals, expert review, and staged approvals. The deck closes by inviting outside groups to collaborate on planned experiments at those facilities.
doe-osti-2999129-lynm-containment-hydrog:
Kristopher Kuhlman, Melissa Mills and Brittney Seaburn of Sandia National Laboratories update a containment data set in report SAND2025-12518, printed September 2025. The work concerns LYNM, a site where models must predict how water and gas move through rock around buried structures. Such two-phase flow, water and air sharing the same pores, depends on how pore sizes in the rock are spread.

New data come from core samples drilled in the P-tunnel. Mercury intrusion tests forced mercury into the rock under rising pressure, revealing both bulk behaviour and the full pore-size spread. The team fitted the van Genuchten model, a standard curve for such data, to the new measurements. A chapter then weighs what the fresh numbers change for future predictions, and an appendix shows sample photos. It is a data update, issued yearly, rather than a new theory.
doe-osti-3000475-investigation-of-new-su:
Alex Gurevich of Old Dominion University leads this final report, with Jean Delayen and Chang-Beom Eom among the senior investigators, on materials for the next generation of accelerator cavities. Superconducting radio-frequency cavities drive particle beams, and today's best are pure niobium pushed near its physical limits. A better material must keep magnetic vortices, tiny whirlpools of field, out of its walls under strong radio-frequency fields. The field where vortices first break through is a key score.

Judging thin films by standard magnet tests is tricky, since sample shape and edges distort readings. The team built a dedicated rig: a small superconducting solenoid presses up to 500 millitesla onto the film surface, while three Hall probes watch for the moment flux punches fully through. The setup suits films and multilayer coatings alike. The report details the instrument and the candidate materials it can now rank fairly.
doe-osti-3000806-pcor-partnership-initia:
Wesley Peck, Nicholas Kalenze, Jose Torres and co-workers at the University of North Dakota close the PCOR Partnership initiative in this final report. It is 2025-EERC-10-06, dated October 2025, under cooperative agreement DE-FE0031838. PCOR is the Plains CO2 Reduction partnership. It is a regional push to speed carbon capture, use and storage across ten states, from Missouri to Alaska, plus four Canadian provinces.

Since 2019 the partnership has worked the practical blockers: regulations and permitting, storage site screening, and monitoring methods regulators can accept. Its publication list runs from subsurface stress assessments for basal reservoirs to stacked storage studies. A Fort Berthold screening assessment appears too. So do monitoring papers covering fibre-optic sensing, soil gas checks and even blockchain accounting. The final report gathers that regional record, and the lessons for deploying carbon storage at commercial scale in the plains and north.
doe-osti-3002294-boiler-experiment-mater:
Nick Russell, Yukinori Yamamoto, Tim Graening, Timothy Lach, Marie Romedenne, Janelle Wharry, and Kory Linton give a status report, ORNL/TM-2025/4007, dated September 2025. It covers the BOILER experiment, which tests alumina-forming austenitic steels. These steels grow a protective alumina skin and resist liquid lead, making them candidates for parts in lead-cooled fast reactors.

The report first characterizes the experiment's materials, including how nickel content varies across the steel heats. Pre-oxidized samples were prepared to carry their protective layer into service. Then it reports the irradiation status of test capsules in the High Flux Isotope Reactor, with build schematics for capsules BLR01 through BLR08 and several furnace test capsules. Readers get both the starting condition of each specimen and how far its reactor exposure has progressed.
doe-osti-3003126-rapid-sacr-observations:
M. Oue, S. Freeman, P. Gatlin, P. Kollias, B. Dolan, K. Rasmussen, W. Petersen, and S. Giangrande report a storm-watching campaign in DOE report DOE/SC-ARM-25-023, dated November 2025. The RAPID campaign placed rapidly scanning radars at the Bankhead National Forest site in Alabama. Its quarry was convection: the rising air currents that build thunderstorms over the southeastern United States.

Most storms caught were isolated cells or clusters during August and September. About 75 percent of cells were shallow, with 20 dBZ echo tops below six to seven kilometers. The authors advise starting earlier in the season, in May, to catch more storm types. They also recommend lower scan angles to capture shallow clouds better. Most isolated cells formed in the local afternoon. The lessons shape the next deployment's scan plan.
doe-osti-3004269-vexcel-imaging-s-suitab:
Meghan Touat, Amir Osman, Stan Seiferth, and Orrin Thomas put a commercial imaging system on trial in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4286, dated November 2025. The question is whether Vexcel Imaging data can support automatic verification: checking that mapped features sit where the imagery claims, without a human measuring points by hand.

The check uses NOAA's CORS network, a nationwide set of precisely surveyed stations, as ground truth. Measured image coordinates are compared with the stations' projected positions, site by site. Residual plots in pixels show where the imagery agrees and where it drifts. Strong agreement clusters near zero residual; outliers flag problem areas. Photogrammetry calibration literature frames the method. Verification like this underpins trust in automatically produced maps for government users.
doe-osti-3005294-recovery-simulator-and-:
Patrick Maloney, Meng Zhao, Xinda Ke, and fourteen colleagues at Pacific Northwest lay out a mathematical framework in an October 2025 report. Their subject is grid recovery after a major disruption. The recovery simulator and analysis tool, RSA, decides which repairs to do in which order when crews, parts, and time are all limited.

The core is an optimization: maximize load served, or customers reconnected, by co-scheduling generation that cannot black-start, transmission lines, feeders, and substations under a labor budget. Linear programming picks the pathway, weighing short-term wins against the full restoration. An appendix shows how to reformulate maximum functions into mixed-integer linear constraints, the kind of detail implementers need. Operators can rehearse outage scenarios against the model before the real storm arrives.
doe-osti-3007590-2020-budget-request-for:
Five years of the Computational Science Graduate Fellowship are closed out by Shelly Olsan of the Krell Institute in Ames, Iowa, in the final report for DOE award DE-SC0021110. The fellowship, running since 1991, trains graduate students to apply high-performance computing to hard science and engineering problems. This award covered September 2020 through August 2025. The hosted text carries frequent character-level OCR noise, though its content stays readable.

Every fellow completes a twelve-week practicum at a DOE national laboratory, working on live research with access to world-class computers. The report argues that computing now underpins nearly every field, from energy to artificial intelligence, so the workforce pipeline matters nationally. Fellows from earlier practica often compete strongly for laboratory jobs when openings appear.
doe-osti-3009110-photosynthesis-protein-:
Final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0016317, by Andrea Markelz, investigates how whole-protein vibrations steer energy in photosynthesis. The proteins under study are the Fenna-Matthews-Olson complex and the Orange Carotenoid Protein, measured with terahertz spectroscopy.

The hypothesis under test is that long-range scaffold motions, not just local pigment jiggling, set energy gaps and couplings between pigments. Instruments combined time-domain terahertz spectroscopy with near-field detection across 80 to 300 kelvin, in solution and in crystals. A new analysis method, Normal Mode Ensemble Analysis, ties measured spectra to specific backbone motions. The orange-to-red switch of the carotenoid protein anchors the photoprotection side of the study.
doe-osti-3012944-synthesizing-novel-h2-s:
CRADA final report LBNL-2001731, dated January 13, 2026, closes the SENSOR project. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory ran it with Baker Hughes Energy Transition LLC. Wibe de Jong led the Berkeley Lab side. The project name spells out its aim: novel hydrogen sensors for operational resilience in pipeline infrastructure. Hydrogen leaks easily and embrittles pipeline steel. Sound detection thus matters more as hydrogen moves into wider use.

Rather than bench chemistry alone, the team built a screening framework. It pairs high-performance computing with artificial intelligence. Machine learning models were trained to simulate hydrogen inside metal-organic frameworks. These porous crystals could serve as sensing materials. One test case was a copper squarate framework. The report also lists the project's subject inventions and publications, next to its funding table.
doe-osti-3013849-principles-and-options-:
Devyn Powell and Jeremy Twitchell of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory wrote this July 2025 guide on designing battery energy storage zoning ordinances. As battery projects multiply, local governments must write land-use rules for them, often from scratch. The report gives those governments principles and ready options instead of a one-size template, since community concerns and state laws differ.

Topics a zoning ordinance must settle include where storage may site, setbacks, noise and fire safety conditions, screening, and decommissioning duties. Each option is presented with its trade-offs, so planners can see what stricter or looser wording does to projects and neighbors. The guide draws on the lab's energy storage policy work and is aimed at county and municipal staff facing their first battery application.
doe-osti-3013882-understanding-aging-mec:
Sandia report SAND2026-15554 studies lithium battery aging with nuclear magnetic resonance. Keith Fritzsching, Katharine Harrison, John Borchardt, and eight co-authors wrote it. They worked both in working cells and in dismantled ones. Batteries fade through chemical side reactions that are hard to watch directly. NMR can identify the molecules involved. But metal cell parts block the magnetic fields the method needs.

The team fabricated model pouch cells. Some versions used thinner materials at the center, to test how deeply the field penetrates. Analytical and numerical models of field penetration were checked against two validation geometries. Separators pulled from cycled cells were examined with high-resolution magic angle spinning NMR. X-ray fluorescence tracked electrolyte degradation products in the same samples. The methods aim at a step-by-step account of aging, rather than simple capacity bookkeeping.
doe-osti-3015073-optimizing-fleet-operat:
A July 2025 slide deck by Kotz and Anderson tallies fleet telematics savings. It is drawn from the Energy to Communities program. Telematics units report how vehicles are actually driven and used. The deck prices what a city fleet gains by acting on that data.

A cited city audit put the cost of dangerous driving, emissions, and waste tied to vehicle use at about 10.5 million dollars a year. It judged that two added staff positions, at roughly 340,348 dollars, would pay for themselves. The savings and lower liability claims would cover them. The deck's own table puts potential savings at 2,307 dollars per vehicle per year. Inventory optimization leads at 695 dollars. Safety follows at 553, then reporting at 312. Idling and aggressive driving cuts sit behind them.
doe-osti-3015298-synthesizing-novel-h2-s:
CRADA final report FP00016865, dated January 13, 2026, covers hydrogen leak sensors designed by computation. It joins Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory with Baker Hughes Energy Transition. Hydrogen's small molecules leak easily. They also embrittle pipeline steel. Blending hydrogen into gas networks, or building its own lines, demands detection at very low levels. Wibe de Jong was the Berkeley Lab contact.

The team built a high-performance computing and AI screening framework. It runs over metal-organic frameworks, a porous family with many candidate forms. Thousands of options are first screened with cheap semi-empirical methods. The screen checks them against known test data and basic structure checks. The reduced set then gets closer study. The goal is a sensor that spots leaks early enough to keep pipeline hydrogen systems safe at industrial scale.
doe-osti-3015787-southeast-regional-co-s:
Ben Wernette of the Southern States Energy Board and presenters from universities, state surveys, and firms gave this closeout slide deck on September 17, 2025. It closes out SECARB-USA, the Southeast Regional Carbon Utilization and Storage Acceleration Partnership, funded under award DE-FE0031830. Kenneth Nemeth led the project as principal investigator, and Brian Hill and Carlos Uroza were among the presenters. The partnership worked on carbon capture and storage across the American Southeast.

The deck reviews the partners, the project timeline, and basin studies, then gives storage capacity estimates for candidate sites. It notes that the Southeast produces over 1.2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide a year, about 30 percent of the national total. Site tables pair stored amounts with porosity and storage efficiency factors drawn from cited studies. Closing slides sum up what the region needs to move storage projects toward real use.
doe-osti-3015983-low-cost-production-of-:
Atlantic Biomass LLC's Phase I final report for STTR award DE-SC0024998 was led by Robert Kozak. Research partners were Frederick C Michel of Ohio State University, Shekhar G Shinde and his team, and Daehwan Kim of Hood College. The project tried to cut the cost of sustainable aviation fuel by starting from perennial grasses, grasses that regrow each year without replanting.

Their method mills the grass in a ball mill at the same time enzymes break it down, so milling and sugar release happen in one step. Tests showed enzymes kept working during milling and later fermentation, turning the intermediate cellobiose into glucose without extra cost. Leftover solids came out clean enough to serve as feed for pyrolysis or gasification. A third finding ties results to the ratio between grass piece length and the mill's inner size.
doe-osti-3017353-structure-aware-unsuper:
Hyojin Kim of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this February 2026 final report, LLNL-TR-2015330, for a Defense Threat Reduction Agency basic research grant. The project built structure-aware, unsupervised machine learning for drug discovery. Unsupervised means the models learn patterns from molecular data without labeled answers. Structure-aware means the three-dimensional shape of drug and target drives the learning.

The proposed framework uses multiple instance learning, judging a binding case by its set of docking poses. Graph networks, named SG-CNN and EGNN in the design, read each protein-ligand complex structure. A pose-wise attention network then weighs which poses are accurate and which are not. Attention focuses the final binding call on the poses that deserve it. For drug hunters, better pose judgment means fewer wasted syntheses. The report lays out the framework, its goals, and its results in the agency's standard final report form.
doe-osti-3018377-characterization-of-neu:
Jeffrey Smith Burggraf and David L Chichester of Idaho National Laboratory wrote this October 2025 report, INL/RPT-25-88190, on neutron emission rates of commercial californium-252 sources. Californium-252 is the workhorse neutron source for experiments and instrument checks. Yet commercial sources often arrive without traceable calibration or stated errors, a quiet problem for anyone modeling from their output.

The team built the missing calibration chain. A pulse-shape scintillator was calibrated against a time-tagged californium fission chamber made at Oak Ridge over forty years ago. Because the old chamber's isotopes have decayed since manufacture, Bateman equations modeled its isotopic evolution, including how the average neutrons per fission drifted over time. The calibrated scintillator then measured absolute emission rates for several such sources. Fast-neutron experimenters get numbers they can finally cite with uncertainties attached.
doe-osti-3018520-irrigation-infrastructu:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory set a baseline for western irrigation in this February 2026 report, prepared for the Department of Energy. Jered F Jorgensen, Kelsey L Adkisson, Sarah E Barrows, and co-authors mapped the region's conveyance network. Canals, laterals, and pipelines across 17 western states were inventoried by extent and material. The team then estimated what modernization could save. Water losses, energy use, and farm economics were all modeled. Between low and high loss scenarios, 16 to 26 percent of diverted water may seep away in transit.

The scale is striking: the spread between the loss scenarios approaches half the volume of Lake Mead. Lining canals, piping open laterals, and automating deliveries form the modernization menu. Before this baseline, benefit claims rested on scattered district studies. Planners now have one accounting of the infrastructure. That accounting is the reference point against which future modernization programs will be measured.
doe-osti-3021255-boride-based-ceramic-su:
Morgan State University final report for DOE NETL award DE-FE0031906, led by Yucheng Lan with Maohong Fan and Hertanto Adidharma. It covers an August 2020 to July 2025 project on temperature sensors for extreme environments. Thermocouples that read the hottest parts of power plants and industrial systems fail when their metal wires degrade. The team pursued boride-based ceramics, which tolerate super-high temperatures and harsh chemistry that defeat conventional sensors.

Work spanned synthesizing boride materials, milling them into nanopowders, and forming nanocomposites. It also meant gauging the Seebeck coefficient. That is the voltage a material generates per degree of temperature difference, which is what makes a thermocouple work. Ball milling ground gram-scale boride batches to nanoscale powders over several hours. Stability testing checked whether the ceramics hold up in service conditions. The report also records the graduate students trained through the project.
doe-osti-3021517-cyber-informed-engineer:
Guide DOE/GO-102026-6269, produced by NLR and INL with a thirteen-author team, applies Cyber-Informed Engineering to electric power making. The approach means designing systems from the start so that a cyberattack cannot easily become a physical disaster. The guide covers design, setup, and upkeep for engineers, operators, and cybersecurity staff.

Eight power technologies get their own sections: natural gas, nuclear, wind, solar, hydropower, bioenergy, geothermal, and hydrogen. Each section presents the method, names a critical digital challenge, and applies the principles to it. A recurring tip favors nondigital backups: gravity-driven spillway gates that open on rising water, and spring-loaded relief valves that need no electricity or network. Worked use cases close the guide.
doe-osti-3024059-spatial-heterogeneity-i:
Gourihar Kulkarni of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory reports the SHINE field campaign in DOE/SC-ARM-26-006, dated February 2026. SHINE stands for Spatial Heterogeneity in Cloud Condensation Nuclei, the tiny particles on which cloud droplets form. The campaign worked in the Bankhead National Forest region of northern Alabama, at the ARM facility's main site plus two supplementary sites, each running a particle counter.

Three objectives structure the work. The first maps how aerosol properties spread out in space and time across the three sites, M1, S20, and S30. The second does the same for cloud condensation nuclei concentrations. The third tests closure, whether the nuclei counts measured directly agree with counts inferred from the aerosol measurements, under local production and transported pollution alike.
doe-osti-3030050-enabling-high-si-conten: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and Perceptra closed a joint project under CRADA FP00010448, in a short final report dated July 31, 2025. Gao Liu was the Berkeley Lab technical contact, and Roger Basu was the partner contact. The work backed fabrication of lithium-ion battery anodes with high silicon content, using conductive binders and smooth solution-deposited coatings. The form lists Energy Department funding to the lab of 6,265.28 dollars and records no publications or subject inventions.
doe-osti-3030855-southeast-regional-co-s:
Kenneth Nemeth and Kimberly Sams-Gray of the Southern States Energy Board report under award DE-FE0031830 for SECARB-USA, the Southeast Regional Carbon Dioxide Utilization and Storage Acceleration Partnership. The study mines existing databases of carbon dioxide sources and sinks across the Southeast. The region spans Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, and Mississippi, among other states. The goal is to find where captured gas could go underground, and which areas stay untested.

Three under-explored zones get site sketches. In Shelby County, Alabama, about 10 facilities within 25 miles emit nearly 10 million tons of carbon dioxide a year, and a test well probed the Knox Group carbonates. Other sketches cover Cartersville in Georgia and a Virginia-West Virginia-Kentucky zone in Botetourt County.
doe-osti-3362584-ferc-2222-amp-der-polic:
Michael Jewell tracks grid policy in this September 2025 tracker report on FERC Order 2222. The federal order lets small distributed energy resources, home batteries, solar, and flexible loads, band together as aggregations and sell into wholesale power markets. Grid operators must file plans to allow it, and the report follows each filing fight month by month for practitioners who need the state of play.

On July 10, 2025, the commission denied a rehearing plea from Voltus over the Midcontinent operator second compliance filing, standing by its ruling on an interim resource type. On July 22 it approved a PJM start date of February 2029 by letter order. In August, the New York operator moved to allow mixed aggregations and to drop tariff edits it no longer needed.
doe-osti-3362702-flow-forecasting-on-new:
Cameron Bracken, Youngjun Son, Mucun Sun of Idaho National Laboratory, and Vincent Tidwell report on river forecasting for Great River Hydro in CRADA 549, dated April 2026. Great River Hydro is New England largest conventional hydropower producer, running plants on the Connecticut River in Vermont, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts. Several plants must run with the river flow, so tomorrow inflow guess sets both power output and market bids.

Two rival forecasts, labeled A and B, were scored on generic and custom metrics. Forecast B won overall, but A beat it in some months, which shows why picking one fixed forecast is hard. Custom metrics zoomed in on the 1 to 2 day window, where the firm bids into the day-ahead market and can still adjust releases. Spring snowmelt season, April to July, got special attention.
doe-osti-3364616-final-prototype-microre:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report dated September 2025, by Steven J. Maheras, Shane A. Foss, Steven D. Bauman, and Michael D. Steele, sets the planning framework for shipping prototype microreactors safely. Microreactors are factory-built units producing under 50 megawatts of electricity, small enough to move by truck or rail. Because they may travel fueled, transport rules and public engagement must be settled before the first shipment.

The framework adapts lessons from the transuranic waste shipping program, which built public trust along its routes over decades. Chapters cover safety messaging, coordination with corridor states and Tribes, and timely answers to media and officials. Audiences range from citizens along the route to public safety officers. The document fulfills a fiscal year 2025 milestone and gives the microreactor program a ready communications and safety structure.
doe-osti-3364618-determining-stability-m:
Fermilab technical memorandum FERMILAB-TM-2748-STUDENT records a student project by Arnaldo Rodríguez González of the University of Puerto Rico at Mayagüez, supervised by Tengming Shen. The subject is quench protection in superconducting magnets: how much stray heat a magnet winding can absorb before it suddenly loses superconductivity. In an adiabatic magnet, no heat escapes, so the margin is thin and worth computing carefully.

The project compares two approaches. The older MIITS method estimates heating with a simplified integral, while a three-dimensional finite element model built in ANSYS follows temperature through the actual strand geometry. Single-strand and multi-strand cases were run, and minimum quench energies were extracted from each. Comparing the two tells magnet designers when the quick method suffices and when the full simulation is worth its cost.
doe-osti-3364695-cytrics-assessment-repo:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2026/4609 assesses the mobile apps that control whole-home battery systems. Jen Sims performed the study with Kyle McCready of Idaho National Laboratory and Tyler Williams of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Part of the CyTRICS testing program, the November 2025 study asks how much risk hides in the software supply chain behind products such as home energy storage units.

Analysts reverse-engineered eight applications, ran them on test devices, and watched their network traffic. Seven of the eight apps shared seventeen third-party libraries, covering analytics, messaging, and telemetry. Permissions overlapped heavily too, including Bluetooth discovery, location, and persistent background running. One compromised shared library could therefore reach several brands at once. The findings argue for supply chain scrutiny before these apps tie into anything more critical.
doe-osti-3374715-land-surface-temperatur:
Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report DOE/SC-ARM-26-019, dated June 2026, follows a balloon-borne look at how land surface temperature shifts through the day. The five authors are Chongai Kuang, Darielle Dexheimer, and Casey Longbottom. B. Peterson and C. Ruiz complete the team. Their site was the Bankhead National Forest in Alabama. The short name for the campaign is LASTT-BNF.

A tethered balloon carried the cameras above the forest. One rig paired a Mirage mid-wave infrared camera with a Sony camera. A second rig swapped the Sony for a GoPro. Flights were timed for morning, afternoon, and evening shifts in surface heat. Cloud cover was part of the study too. Broken clouds throw patchy shade, so the canopy and clearings warm at uneven rates.
doe-osti-3375392-precision-of-endf-and-e:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2017917, by Dermott E. Cullen and dated April 2026, asks how much truth survives inside the standard nuclear data file formats. ENDF and ENDL files store the cross sections that reactor and weapons codes read. Their fixed field widths cap how many digits each number can hold. Cullen tests what that cap does to the physics, with heat as his main lever.

One case follows capture resonances as a sample warms from zero to 293.6 kelvin. Doppler broadening smears the sharp peaks until they nearly vanish. At zero kelvin, rebuilding the data to a tolerance of one part in ten thousand took almost two million energy points. Most of those points wash out once heat is added. Cullen argues the unresolved resonance scheme could state the same facts more simply and with less error.
doe-osti-3378173-ultra-high-operation-te:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-17241, printed February 2026, documents the test facility and performance testing for HOTSSTAR. HOTSSTAR is a solar thermal air receiver made by additive manufacturing. It is built from a silicon carbide matrix and runs at ultra-high operating temperatures. Eight Sandia authors are printed, led by Kenneth M. Armijo. Reza Sarrafi-Nour, Joseph Shiang, and Stephanie Cavallaro of General Electric Aerospace join them.

The receiver belongs to a demonstration project at the National Solar Thermal Test Facility. There, a field of mirrors concentrates sunlight onto it. The report covers the experimental setup, heat exchanger modeling, and integration of the test module. An infrared camera measures temperature. An on-sun test campaign follows, with flux calibrations and checkout procedures before performance runs. The aim is a receiver that survives heat levels metal alloys cannot.
doe-osti-3399431-atmospheric-plasma-for-:
Atmospheric Plasma for Cathode Relithiation and Up Cycling, CRADA final report NLR/TP-5700-99428 from July 2026, closes agreement CRD-23-24422. Ryan Brow is the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact and cited author. Funding came from the Advanced Manufacturing and Materials Technologies Office.

A spent lithium-ion cathode is not dead material; it has mostly lost lithium. Relithiation puts the lithium back, restoring the cathode for new cells without dissolving it down to raw metals, the expensive route conventional recycling takes. Doing that treatment with an atmospheric plasma, a plasma struck in open air rather than in a vacuum chamber, aims at a process cheap and fast enough for production lines. The cooperative project developed that route with a partner, and this report is its final record.
doe-osti-3407897-progress-report-on-sfr-:
Argonne report ANL/CFCT-22/30 Revision 1 tracks progress on qualifying data for sodium fast reactor metallic fuel. Kun Mo, Aaron Oaks, and Carolyn Tomchik are the named authors in the evidence record. The data sit in the FIPD database named in the text.

Old test data must be checked before designers can trust them for new reactors. The report pulls past irradiation and physics records into one qualified set. Past papers and lab reports supply the base facts, each cited in full. Qualified data let fuel designers work from checked numbers instead of scattered files of mixed quality.
doe-osti-3419725-guideline-for-character:
NLR/TP-5700-100173 is a August 2026 report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies that guides developers in judging a site for solar thermal use. Steve Schell, Matthew Emes, Stephanie Meyen, and Matthew Neber wrote the guideline. Good sites need strong sun, fit land, and few shading blocks.

One section covers shade from terrain and structures. Mountains, ridgelines, and trees can cut startup and peak output, mainly in winter. Towers and wind turbines count as man-made shade sources. Each shade source should be checked against sun paths for the site. Early site screens save costly redesigns later in a project.
doe-osti-3422010-innovating-high-through:
In August 2026, the National Laboratory of the Rockies released report NLR/TP-5700-99665, which reports work on high throughput hydrogen fueling stations. Shaun Onorato, Jennifer Kurtz, and Spencer Gilleon were the lab contacts. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-18-00773. Heavy vehicles need fast, large fills to match diesel habits.

On October 6, 2022, the team fueled 82.3 kilograms in 6 minutes and 33 seconds. Average flow hit 12.6 kilograms per minute, with a peak of 23. Hydrogen arrived pre-cooled to minus 40 degrees Celsius. Such fills show that fleet-scale hydrogen stops can run at practical speeds. The project targeted average flow rates of ten kilograms per minute for station design.
doe-osti-3451997-residual-stress-develop:
In May 2026, Oak Ridge National Laboratory released report ORNL/TM-2026/4673, which studies residual stress and warping in wire-arc printed metal parts. Aslan Nasirov leads a ten-author team under CRADA number NFE-23-09584. Wire-arc deposition builds big parts fast, but heat leaves stress locked inside.

Models split the base contact into two zones. One zone grips with rough friction and blocks sliding. The other lets gaps open, with a friction factor of 0.2 applied. The table beneath is fixed in all directions in the model. Builders can predict part warp and plan fixtures before printing costly pieces.
doe-osti-3484652-recent-updates-to-the-l:
Los Alamos document LA-UR-26-27601, by Mark W. Paris and issued August 24, 2026, updates the Los Alamos EDA R-matrix code. EDA evaluates nuclear reaction data for users. The hosted text is short and technical, so this note stays brief.

A new design centers on objects that hold one compound-system model each. A companion object holds a full evaluation with data and constraints. One equation gives the R-matrix change with channel radius in Riccati form. That form doubles as a stability check and a future fit constraint. Evaluators get a more modular code for data work.
doe-osti-3547198-hawaiian-hoary-bat-repo:
Sandia report SAND2026-25421, by Amanda K. Jones, surveys the Hawaiian hoary bat at the lab's Kauai Test Facility. The bat is the only bat species expected in the area, the report notes. Acoustic recorders captured bat calls at set sites.

Software called Kaleidoscope sorts calls by amplitude, shape, length, and frequency. Any call classed as a bat was credited to this species. Noise files were tallied separately from bat calls at each site. The species code LASCIN labels the bat in the data. Facility managers learn when bats use the site, guiding work timing.
doe-osti-3914962-facilitating-connection:
Paige Skur and Denise Barber of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this September 2026 report, NLR/TP-6A50-98547, on the American-Made Network. The Energy Department set up the American-Made program in 2018 to fund new energy ideas through prizes and contests, not just grants. The Network branch links prize teams with skilled helpers across industry.

The report explains how those links work in practice. Network members called Power Connectors coach teams, open doors to experts, and share hard-won know-how. One case follows Jade Garrett of Positive Deviancy, who backed more than 450 teams across 63 prizes in seven years. Readers get a clear view of how a prize program can give small teams reach they could not build alone.
experimental-determination-of-the-veloci:
Michelson's Experimental Determination of the Velocity of Light reports his early precision measurement at Annapolis. Albert A. Michelson was then a Master in the United States Navy. The work was done at the U.S. Naval Academy at private expense. Simon Newcomb's note of February 20, 1880, frames the paper.

Newcomb links light speed to finding the solar parallax by the best method then known. The contents lay out the theory of Michelson's new method first. Apparatus and constants follow, then formulas and grouped observations. Separate results, error discussion, and objections fill the later sections. Michelson takes sole credit and responsibility, Newcomb stresses. The paper marks a young officer's entry into exact physical measurement.
frank-on-a-gun-boat:
Castlemon's Frank Nelson enlists in the Navy and learns the ropes aboard a river gunboat. The Gun-Boat Series chapters promise a midnight alarm, a discomfited rebel, capture, and an escape chased by blood-hounds. A faithful friend and a spunky rebel share the adventures.

Taken prisoner, Frank is confined in the lower part of a fort, directly in range of the iron-clads' shells. He expects to be struck every moment as the pieces fly about him. He knows the rebels cherish an especial hatred toward gun-boatmen. Harry Castlemon published Frank on a Gun-Boat in 1892, decades after the war that made his name.
frus-1952-54Guat:
Guatemala from 1952 to 1954 fills this retrospective volume, a documentary history of PBSUCCESS. The CIA operation ended with the 1954 coup that removed President Jacobo Arbenz from power. Agency files form the core of the record.

An earlier plan, PBFORTUNE, first weighed in 1951, appears in the sources note. The main run then tracks the operation as built and run. A third project, PBHISTORY, mined the fallen government's papers. Cryptonyms and pseudonyms fill the lists. The volume is a rare inside view of a covert action, from first pitch to final use of captured files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DoleRobertSenat: Howard Kurtz, the Washington Post's media writer, examined how the press covered what the headline calls the Dole Affair, involving Senator Robert Dole. His piece, Behind the Scenes, looks at the reporting itself rather than at the underlying events. The surviving record gives the author, paper, and subject, but no date or findings, so the article stands as an example of Kurtz's media criticism from his Post years.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KautenMarieMat_: Harold Weisberg wrote to Mr. and Mrs. Kauten on January 22, 1977. The archive's entry gives the correspondents and the date and nothing of the contents. Weisberg's letters went out by the thousands, to sources, readers, and friends of his work. This one stands as a single dated entry in that correspondence, its subject unrecorded.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ODanielPat_ODan:
The Dallas Times Herald reported on March 19, 1968, that Pat O'Daniel wanted a state investigation of President Kennedy's assassination. O'Daniel was then a candidate for governor of Texas. His call asked Texas to run its own inquiry, five years after the shooting and four after the Warren Report.

Demands for a new inquiry were a constant of the case's politics. Most came from private critics; O'Daniel's came from a man running for office in the state where the crime occurred. The article records his request and its setting in the 1968 campaign. It shows the assassination still working as live politics in Texas, not merely as history argued in books.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WatergateSpoofs: Tom Huth reported for the Washington Post on a strange Watergate side business: anti-Nixon novelties were selling fast. Even during a television recess in the hearings, vendors found buyers for jokes at the president's expense. Huth's article treats the trade as news about the public mood. When a scandal becomes souvenirs, anger and humor are clearly sharing the same street.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
Fifty years after the scandal broke, this briefing book, number 870, looks back at the CIA's secret role in Chile. Peter Kornbluh edited it, and it was published on September 9, 2024. Its documents center on Henry Kissinger and what he told people about that role.

The records show Kissinger misled the president, the cabinet, and reporters about CIA activity in Chile. He told journalist Ted Koppel the issue was total nonsense, even as a New York Times exposé sent the White House into anger and panic. A secret White House memo captured his view that America should not let a country go communist.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_The:
Fifty-five years after the Cuban Missile Crisis, William Burr and Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 606, published in October 2017. It gathers papers on parts of the crisis that planning documents reveal. One is an occupation proclamation drafted for Cuba.

The proclamation ordered all persons in occupied territory to obey all orders promptly. It was written for an invasion that never came. CIA post-mortems also admitted a photo-gap on missile sites, caused by limits placed on U-2 spy flights. Together the papers show how close Washington came to occupying Cuba, and how blind spots shaped the crisis.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
In April 1995 Russian forces destroyed the Chechen village of Samashki, killing many civilians. Svetlana Savranskaya and Matthew Evangelista edited this briefing book, number 702, published in April 2020. It examines the massacre and the American response to Russia's war in Chechnya.

The pairing of the two presidents in the title is the analytical point. Boris Yeltsin's Russia was then a partner the Clinton administration wanted to keep, which shaped how Washington reacted to atrocity reports. Documents on the response let readers weigh friendship against evidence. The Samashki case became a test of whether the new post-Cold War relationship had room for human rights pressure.

During the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, Soviet submarines carrying nuclear torpedoes were being hunted by American ships above them. Sixty years later, this National Security Archive posting gathers the core declassified records on those submarines and on how close one of them came to firing its nuclear weapon.

At a 1997 conference, brigade chief of staff Vasili Arkhipov gave signs that confirmed the near-use of a nuclear torpedo aboard his submarine. The commanders involved had kept the story quiet for forty years. The records here let readers piece together the underwater half of the crisis, a part long hidden even while the standoff between Kennedy and Khrushchev above the surface became famous.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cuba_Luis_Posada_: Luis Posada Carriles, the Cuban exile militant who spent decades in the CIA's orbit and was accused of bombing a Cuban airliner in 1976, died at ninety. A National Security Archive briefing book page carries his obituary under a headline drawn from the agency's own reported phrase for him: a CIA-created Frankenstein, a asset who escaped his makers' control. Posada was never convicted for the bombing and lived his last years in Miami. Only the page capture survives here, marking the Archive's notice of a violent Cold War life.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Freedom_of_I:
President Lyndon Johnson signed the Freedom of Information Act with reluctance in 1966, and the law turned sixty in July 2026. A National Security Archive posting marked the anniversary by calling the act a national transparency treasure: the tool that lets Americans request, obtain, and study the records of their own government.

Few organizations have used FOIA more than the Archive itself, whose lawsuits and requests built much of the public record on modern American foreign policy. An anniversary piece from that source doubles as a user's report on what the law has achieved and where it strains, in delays and denials. Readers get a short history of a statute that quietly underpins a great deal of reporting, scholarship, and public argument.
if-not-silver-what:
John W. Bookwalter, a maker and land owner from Ohio, argued the money question in this 1896 book. He opens with a speech by A. J. Balfour against a gold standard that keeps rising in value. Bookwalter says his farm-linked trade forced him to study coinage at home and abroad.

His case favors silver and a double standard of gold and silver. He traces past panics, bank strain in England, and the role of France in holding both metals. Farmers and makers, he holds, bear the cost when money grows scarce. The book is a plain brief from the silver side.
island-tales-on-the-makaloa-mat:
Jack London set the seven stories of On the Makaloa Mat in Hawaii, and the collection appeared in 1920, after his death. The title story opens on Martha Scandwell, a wealthy Waikiki matriarch under her great hau tree, telling tales of the old islands. Other stories take up the bones of the chief Kahekili, a Chinese servant's tears, surfing, and the memories of old Hawaiians.

London mixes plantation wealth with native legend, and the races of modern Honolulu crowd his pages: Japanese servants, Chinese nurses, haole fortunes, and kanaka storytellers. His Hawaii is beautiful and haunted at once. Readers who know London for dogs and snow will find the same strong storytelling working in heat and surf.
life-history-of-the-kangaroo-rat:
Charles T. Vorhies and Walter P. Taylor wrote this 1922 government bulletin. The Agriculture Department issued it as Bulletin Number 1091. Arizona's Agricultural Experiment Station shared in the work. Its subject is the banner-tailed kangaroo rat of the Southwest.

Chapters cover identification, occurrence, habits, food, and burrow systems. The authors also study the rat's commensals, enemies, and abundance. Economic considerations close the report for farmers and ranchers. Forty pages of close observation make it a model species life history. Plates show the banner-tailed kangaroo rat in its desert home. A forty-item bibliography supports the authors' field observations.
lights-and-shadows-of-new-york-life-or-t:
James D. McCabe Jr. describes New York in all its phases here. The National Publishing Company sold the book by subscription only. Its subtitle promises the great city's sights and sensations. Engravings show noted places, life, and scenes throughout.

McCabe promises accounts of splendors and wretchedness alike. Marble palaces and dark dens stand side by side in his plan. Rings, frauds, charities, mysteries, and crimes all receive coverage. Leading men, politicians, and adventurers complete his city portrait. Grand Central Railway Depot illustrates the subscription prospectus handsomely. Agents called on residents who wrote the publishers for copies.
mauprat:
George Sand's novel Mauprat appears here in Stanley Young's English version. Front essays tell of Sand's life and of her place in letters. Edmund Gosse wrote the life, and the author's own preface follows.

One essay calls Sand the greatest woman writer the world has known. It praises her candor, her free spirit, and her warm heart. Her foes, it says, feared her warnings and her plain truth. The tale itself bears her famed pen name, George Sand, on its title page. The preface by the author stands just before the tale starts. Life, praise, and the tale itself give three views of one writer.
mob-rule-in-new-orleans-robert-charles-a:
Ida B. Wells-Barnett published this pamphlet in 1900, interrupting a larger work to write it. A mob in New Orleans had roamed the streets day and night. Its members beat, shot, and killed Black residents at will, despising all law. Wells-Barnett tells the story of Robert Charles and his fight to the death.

She builds her account from the New Orleans Times-Democrat and Picayune. Both papers, she notes, condemned the mob and defended law and order. The pamphlet also prints lynching statistics and recalls the burning of Sam Hose in Georgia. Wells-Barnett shows he killed his employer in self-defense, not in crime.
nasa-tm-19640023646-an-ultraviolet-spect:
Kenneth Hallam and John Mangus of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper. They presented it at a Tokyo optics meeting on September 1, 1964. It describes a tool for studying ultraviolet light from space. The tool was built for OSO-B, the second Orbiting Solar Observatory.

A spectrophotometer splits light into its colors and measures each part. This one was meant to analyze ultraviolet output from stars and nebulae. Its slit sits at the focus of a six-inch reflecting telescope. Earth's air blocks ultraviolet light, so the tool had to fly. The paper details a key early step toward space-based ultraviolet astronomy.
nasa-tm-19650003085-stability-and-contro:
M Leroy Spearman and Gerald V Foster tested a swing-wing aircraft shape in the Langley supersonic pressure tunnel. The outer wing panels were swept back seventy-five degrees. Testing ran at Mach 2.01, just over twice the speed of sound.

Their summary reports a fairly straight-line change in pitching moment as lift rose. That meant the static margin could fall to about five percent at low lift before the shape turned neutrally stable. In plain terms, the swept shape stayed predictable at high speed. Such results guided later variable-sweep designs.
nasa-tm-19650025631-a-summary-of-hingele:
John F Ward and a Langley colleague summarized research on helicopter rotors built with no hinges, in a report whose scan is partly garbled. A normal rotor blade flaps on hinges as it turns. A hingeless rotor instead flexes as one stiff structure. Langley work included an early flight test program using a three-blade hingeless rotor fitted to a helicopter.

Wind tunnel testing of a scaled research model formed the second strand of the work. Such rotors promise simpler hubs and sharper control response for the pilot. They also raise hard questions about loads and vibration in the blades. The summary gathers the flight and tunnel strands in one place, so rotor designers could weigh the gains against the costs.
nasa-tm-19660008283-an-analysis-of-the-t:
Robert Siegel and Joseph M Savino at Lewis Research Center analyzed a freezing problem with many uses, in a paper offered for an August 1966 heat meeting in Chicago. A warm liquid flows over a wall that is cooled from the other side. A frozen layer grows on the wall as the liquid passes. The growth changes with time, which is what transient means here.

The frozen layer insulates the wall as it thickens. That slows further freezing in a self-limiting way. Flows of this kind appear in casting, in cooling systems, and in fuel handling. Siegel and Savino give an analysis that predicts the layer's growth, so engineers need not rely on trial and error alone.
nasa-tm-19660015112-a-lunar-ephemeris-wi:
Theodore L Felsentreger at Goddard published a lunar ephemeris in March 1966 with an unusual reference frame. An ephemeris is a table of positions over time. Felsentreger gives the Moon's positions referred to Earth's equatorial plane. Most tables of the era used a different plane. His choice suits users who work in Earth-based coordinates, such as tracking stations and orbit computers.

Daily motions of the Moon's angular orbital elements are part of the work, per the catalog note. Apollo planning made precise lunar positions a daily need. A table in the user's own frame saves conversion errors. Felsentreger's ephemeris served the missions then being prepared, when the Moon was about to become a workplace.
nasa-tm-19660024047-stability-and-contro:
Ross B Robinson and M Leroy Spearman tested a lightweight glider reentry shape in Langley's four by four foot supersonic pressure tunnel. Testing ran at Mach 1.89, just under twice the speed of sound. The shape was an all-wing design with a diamond planform. A small fuselage sat on top of the wing, the summary says. Flight attitudes studied were those of normal flight in the air, at fairly low angles of attack.

A glider that returns from space must fly well at both extremes of its journey. Supersonic stability and control in the air are the middle part of that problem. Robinson and Spearman report the characteristics measured for this diamond-wing layout. Lightweight glider concepts were a leading alternative to capsules in that period of reentry research.
nasa-tm-19660029426-a-theoretical-and-ex:
Charles Borden Johnson wrote this work as a master's thesis in aerospace engineering at the Virginia Polytechnic Institute in August 1966. His test case is a flat plate fitted with a flap at its trailing edge. The plate flies, in a wind tunnel, at Mach 8, eight times the speed of sound.

Johnson combined theory with experiment. He measured how the pressure spread across the plate and how the flow separated near the deflected flap. He varied the Reynolds number, the flap angle, and the wall temperature to see each effect. Flow separation at such speeds matters for vehicles that fly in the upper atmosphere.
nasa-tm-19670001914-nasa-selective-disse:
Gifford A. Young, of the Scientific and Technical Information Division at NASA headquarters in Washington, D.C., wrote this program description in June 1966. It explains NASA's selective dissemination of information program, an early computer system for matching new documents to the interests of individual researchers. The system ran on the IBM 7090/94 computer.

Twice each month, the system compared more than 2,000 documents against the stated interests of over 700 participants. Those users sat at ten NASA centers and eleven Air Force centers. Interest profiles could use single key words, short phrases, excluded terms, and percentage matching. Output came as abstract cards, with a response card for requesting full texts. The report covers operating experience, program changes, and availability, and notes a move to newer IBM machines in February 1966.
nasa-tm-19670005589-low-torque-three-pie:
Report TR-426, issued on September 15, 1966, by the Directorate for Design Engineering at NASA's Kennedy Space Center. It covers a three-piece valve seat built for high-pressure pneumatic valving. A valve seat is the surface a valve closes against to seal. This design aimed to seal well while needing little turning force to operate.

Three different materials served as seating rings during qualification testing. The test series included water proof tests, pneumatic proof tests, repeated cycle tests, and seat erosion tests. Pressures ran from 6,000 to 10,000 pounds per square inch. All three materials performed satisfactorily across that range. The report concludes that, for design purposes, the choice among the seating materials is not particularly critical.
nasa-tm-19670013515-communications-syste:
H. E. Smith, of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on December 6, 1966. Astronauts trained for weightlessness underwater, floating in tanks that simulate zero gravity. Crews in and around the tank needed to talk to each other clearly.

Smith describes a two-way communications system built for that training. It connects nine personnel stations and a public address system. Underwater speakers let the safety divers hear what is said. The report also gives operating instructions for the system, so training crews could run it day to day.
nasa-tm-19700014017-the-as-205-csm-101-l:
Gordon W. Solomon of the Marshall Space Flight Center prepared this data report on September 10, 1968. It gives the planned flight path for the AS-205 launch vehicle carrying the CSM-101 spacecraft. The volume is Revision 1 of the operational trajectory, the working path planners expected the flight to follow.

Solomon lays out the predicted path, the mission goals, the ground rules, and a tracking summary. The plan placed the S-IVB stage and spacecraft into a low elliptical orbit, one hundred twenty by one hundred fifty nautical miles up. Later sections cover vehicle traits, guidance and control, powered flight, and the spent stage. The flight would further check launch vehicle and spacecraft systems in orbit.
nasa-tm-19700016330-irradiation-effect-a:
Charles L. Younger and Fred A. Haley of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 meeting on radiation effects in materials. It studies what radiation does to titanium and titanium-base alloys at very low temperatures. The property at issue is tensile strength, how the metal acts when pulled.

Metals in space and nuclear service face both deep cold and steady radiation. The authors test how the two act together on these alloys. Builders need such data to know if a part will stay strong in service. A metal that turns brittle in cold, irradiated use can fail without warning.
nasa-tm-19700025035-investigation-of-lan:
NASA issued this Apollo working paper, number 1180, from the Manned Spacecraft Center program. It investigates a change of landing site during the second phase of the lunar module's powered descent. The change would be made using the primary guidance system, while the craft was already flying down toward the surface.

The calculations ask how much landing area stays open to the crew at that late stage. They track how guidance commands, pitch angle, and thrust would change for an alternate site. Charts show the reachable footprint from three different ranges during the descent. A closing section weighs whether the crew could still see the new landing site well enough to use it.
nasa-tm-19700025124-radiation-pattern-ca:
R. Miezis and R. F. Schmidt of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in June 1970. It gives radiation pattern calculations for the ATS-F antenna. The antenna was a deployable reflector made of forty-eight panels that would unfold in orbit, far too large to launch already open.

The work begins with two ways of finding the reflector's surface normals, one analytic and one numerical. It then builds up the computing steps: small area pieces, numerical integration, and the program's input and output quantities. Notes on computer requirements and critical program areas follow. The closing section presents the computed results for ATS-F itself, the patterns the finished antenna was expected to beam out.
nasa-tm-19700026419-circumlunar-comminic:
John T. McNeeley and Ellis W. Henry of the Advanced Mission Design Branch wrote this internal note on June 20, 1968. It was issued by the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. It studies radio contact around the Moon using two satellites in lunar polar orbit, passing over both poles as they circle.

The note first fixes the orbit layout the two relay satellites would fly. Deployment and phasing come next, so the pair would stay spaced as the plan requires. Guidance needs, orbit lifetime, and the speed changes required are worked through in turn. A table reports the communication coverage the two satellites could achieve, counted in tracking intervals and percentages.
nasa-tm-19700026436-an-analysis-of-point:
Houston's Manned Spacecraft Center issued this analysis of point-to-point communication for the lunar flyer program. The flyer was a proposed small craft for moving astronauts across the Moon's surface. Radio links between two points on that surface were the problem at hand, especially near the edge of direct sight.

The study seeks the best radio frequency for links near the line-of-sight horizon. It assumes a small transmitter and works through two antenna heights for the link. Losses counted in the circuit budget include free-space loss and diffraction loss where the lunar surface blocks the path. Ground proximity loss, antenna gains, and receiver sensitivity each get a short explanation before the comparison.
nasa-tm-19700032536-contact-resistance-o:
T. H. Wilkinson of the Marshall Space Flight Center ran the tests reported in this technical memorandum. It measures the contact resistance of electroplated conductors in flat conductor cable. Low resistance at each contact keeps signals clean and power losses small.

Three kinds of conductor were tested in a special receptacle. They were gold over nickel plate, cleaned nickel plate, and uncleaned nickel plate. Tests ran indoors, outdoors in winter cold, and after hundreds of mating cycles. The gold-plated contacts showed the lowest resistance, the report states. Cleaned nickel contacts still fell within the acceptable limits.
nasa-tm-19710019413-virtual-image-displa:
An Ames Research Center memorandum, NASA TM X-2327, reports a simple way to make flight simulator scenes look far away. Cheap uncorrected plastic lenses formed a virtual image of the flight scene. A virtual image seems to sit at a real distance, not on a nearby screen. That depth cue makes landings in a simulator feel far more realistic.
